articles.title: LNG Canada to use Chinese steel on $33-billion expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
articles.summary: LNG Canada will once again use Chinese steel for the "specialized fabrication capability" it says it requires for its $33-billion Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.

image.caption: Wudang, a liquefied natural gas (LNG) tanker, fills up at an LNG Canada facility in Kitimat, B.C., on Nov. 13, 2025. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
LNG Canada will once again use Chinese steel for the "specialized fabrication capability" it says it requires for its $33-billion Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
China Offshore Oil Engineering Co., Ltd. made LNG Canada's first 2 processing units now in operation

When the proposed expansion led the list of early projects referred to the new federal Major Projects Office in September 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters these ambitious building projects would be "at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy."

In fact, the joint venture will buy more components from the state-owned China Offshore Oil Engineering Co., Ltd. (COOEC), which also manufactured its first two liquified natural gas processing units, known as trains, now in operation.

items: LNG Canada to move forward with Phase 2 expansion project in Kitimat, B.C.
LNG Canada gets go-ahead for massive expansion in B.C.

blocks.text: On Tuesday, LNG Canada announced an expansion of the facility’s production capacity, adding two more trains for a total of four on the site, increasing its production from 14 to 28 megatonnes per year once Phase 2 construction is complete, likely in the early 2030s.
At the event marking the final investment decision, CBC News asked the prime minister if the expansion would be built with Canadian or Chinese steel.
"It’s a great question for the proponents of Phase 2," Carney said. "I’ll leave it to them."

"There will be full opportunities to buy Canadian steel, and we'll continue to invest in the Canadian steel industry to make sure that's the case. But it will be for them to decide," the prime minister said.
Accordingly, CBC News asked LNG Canada where it intends to source steel for its expansion.

"For the plant construction in Kitimat, the challenge is not a preference for offshore steel, but the specialized fabrication capability required for modules of this scale and complexity," LNG Canada spokesperson Paul Hagel wrote in an email.

"There are no fabrication yards in Canada that can manufacture and deliver the additional modules required for Phase 2. Only five fabrication yards globally have the combination of space, capacity, quality systems and marine access required for this scope of work, including COOEC in China, which successfully fabricated modules for LNG Canada’s Phase 1."
Chinese state-owned producer holds 15% stake
Shell Canada Energy is the majority operator and project leader in Kitimat, holding a 40 per cent stake in LNG Canada.

State-owned PetroChina, the largest oil and gas producer, supplier and global investor in China, is a 15 per cent shareholder. The other three partners in the joint venture are Malaysia’s Petronas (25 per cent), Japan’s Mitsubishi Corporation (15 per cent) and the Korea Gas Corporation, or KOGAS (five per cent).
LNG exported from Kitimat is distributed by these five energy giants to Asian markets, based on their relative stake in the project.

Prior to a final investment decision for Phase 1 of the Kitimat facility in 2018, the joint venture sought and received an exemption from steep anti-dumping and countervailing duties that had been levied on fabricated industrial steel from China to protect Canada’s steel industry.

Canada is among many countries that implement safeguards based on threats identified by its domestic steel producers. State-subsidized Chinese steelmakers produce more than China’s domestic economy requires. The surplus ships overseas, undermining the cost-competitiveness of steel manufactured in countries like Canada that have higher-paid, unionized workers and higher environmental standards.
The value of the concession the federal government made to LNG Canada for Phase 1 was estimated at $1 billion.

items: Minister concerned over B.C. Ferries' construction deal with Chinese shipyard
Canadian shipyard slams B.C. Ferries' contract with Chinese shipbuilder

blocks.text: The 2019 remission order published in the Canada Gazette said that LNG Canada, as well as the Singapore investors behind the Woodfibre LNG project in Squamish (slated to come online in 2027), had told the finance department there was no Canadian capacity to produce what they needed.
They also framed the cost impact of these duties as having a "negative impact on investment decisions."
In other words: without it, the deal may not have gone ahead.
However, the duties in effect when the use of Chinese steel first drew negative attention in 2018 expired after five years and have not been renewed.
LNG Canada told CBC News there are no tariffs now on importing steel components from its Chinese supplier.

The office of Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne told CBC News that the Canada Border Services Agency determines whether additional levies are required on Chinese steel to avoid predatory dumping. In this case, the measures were dropped and Canadian producers have not objected, because these particular components don’t directly compete with what they make.

In 2024, other surtaxes and tariff rate quotas (volume restrictions) were placed on a list of specific Chinese steel products that could threaten the viability of Canada’s domestic industry. That list, however, does not include what LNG Canada is importing.
Compressor stations target 70% Canadian steel

Other aspects of the Kitimat expansion may, however, use Canadian steel. For example, in order to expand storage and production at the export terminal, Coastal GasLink needs to expand the volume of gas moving in its pipeline network to Kitimat.

The new compression stations required along the pipeline will be "targeting almost 15,000 tonnes of steel from Canadian suppliers or mills, representing approximately 70 per cent of the steel required for that work," the LNG Canada spokesperson wrote.

That apparent prioritization of Canadian supply chains would be more consistent with the assurances the prime minister gave in September 2025, when LNG Canada’s Phase 2 expansion led the first list of priority referrals to the new federal Major Projects Office.

"These major projects will be at the heart of our new, comprehensive Buy Canadian policy," Carney said in his remarks a year ago. "To strengthen Canada’s independence, resilience and security, we will build with Canadian steel, lumber, aluminum, and by Canadian engineers and tradespeople. We will be our own best customer."

Unlike public purchasing contracts now subject to the federal government’s Buy Canadian procurement guidelines, the supply chains used by private sector energy companies are, as Carney noted Tuesday, up to them to decide.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Janyce McGregor has been a member of the Parliamentary Press Gallery in Ottawa since 1998. She joined CBC News in 2001 as a national news and current affairs producer. After a writing and producing stint with the parliamentary bureau's online desk, she switched to daily on-air reporting and now serves morning audiences on CBC Radio's World Report and CBC News Network.

articles.title: ‘The enemy is tearing our city apart’: terror in Kyiv as Russia ramps up attacks
articles.summary: Mayor Vitali Klitschko says Kyivans can no longer pretend it is ‘peacetime’ amid strikes on school, hospital and bridge

blocks.text: Valeriya Tkachenko was dropping her son off at school in central Kyiv when the air raid alert sounded. Staff hurried the children and parents into the shelter, where the frightened lawyer spent the next two hours with her son.
“I’m scared to death all day about what could happen to my son,” she said as she emerged from the shelter, already late for work.
A day earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone had struck a school nearby. “And I can’t plan anything any more,” she said. “It’s not sustainable like this.”

blocks.caption: Smoke rises after a Russian drone hit the Academy of Sciences building in Kyiv on Monday. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian
Firefighters tackling a blaze in the city centre. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Across the city on Friday morning, Artem Marchenko, an IT worker, was forced to abandon his car and walk for 20 minutes across the Pivdennyi Bridge on his way to work after repeated Russian strikes damaged the crossing.
He feared Russia would soon target Kyiv’s other bridges, paralysing movement across a city of about 3 million people, the two halves of which are divided by the Dnipro.
Kyiv is entering its most difficult period since the early days of the invasion, as intensifying Russian attacks reshape everyday life in a capital that Moscow is seeking to plunge into darkness.

For weeks, the main worry in the capital had been the coming winter, when Russia is expected once again to try to plunge Ukraine into darkness and cold. But a sharp escalation in Russian attacks has left many residents feeling that some of the hardship they had been bracing for is already here.

blocks.caption: Rescue workers running to a shelter during an air threat. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: “The capital is in a very dramatic situation. And it’s no longer possible to pretend that we can live now as we do in peacetime,” the Kyiv mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said on Friday. “The enemy is tearing Kyiv apart.”

This week alone, Russian missiles and drones have struck offices, datacentres, a school and hospital and one of Kyiv’s main bridges. Moscow has also started its attacks on Ukraine’s energy, targeting a thermal power plant and other energy facilities, leaving several neighbourhoods without power and water by morning.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy underlined the apparent shift in Russian tactics in an interview with the Financial Times this week, saying Vladimir Putin had recently ordered his commanders to abandon the rules of war.
“They want Ukrainians to leave the capital … and show that if you don’t have the capital you don’t have the capital,” Zelenskyy said in separate comments to reporters.

blocks.caption: A volunteer medic crew on patrol in Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Until recently, Kyiv had retained a deceptively normal rhythm, while cities closer to the front, including Kharkiv and Dnipro, absorbed the brunt of daily missile and drone attacks. Now, residents joke grimly that the balance is beginning to shift, with those cities at times feeling safer than the capital.

The city is confronting a particularly dangerous combination of an acute shortage of Patriot interceptors for ballistic missiles and a new generation of faster, jet-powered Russian drones that are harder to shoot down.

Kyiv is racing to fast-track a new generation of interceptor drones capable of taking down the jet-powered models. Several are already in use, according to three defence industry sources, though they said it could still take weeks or months to deploy them at a scale sufficient to provide meaningful protection for the capital.
At the same time, Russia’s advances on the battlefield remain relatively slow and are coming at enormous cost.

Moscow captured about 361 sq km in September, according to the military analyst Konrad Muzyka, an increase on recent months but still far short of the pace needed to seize the rest of the Donbas before winter, when offensive operations typically become more difficult.

blocks.caption: A man with a tattoo reading ‘immortal’ standing near the site of a Russian drone strike in Kyiv. Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ukraine, meanwhile, has clawed back about 126 sq km in a series of counteroffensives in the east, being conducted under the codename Vivaldi. That slower-moving battle on the ground is increasingly at odds with what is happening far behind the front. The contrast reflects a broader shift in the war, as Ukraine’s major cities come under growing pressure.

“You can be quite successful in the land domain, but if you are vulnerable in the air, especially in the rear, that is the vulnerability your opponent is going to exploit,” said Mykola Bielieskov, a military analyst at Ukraine’s government-run National Institute for Strategic Studies.

Ukrainian officials have been warning their European counterparts about the scale of the looming threat. According to the New York Times, Ukraine’s energy minister, Denys Shmyhal, recently briefed European counterparts on an intercepted Russian plan to use as many as 1,000 missiles, drones and bombs against the country’s energy system. The targets included electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants and boiler houses, in what appeared to be an effort to plunge Ukrainian cities into darkness and cold and create a humanitarian crisis.
“Russia plans to freeze Kyiv out, to throw it back into the Stone Age,” said one senior western diplomat in Kyiv, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Western diplomats say publicly that they intend to remain in Kyiv, mindful that leaving would hand Moscow a propaganda victory and risk creating the impression that Ukraine was being abandoned. However, privately two senior diplomats said contingency plans were being drawn up to relocate embassies to Lviv or eastern Poland if Russia began deliberately targeting foreign missions.
“The situation is obviously deteriorating fast,” the diplomat said.

articles.title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll
articles.summary:
Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on…

blocks.text: India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.

The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.

Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.

blocks.caption: Abhijeet Dipke addresses supporters in Mumbai on Friday. Photograph: Indranil Mukherjee/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).

The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.

blocks.caption: Supporters of the All India Students Association demand the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar at a protest in Bengaluru. Photograph: Idrees Mohammed/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.

The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.

“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”

Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
after newsletter promotion
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.

blocks.caption: A demonstrator holding a placard wears a mask depicting the face of Gyanesh Kumar. Photograph: Francis Mascarenhas/Reuters

blocks.text: The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared ​aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.

Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.

Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.

Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election ​commission office in Delhi next week.

articles.title: Woman in alleged Cornell gang-rape case was ‘failed’ by system, New York governor says
articles.summary: Kathy Hochul briefs journalists with state attorney general Letitia James, who will be taking over the entire case

blocks.text: Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, said on Friday that she would “ensure” that all the facts of the alleged gang-rape in a fraternity house at Cornell University “are brought into light” while harshly criticizing the institution for how they handled the 2024 case.
Hochul, a Democrat, said the woman in the case, was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including the police and the county prosecutor.
“I’m deeply disturbed at Cornell University’s police and how they handled this,” Hochul said of the Ivy League university in Ithaca in upstate New York.
In a rare legal development, Hochul late on Thursday announced that the state attorney general, Letitia James, was taking over the entire case as a special prosecutor.
“I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul said in a press conference on Friday morning alongside James.

“Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, they will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law,” James said. James will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury in a process that could lead to the pressing of criminal charges.
Hochul sharply criticized the investigation that began in 2024 after the woman in the case went to the police.

“In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang-raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney,” Hochul said, of the alleged assaults.
The governor also criticized what she called “a gap in state law” relating to claiming a sexual crime was committed when the alleged victim was voluntarily intoxicated.
She said: “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang-rape. Period.”
Hochul said on Thursday she was appointing James after she “lost faith” in the district attorney’s ability to oversee the case after he decided not to prosecute the case in 2024, among other reasons.

A former Cornell University student, who identifies by the pseudonym Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in September alleging she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024, when she was 20. She said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. The case has sparked national outrage, roiled the campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for Jane Doe, said his client was “not doing well” amid the uproar.

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Germany's Franz Reindl elected new IIHF president
articles.summary: Franz Reindl has been elected president of ice hockey's world governing body. The former forward was a member of West Germany's Olympic bronze medal-winning team.

image.caption: Franz Reindl's term as IIHF president runs until 2030 Image: ActionPictures/IMAGO

blocks.text: Franz Reindl came from behind to narrowly beat Petr Briza of the Czech Republic in a run-off vote to become the International Ice Hockey Federation's new president on Friday.

Reindl had trailed Briza 48-36 in the first round of voting but picked up crucial votes after Aivaz Omorkanov of Kyrgyzstan was eliminated. He then beat Briza 60-57 in the runoff held on the Spanish island of Tenerife. Six of a total of nine candidates had withdrawn prior to the election.

The 71-year-old German, who had been a member of the IIHF Council since 2016, succeeds Canadian-born Frenchman Luc Tardif, who had announced in March that he would not seek a further term in office. Reindl's election comes 5 years after he had finished as runner-up to Tardif. His term runs until 2030.
Wealth of experience

Reindl has done it all in German ice hockey, having been a player and coach, as well as serving as the first CEO of the top-flight professional league, the Deutsche Eishockey Liga (DEL), from 1994 to 96. He also headed the organizing committees for three World Championships – in 2001, 2010 and 2017. From 2014 to 2022 he served as president of the German Ice Hockey Association (DEB), overseeing an upturn in the fortunes of the men's national team, who won the silver medal at the Pyeongchang Winter Olympics in 2018.

blocks.caption: Franz Reindl served as interim coach of the men's national team, here during the 2004 World Cup of hockey Image: Christof Koepsel/Bongarts/Getty Images

blocks.text: "Franz Reindl has shaped German ice hockey for decades—as a player, but above all through the various key roles he has held within our federation," the current DEB chairman, Frank Lutz, said.
"The fact that the international ice hockey family is now entrusting him with the leadership of the IIHF is a great tribute to his work."
Successful playing career

Like Briza, who was a goalie for the Czechoslovakia team that won bronze in Albertville in 1992, Reindl was also an Olympic bronze medalist, having been a member of the 1976 West Germany team who beat the United States and Finland to finish third in Lake Placid.
Domestically, Reindl played 669 games and scored 423 goals for SC Riessersee and SB Rosenheim over 16 seasons in the Eishockey-Bundesliga, the predecessor to the DEL.

Tardif's years as IIHF president were marked by two major events; the return of National Hockey League players to the Olympic tournament in Milan Cortina this year, and the exclusion from international play of Russia in 2022 over the country's full-scale war on neighboring Ukraine.
Reindl is the second German to be elected IIHF president after Günter Sabetzki, who held the post from 1975 to 1994.

articles.title: Argentina launches cash-for-citizenship scheme
articles.summary: Investors seeking the fastest but most costly route to Argentine citizenship can choose between a non-refundable gift of $350,000, or buying a government bond for $800,000, if they think that will…

image.caption: Fancy an Argentine passport? The clue's in the name: it's obtainable with silver — or, more specifically, US dollars.Image: Tetiana Chernykova/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Argentina's government launched a scheme it hopes will attract wealthy investors and simultaneously "further strengthen the Argentine Republic's fiscal and financial position," offering people the chance to apply for citizenship via investment and thus bypass the more typical procedures.

Economy Minister Luis Caputo and Cabinet chief Diego Santilli launched the citizenship-by-investment program amid the "Argentina Week" business event in Paris, saying it would start accepting applications during the fourth quarter of 2026.

"This announcement is part of Argentina's drive toward international openness and integration, accompanied by reforms aimed at strengthening the investment climate and attracting capital," the Economy Ministry said in a statement.

Argentina's President Javier Milei has tried to portray himself as a cost-cutting pro-business leader restoring stability to one of the world's most fragile economies, which has defaulted on or restructured parts of its national debt multiple times just this century. Its most recent emergency loans scheme from the IMF and World Bank was approved last April.

blocks.caption: Luis Caputo announced the move amid the 'Argentina Week' event in Paris trying to drum up business and investmentImage: Teresa Suarez/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What are the details of the citizenship-by-investment program?
The program plans to offer "two simple and transparent mechanisms" to the primary investors seeking citizenship for themselves and perhaps for their immediate family.

The first is "making a direct, non-refundable contribution of $350,000 (roughly €310,000) to the National Treasury," the Economy Ministry said. The other higher risk, higher reward approach will be "subscribing to a $800,000 public bond created specifically for this program."

The principal applicant's spouse and children aged 25 or under can then also apply, albeit themselves having to pay smaller fees. Spouses and childless children aged 18-25 would be charged $100,000 each, and minors would have to contribute $25,000 each.

"Under this scheme, a typical family unit consisting of a principal applicant, their spouse, and two minor children could apply for Argentine citizenship for a total of $500,000," the ministry said, referring to a sum equating to well over a century earning Argentina's nominal median wage.
Argentina loses 33 companies a day under Javier Milei

Argentina said it would incorporate recommendations from the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) to ensure the adoption of international best practices and "comply with applicable standards regarding the prevention of money laundering, terrorist financing, and financial transparency."

"We continue working to strengthen Argentina's ties with the world, project the value of our citizenship internationally, and consolidate the country as an open and reliable nation," Economy Minister Caputo said online.

articles.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak surpasses 4,000 deaths amid violence and mistrust
articles.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak has recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities say, as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.

image.caption: A health-care worker in protective clothing is disinfected by a colleague inside a treatment centre for Ebola patients in Beni, North Kivu province, eastern Congo, on Saturday. (Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak has recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities say, as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.
Health workers protest lack of pay; Congolese politician beaten to death over response to outbreak
The Democratic Republic of the Congo's Ebola outbreak has recorded more than 4,000 deaths, authorities said, as they struggle to contain the spread of the virus.

The latest figures released by the health ministry on Thursday showed that 4,018 people have died, making up nearly half of the 8,300 confirmed cases, in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
Congo announced an outbreak on May 15, caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no known treatment or vaccine.

Some health workers gathered in Bunia, the capital of northeastern Ituri province, the heart of the outbreak. They were demanding payment for wages owed, but were quickly dispersed by officials. The protesting workers included surveillance team members, who identify people exposed to infected patients. They waved placards saying, "No money, no data!" and "No payment for months."
Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.

A senior UN official said that an Ebola-hit camp housing a transit centre for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
Julien Harneis, the UN senior Ebola co-ordinator, said creating Ebola transit and treatment centres has been a struggle, requiring money and staff, all of which are in short supply.

"When we lose a centre, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need," Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.

The worker arrived late on Thursday night after being flown to the Netherlands on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.

items: Suspected Ebola case at Montreal hospital turns out to be a false alarm
Ebola outbreak now deadliest in Congo’s history

blocks.text: "The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country," MSF said.
More than 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
Community resistance hampering containment efforts
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm about the virus's rapid spread into new health zones, stretching limited resources.

Africa CDC said in its latest news conference that the number of newly confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to co-operate in some of the hot spots. While the spread of the disease has slowed down in some areas, it has accelerated in others, creating what experts see as a delicate situation.

items: Moderna authorized to test vaccines to fight Ebola virus in Congo
Aid cuts have slowed fight to contain Ebola in central Africa, doctors say

blocks.text: Confirmed cases have slowed in recent weeks, from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.

A Congolese politician was attacked and beaten to death earlier this week for defending government measures in dealing with the outbreak, highlighting tensions that have stretched both the health community and local resources.

The attack on Marie-Célestin Karondwa, a local official with Congo's ruling Union for Democracy and Social Progress party, took place on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hot spot in eastern North Kivu province. His house was set on fire afterward, and he died at a hospital from his injuries.
Widespread mistrust of health workers and the authorities has hampered efforts to slow the Central African nation's 17th Ebola outbreak.

Authorities last month launched a village-centred approach, but those efforts face resistance from residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country's government for reasons ranging from how it's managed past Ebola outbreaks to chronic corruption.

articles.title: Water-intensive businesses brace for Super El Niño
articles.summary: Amid the looming effects of Super El Niño, some establishments in water-intensive sectors are adapting to the dry conditions of the season, with several switching to crops that require minimal water…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 10:13pm

Amid the looming effects of Super El Niño, some establishments in water-intensive sectors are adapting to the dry conditions of the season, with several switching to crops that require minimal water use.

In a "24 Oras" report by Bernadette Reyes on Friday, resort farm owners Ysrael and Romalyn Dantay shared that they shifted from growing leafy vegetables to plants that require less water, while also implementing rainwater harvesting measures.

“Na-experience namin ang bilis ng evaporation ng swimming pool so we need to refill everyday. ‘Yung tubig-ulan ngayon pa lang, dahil madalas ang ulan, sinesave na namin for future use,” Romalyn Dantay said.
(We experienced fast evaporation in our swimming pool, requiring us to refill it daily. Now, while rainfall is still frequent, we are already harvesting rainwater for future use.)

According to the National Water Resources Board (NWRB), under the Water Code, domestic use and agricultural irrigation are prioritized for water supply should the effects of El Niño worsen, rather than recreational facilities such as resorts and golf courses.

“Ang gusto natin bawas bawasan ang requirement nila. Hangga’t maaari, kung pwede sila makapag-recycle. Sabi nga natin ‘yung paggamit ng mga tubig-ulan [o] rainwater harvesting ay kung pwede nila i-consider sa mga golf course,” NWRB Executive Director Sevillo David said.
(What we want is for them to reduce their water requirements. As much as possible, they should recycle. As we have mentioned, golf course operators should consider rainwater harvesting.)
While households are assured top priority for water supply, several families are already storing rainwater.
Nora Pura, a resident, said they want to avoid queuing up and competing for water from delivery trucks again.
“Naranasan na po namin siyempre ang hirap, maghihintay ka ng pagdating ng truck. Agawan, ‘di po ba?” Pura said.
(We experienced the difficulty before—waiting for the truck to arrive and competing for water, right?)
The NWRB said the water supply in Metro Manila will remain a priority, along with irrigation for crops that require continuous water, such as rice.

“Mas priority po yung water supply dito sa Metro Manila. Kung ikukumpara natin sa irrigation, pero sa irrigation, ‘pag nakapagtanim na ‘yung mga kababayan natin, kailangan natin i-sustain lalo ‘yung palay,” David said.
(Water supply in Metro Manila remains the top priority. Compared to irrigation, however, once our farmers have planted, we need to sustain their crops, especially rice.)
According to David, authorities will study whether adjustments to existing protocols are necessary, but domestic consumers will remain the top priority. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: I've seen nearly 500 executions - but never one like Christa Pike's
articles.summary: Texas reporter Michael Graczyk has seen botched executions in his time, but not one in which an inmate survived.

blocks.text: Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of pentobarbital-filled syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set, according to AP, but does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Governor Bill Lee halted executions in the state after Wednesday night's failure, ordering an independent review into procedures. Botched executions have come under scrutiny over the past decade, since a shortage of the drugs used led some states to change the formula, or procure drugs from more questionable sources. Some states even brought back death by firing squad as an alternative.

items: The secret hunt for lethal drugs used in US executions

blocks.text: Pike is now in hospital where she is receiving "life-saving care", according to her lawyer.

It's not uncommon for lethal injections - the most frequently used form of capital punishment in the 27 US states where the penalty is legal - to be "botched". The Death Penalty Information Center, a think-tank that does not take a stance on the death penalty, lists 64 botched executions since 1982, 51 of them lethal injections. In at least seven of those cases, the executions were halted because the IV line could not be set.
But Graczyk has never seen an execution fail after the injection was delivered.
"That has never happened here," Graczyk said of the Lone Star State.
Graczyk, who covered a wide range of topics for the AP during his 46 years with the news service, considers his prolific attendance at executions to be an important part of the job.
"There is no [greater] authority, power, or whatever you want to call it, that state or federal government has over us than the power to take our life," he said.

There have been 1,683 executions in the US since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre. which is when the US Supreme Court re-instated the death penalty. Texas has carried out by far the most of any state, with 602 executions. In 1982, it became the first state to use lethal injections to execute people.

items: Why the death penalty is on the rise in US

blocks.text: "I always thought it was important for someone who has no stake in the outcome of a case to be there and to see the law being carried out and to make certain that it is done properly," Graczyk said.
"That someone is there to see it and tell others: Here's what I saw. Here's what happened."
He feels a particular responsibility to remember victims in his coverage and it's especially disheartening when he writes a story about an execution that doesn't make big news.
"I feel bad for the victims in the case," he said. "They are the forgotten folks. They always have been."

"Today, all the emphasis is on the inmate in Tennessee," he said. "No tears are being shed, other than the victim's immediate family, for the victim … and I understand that's the business we're in, but it doesn't mean it's right."

Pike's victim was Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old originally from Florida who loved to roller skate, smile and help others, according to descriptions given by her friends and family. Slemmer was tortured and killed by Pike, then 18, and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, after they met her at a job training camp.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, was present in Tennessee on Wednesday for the execution attempt, telling NBC News afterwards that it "was a mess".
Texas, where Graczyk lives and works, does not allow observers in the execution chamber when the IV is being inserted, he said.
"So when we get into the chamber, the inmate's already hooked up."

In a lethal injection execution, the IV would typically be inserted in the crook of the person's arm, Graczyk said. But if that didn't work, sometimes it would go into the top of their hand, their leg, neck or other sites.
During successful executions, Graczyk said inmates become "visibly unconscious after just a few seconds". They are usually pronounced dead 20 to 40 minutes after the fatal dose is given, he said.

He still remembers the death of Jonathan Nobles, who was executed by lethal injection in Texas in 1998. He'd been handed the sentence after his conviction for the brutal 1986 stabbing murders of two Austin women, Kelley Fraquhar and Mitzi Johnson-Nalley.
Nobles sang "Silent Night" as his last words.
"He gets to 'Round yon virgin' and he stops talking," Graczyk told BBC News. "That's how long it took for the drug to kick in so he wasn't conscious anymore."
That scene has stuck with Graczyk for nearly 30 years.

"To this day, when I'm in church on Christmas, and the choir is singing Silent Night, and all the congregation is joining in Silent Night and they're all, you know, in the spirit of the season and the joy of the season, and I'm thinking of this execution, I'm sure I'm the only one in that congregation that is having that kind of recollection."
When people hear about his career covering executions, he said, they are usually curious.
"Most people don't get to watch someone die," he said.
But when people ask him about what he has witnessed, he tells them "it's not the only thing I did or do or have done".

articles.title: Palestine Action crowdfunder for UK supreme court challenge blocked due to US sanctions
articles.summary:
Exclusive: CrowdJustice platform says US firm Stripe, its payment processor, ‘cannot support accounts or transactions’ linked to group

An online crowdfunder to raise money for

blocks.text: An online crowdfunder to raise money for the UK supreme court challenge to the ban on Palestine Action has been blocked as a result of US sanctions against the direct action group.
CrowdJustice, a UK company, has declined to host a fundraiser for legal fees to fight proscription because the platform uses the US company Stripe as its payment processor.

In an email seen by the Guardian, CrowdJustice said Stripe had confirmed “that it cannot support accounts or transactions linked to, or for the benefit of, Palestine Action. This includes circumstances where funds are being raised for legal proceedings.”
The US sanctions were imposed last month by Donald Trump, using powers introduced by President George W Bush in 2001 shortly after the 9/11 attacks by al-Qaida on the twin towers in New York.

Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, who has brought the legal challenge against the UK ban, said: “Due to CrowdJustice’s and other platforms’ reliance on US services, we are unable to fundraise for legal fees needed for our supreme court challenge.

“On the other hand, the state continues to spend millions of pounds to cover their legal costs to defend the disproportionate and draconian ban, which has led to more than 3,700 arrests for holding signs [allegedly supporting a proscribed organisation]. The British government and the US are putting every possible obstacle in our way, in order to stack the odds against us.”

blocks.caption: Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action, said the group was ‘unable to fundraise for legal fees needed for our supreme court challenge’. Photograph: Abdullah Bailey/Alamy

blocks.text: The Home Office has spent £700,000 defending proscription in the high court, according to the Independent. The total amount spent by the government will be far higher as the case has since been heard by the court of appeal, which overturned the high court’s decision that the ban was unlawful, and moves to the UK’s highest court in November.

When the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, announced her intention to ban Palestine Action under UK law in June last year, placing the group alongside the likes of Islamic State and Boko Haram, a CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees to fund a high court challenge raised more than £300,000 within days.

Ammori said: “Clearly, the powerful have banded together against citizens acting on their conscience against the Israeli war machine and ethnic cleansing of Palestine. It is extremely clear that Palestine Action faces harsher sanctions than Israel.

“The supreme court case is extremely important for our rights to free speech in Britain, but also for the people of Palestine. If we are successful, all prosecutions of protesters who held signs will be rightfully quashed. If not, we will witness thousands of people facing jail for holding placards.”
after newsletter promotion

The former British diplomat Craig Murray, who is separately challenging the legality of the ban on Palestine Action in Scotland, had his own CrowdJustice fundraiser for legal fees taken down after the US designated the group as a global terrorist organisation.

“It’s really disgraceful,” Murray said. “Not only do you have draconian legislation with the proscription of Palestine Action affecting freedom of speech but you’ve then got moves to cripple our ability to fight it legally through the courts, which is just adding injustice to injustice.”

articles.title: Tesco is first supermarket to offer paid ‘safe leave’ for victims of domestic abuse
articles.summary:
Exclusive: Britain’s largest private-sector employer has also trained managers to spot signs of domestic abuse

Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for…

blocks.text: Tesco has become the first supermarket to introduce paid “safe leave” for victims of domestic abuse, giving staff dedicated time to access support, secure their safety and take steps to move on with their lives.

The UK’s largest private-sector employer is offering up to three days of paid leave which can be taken flexibly for activities such as attending court hearings, arranging emergency accommodation, changing locks, securing childcare or separating finances.
Managers across the business, which employs 300,000 people, have also been trained to spot the signs of domestic abuse, support those affected and flag them to specialist services.
Under the new policy, which was developed in partnership with the shopworkers’ union Usdaw, Tesco will not ask those suffering abuse to provide formal evidence to gain access to the special leave.

Tesco is thought to be the first big British retailer to introduce safe leave, but similar policies, such as protected paid leave, emergency accommodation and training staff to spot the signs of domestic abuse, have been enacted at other UK companies, including BP and Vodafone, as well as some local councils.
Daniel Adams, an Usdaw national officer, said domestic violence and abuse affected the lives of at least one in five women, and he urged other employers to introduce similar support.

“Usdaw has long campaigned for support at work for survivors of domestic abuse and we are pleased to have successfully negotiated this new policy with Tesco. Domestic abuse often has an impact on the working lives of survivors, and it is important that employers understand this and the actions they can take to support and protect them,” he said.
“Historically violence against women, and domestic violence in particular, has been hidden, excused and ignored. That needs to change.”
Emma Taylor, the chief people officer at Tesco, said: “We believe we have a responsibility to support colleagues in what are likely to be some of the most challenging moments in their lives.

“That’s why we’re introducing guaranteed safe leave, ensuring colleagues can access practical support and the time they need without worrying about taking unpaid leave or explaining deeply personal circumstances.
“We’re proud to be taking this step and want it to help drive wider action from employers across the UK. No one should have to choose between their job and their safety.”

More than 3 million people suffered some form of domestic abuse in England and Wales last year, most of whom were women, according to the campaign group SafeLives. It says eight women a month are killed by a current or former partner in England and Wales, based on 2023 data.
after newsletter promotion

There was a sharp increase in abuse incidents during the pandemic lockdowns as victims were trapped at home with perpetrators. The permanent shift to working from home since then is seen to have made some people more vulnerable.
The Domestic Abuse Act, which became law in April 2021, includes workplace protection for domestic abuse victims, who can see their place of work as somewhere to seek help and support.

A private member’s bill currently before parliament proposes granting 10 days of paid leave for domestic abuse victims in England and Wales to give them time to deal with the practical and emotional steps.
In 2020, Northern Ireland passed legislation guaranteeing domestic abuse victims 10 days’ paid leave, and similar laws exist in Australia, New Zealand and the Philippines.

articles.title: Can there be solar for all, everywhere by 2030?
articles.summary: Prominent climate leaders have called on governments, businesses, institutions and the public to make a push for solar power before the decade is out, repowering the world with cheap, clean energy.…

image.caption: The open letter calls for solar for all, everywhere — particularly for those who don't have access to electricityImage: Tsvangirayi Mukwazhi/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: In a world set ablaze by war and global warming, with ever worsening climate disasters such as wildfires in Europe and collapsing glaciers in Nepal, solar energy provides the solution of clean, affordable power, prominent climate leaders wrote in an open letterpushing for more solar.

Signed by prominent climate figures such as author Bill McKibben, former UN Climate Secretary Christiana Figueres and Canada's former Minister of Environment and Climate Change Catherine McKenna, the letter makes a clear call. It urges governments, businesses, institutions and the public to come together to provide clean, affordable energy to "everyone, everywhere by 2030" — from the close to one billion people who still lack access to reliable electricity, to the billions more who pay too much for dirty fossil fuels.

blocks.caption: Close to 1 billion people don't have access to reliable electricity — solar power could change thatImage: Moritz Wolf/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: With just a little over three years to go until the decade is out, how realistic is this push?
"It's an ambitious target, but we've blown away in terms of where we thought we would be on solar and renewables," McKenna told DW. "So let's just keep on going."
Where are we currently with solar?

According to global energy think tank Ember,solar power has grown at its highest rate in eight years. In 2025, it increased by a record 30% over the previous year and has risen more than tenfold since 2015.

Solar is the cheapest form of electricity in the history of the world, said McKenna, who founded the climate advisory firm Climate and Nature Solutions, and the global coalition Women Leading on Climate.
"It is scaling way faster than anyone ever imagined."
As is battery technology used to store excess renewable energy.

"The cost of batteries have as well come down as the cost of solar modules," said Eicke Weber, a physicist and former director of Germany's Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems who went on to found the European Solar Manufacturing Council, among other things.
"We have the technologies available and we have enough money to finance it," he said, of a transition to widespread solar access.
In 2025, for the first time in 100 years, renewable energy sources overtook coal power in the global electricity mix, Ember's most recent analysis showed.
Where do we need to get to with solar?
At the moment, installed solar capacity around the world stands at 3 terawatts. 1TW equals 1000 gigawatts, and a single nuclear power plant has a capacity of 1GW.

Currently, the world produces about 1TW of new photovoltaic capacity each year, most of it in China. Weber says in order to fully change global energy supply to renewables, we would need about 50TW, adding that "we have more production capacities than we are selling."
Roughly 655 million people still lack accessto electricity.
"The pace of electrification in Sub-Saharan Africa has to triple to achieve universal access by 2030," McKenna said, pointing out how quickly this gap could be closed with solar.

Areas without electricity have the opportunity to leapfrog straight into clean technologies, she says, bypassing the fossil fuels that are heating the planet. Rising global temperatures are fueling extreme weather events such as drought, storms and flooding around the world.

"And there's a misunderstanding, which is often propagated intentionally by fossil fuel companies, that it's expensive, it's hard, it's unreliable. And that just isn't the case anymore," she said. "To be honest, the most unreliable thing is if you're trying to pass fossil fuels through the Strait of Hormuz."
Is solar for all, everywhere really doable in that short amount of time?

Hans-Josef Fell is used to the argument that certain things cannot be done. Widely known as a pioneer of renewable energy, he drafted Germany's Renewable Energy Sources Act which established feed-in tariffs that catalyzed clean energy growth at home and beyond.

"The Renewable Energy Sources Act unleashed exponential growth that shattered every assumption about what was achievable. It overturned the scenarios and projections that policymakers and experts had considered realistic. In the end, reality outperformed all expectations," said Fell, who now heads the think tank Energy Watch Group.

Fell, who has lived off grid for five years, says achieving a global energy transition requires political and societal will that is "currently lacking around the world because public debate is dominated by fossil fuel interests."

blocks.caption: Solar power has been growing exponentially over the past yearsImage: Thomas Imo/photothek/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to calculations by his think tank, if global energy demand were met entirely by renewables, solar energy would account for roughly 60-70% of the supply. The rest would come from wind power, and other sources, such as bioenergy and hydropower.
Where to go from here?
Countries like China and Pakistan have already pushed ahead.
"It is in our hands right now in the year 2026 to say we drop everything, we concentrate on this problem. We don't need to wait for new research," Weber said.
"It is possible to achieve this, but it would require a very kind of moonshot program," he added, saying it would need serious political backing.

He says while it might be possible for Germany to pull off such as transition in two or three years, if the political will were there, it would likely take longer to achieve on a global scale. "We would need probably till 2040 to say that we have a goal of a worldwide 80%, 90% electricity from renewables."
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions

"I would sum it up this way: if we as a global society tackle this properly, we might actually be able to make it happen," Fell said. "And even if we achieve only 90% of that goal, it would still be a remarkable accomplishment."
McKenna points to the need for blended finance, calling on governments, the World Bank, the African Development Bank and the private sector to put in money.
"What is irrational is continuing down the road of fossil fuels," she said. "That's irrational on the costs, the risks, the impacts. It's an old technology."

articles.title: UK diesel price hits record high of £2 a litre
articles.summary: France proposes that EU nations and IEA release oil and diesel from reserves as Iran war drives up cost worldwide

blocks.text: British motorists face more pressure at the pumps after the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre.

The price of a litre at UK forecourts has risen 40.5% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.
The RAC motoring group said on Friday that the average price had reached 200.01p a litre, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.
Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”
The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.

Petrol prices are also continuing to rise, with a litre of unleaded costing 174.1p on average, a 31.5% increase since 28 February, taking the cost of a typical tank to £96, just over £23 more than before the US-Iran conflict.

Earlier on Friday the transport minister, Keir Mather, sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting the UK was not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.
The Trump administration has told Germany and France to release their diesel stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.

On Thursday, the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency supplies, and Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said on Friday that Europe was discussing the diesel reserves issue with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the US.

In a video conference with G7 leaders, chaired by French president Emmanuel Macron, attendees discussed a proposal from the French government that European nations release 50m barrels of diesel from reserve supplies, and for members of the IEA to release 50m barrels of crude oil, Reuters reported.
The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.
Motorists and small businesses have been struggling with the increasing cost of filling up.

Williams added: “This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders.
“In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”
after newsletter promotion
Capital Economics estimated that a ban on US exports of diesel could raise UK diesel prices from £2 a litre to £3 a litre and push inflation up to 5%, from 3.1% in August.
The fresh high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures.
Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia.

Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait.
Trumphas pushed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to cease Kyiv’s drone and missile attacks on Russian refineries so they can help to relieve the global fuel squeeze.

The Middle East war has also pushed up household energy bills. This week the quarterly price cap rose by 4%, meaning a typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year. The cap is forecast to increase by a further 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.
Reports of talks among European nations to potentially release diesel and oil reserves fuelled a 2.5% fall in the price of Brent crude to $99.78 a barrel.

“This highlights that the main stress in the energy market is no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering,” said Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. “But rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia.”

articles.title: North and South Korea trade accusations over landmines that injured three soldiers
articles.summary: A mine blast that injured three South Korean soldiers has renewed scrutiny of North Korea's actions along the border and raised questions about its strategic goals.

image.caption: North Korea has been fortifying the border after a shift in policy against Seoul, calling it a 'foe' [FILE: June 2019]Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Pyongyang and Seoul are trading increasingly hostile accusations across the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that divides the peninsula, 10 days after three South Korean soldiers were injured by a land mine on the South's side of the border.

The latest tensions may reflect a broader North Korean effort to test South Korea's resolve while extending its control to the outer limits of its territory, including an area that has effectively been a no-man's land for more than 70 years, according to a professor of foreign policy at South Korea's Kyung Hee University.

"The North revised its constitution in March this year and officially stated that they intend to define the absolute geographical limits of the nation, and that includes within the DMZ," said Choo Jae-woo.
"They want to maximize their territory and it is my sense that they would like to push the Military Demarcation Line [MDL] — the half-way point in the DMZ — further south," he told DW.
"I see the placing of landmines on the South's side of the line as a purely political act by the North, an attempt to threaten and intimidate the South."
Why Seoul blames North Korea

The three men were part of an 18-strong patrol clearing a new route through the DMZ as part of an investigation into the activities of North Korean troops in the western sector of the zone. The four-kilometer-wide strip of land has divided the peninsula since the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953.

blocks.caption: The DMZ is a fortified buffer zone between the two Koreas that has been in place since 1953Image: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Shortly before 11 a.m. on September 21, the patrol was around 10 meters south of the MDL when a staff sergeant detonated a mine. A second mine went off as the unit commander approached to provide assistance. Both men were successfully evacuated and have undergone surgery, with a third soldier treated for minor wounds.

The South Korean military has conducted an investigation with the United Nations Command, which administers the armistice on the border, and concluded in a report released this week that the mine was of North Korean origin.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff on Wednesday accused the North of sowing mines to the south of the MDL, a breach of the armistice agreement, and demanded an apology from Pyongyang and a commitment to halt the construction of further fortifications along the border.

"This constitutes a blatant violation of the Armistice Agreement and undermines the spirit of existing inter-Korean agreements and must be halted immediately," Kang Hyun-woo, chief director of operations, said in a press briefing.

"North Korea must immediately cease activities that heighten tensions on the Korean Peninsula, such as its so-called 'border fortification.' We strongly demand an apology and responsible measures from the North," Kang added.
In a statement, the UN Command said it had "determined that an Armistice Agreement violation occurred. UNC is addressing the violation through established Armistice mechanisms."
Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine
Many in the South are demanding more resolute action on the grounds that failure to respond will be taken as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

Na Kyung-won, a politician from the conservative opposition People Power Party (PPP), has demanded that the South Korean military carry out exercises simulating a "decapitation attack" against North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
She has also called for the restart of propaganda broadcasts from loudspeakers on the border and for dissident groups to be allowed to launch balloons carrying propaganda into the North.
A pattern of border confrontations

Yu Yong-weon, also of the PPP, told reporters on Wednesday that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL around 20 times in August and on 30 occasions in September. On each occasion, South Korean troops fired warning shots when the incursions were detected.

An editorial in the Korea JoongAng Daily on Thursday said North Korea must be "held accountable" for the incident, arguing that Pyongyang's denial of responsibility "demands a firm response, clear accountability and stronger border enforcement."

blocks.caption: Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong has accused Seoul of conspiracy after it blamed Pyongyang for the blast in the DMZImage: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The North is not backing down, however, with Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong Un, accusing the South of staging a provocation and threatening to retaliate.

In a statement published by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Wednesday, Kim Yo Jong dismissed the South's allegations as a "self-staged farce" and accused the "South Korean armed gangs" of using the incident to justify political and military provocations against Pyongyang.
Accident or calculated provocation?
Andrei Lankov, a professor of history and international relations at Seoul's Kookmin University, is more willing to view the landmine detonations as an accident.

"It makes no sense to me for North Korea to do this deliberately," he said. "At the moment, the North wants to keep a low profile and do nothing that could provoke the South. There is no gain in a deliberate attack like this."

Lankov believes a more likely scenario is that the mines were shifted from the northern side of the MDL in heavy rain or natural movements of the terrain, meaning that the North's protestations of innocence are genuine.

"I also do not think the South Korean government has any interest in escalating the situation further and that they will hope this is quickly forgotten," he said. "They will want to brush it under the carpet."
Choo, however, is less convinced and senses a growing anger in South Korean society that the government is not standing up to provocations from north of the border.

"I believe that resuming the propaganda broadcasts over the border would be an effective response, but I do not believe this government will do that," he said. "This government is trying very hard to connect with the North, but I see a failure to take a firm line this time being interpreted in the North as a sign of weakness in Seoul.

"Not responding would give Pyongyang a green light to push a little more and then a little more again," he said. "There is a lot of anger here that the government is not doing enough to protect soldiers who are serving on the DMZ, to protect the people and to protect our territory."

articles.title: Reform UK-run council boycotts reporter after row over potholes
articles.summary:
Derbyshire county council accused of ‘worst kind of double speak’ as it denied banning local democracy journalist but said his inquiries will be ignored

Rows over potholes and a viral story…

blocks.text: Rows over potholes and a viral story about a garden gate have led to Reform UK’s latest confrontation with local media, after one of its councils announced it would refuse to engage with a reporter behind the stories.

Reform-run Derbyshire county council has been accused of setting a “dangerous precedent” after withdrawing all cooperation with Eddie Bisknell, a Derbyshire Live journalist who is publicly funded to cover local democracy.
Stephen Reed, the Reform council’s deputy leader, said the reporter would now have to work “twice as hard” to do his job after confirming that Bisknell’s inquiries would be ignored.

It comes after a neighbouring Reform council last year banned journalists from a major local newspaper. Nottinghamshire county council eventually ended its ban on the Nottingham Post and its website, Nottinghamshire Live, after being threatened with legal action.
In the Derbyshire case, Reform said its decision had been made after a “prolonged period of concerns”, which culminated in a story about potholes.

Councillors had hoped to produce positive headlines with a press release stating that the number of potholes in the county had been slashed from 12,000 in April to less than 700 – a figure it described as the lowest recorded in over a year.
However, an article by Bisknell, one of a group of local democracy reporters funded by the BBC, reported that questions had been raised about statistics used in the release.

The block on engaging with Bisknell emerged as the council took issue with another story about how a fence panel had been cemented across a gap in a wall between an 81-year-old woman’s garden and a council car park. The work had been initiated by the previous Conservative-led administration.

However, Reed said the decision to block the reporter had been made before the latest story about the fence appeared. He denied an outright ban had been imposed, saying Bisknell was still able to write about the council and attend public council events – a right enshrined in law. However, he confirmed the council would ignore his requests for information.

“I want to be very clear: non-engagement is not a ban,” he said. “He can still write whatever he wants. What we’ve chosen to do as an administration and as a council is just not respond to his inquiries.

“We don’t think it’s fair to other good working reporters and journalists who actually hold us to account. We want to be scrutinised. We want people to challenge what we’ve done. We want to get good news stories out and we accept that we’re going to have criticism, but it needs to be fair and balanced.”
Natalie Fahy, editor-in-chief for London and the east of England for Reach, which owns Derbyshire Live, said Reform’s decision was plainly a ban.

“We have covered some awful situations at many different councils over the years, and we don’t always expect our relationships with councils to be cosy, but we do expect there to be an open dialogue,” she said.
“To say this isn’t a ban is the worst kind of double speak and something we should all be on guard for, if you consider a free press essential to a functioning democracy.”

Dawn Alford, chief executive of the Society of Editors, called for the decision to be reversed. “Refusing to engage with a journalist because you object to their reporting sets a dangerous precedent,” she said. “A council cannot simply choose which reporters deserve answers. Transparency is a responsibility, not a favour.

“This matters far beyond one journalist or one story. When a public body shuts out a reporter, it is the public who lose access to answers about decisions taken in their name and money spent on their behalf.”
Laura Davison, the NUJ’s general secretary, called on the council to “get off its high horse and respect the democratic norms voters and local communities they represent expect”.

articles.title: What will be Vic Rodriguez’s arguments in his fight vs impeachment threshold?
articles.summary: In his appeal, Rodriguez says he will reiterate his 'intergenerational sovereignty' argument

blocks.text: In his appeal, Rodriguez says he will reiterate his 'intergenerational sovereignty' argument

items: The Supreme Court dismissed petitions challenging the adjusted threshold for conviction in Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment, citing the petitions as premature and the petitioners' lack of legal standing.
Vic Rodriguez, a petitioner and ally of Duterte, plans to appeal the ruling, arguing that the issue is ripe for consideration due to alleged unconstitutional amendments to the Constitution.
The Vice President's camp is still deliberating on whether to file a petition regarding the adjusted threshold, emphasizing the need for careful consideration of their arguments.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
The Supreme Court (SC) junked on Wednesday, September 30, the petitions challenging the adjusted threshold for conviction in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment.
There were three petitions, and one of them was filed by Vic Rodriguez – President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s former executive secretary and now an ally of Duterte.

In the ruling, the SC said it was too early – the petitions were premature – so it junked the cases. The decision also cited lack of legal standing or locus standi of the petitioners. A petitioner must have legal personality or a right to file a petition for a legal action to prosper in court.
The SC, at least based on the available briefer, did not dwell on the merits of the case. The petitions were dismissed on procedural grounds.
Rodriguez said he will appeal the ruling. He argued that the issue is not premature.

“Dito, hinog na hinog na ‘yong kontrobersiya. Bakit? Ginalaw na nga ‘yong ating saligang batas, nagkaroon ng amiyenda, illegal, unconstitutional. Hindi dapat hahayaan ng kataas-taasang hukuman,” Rodriguez said in a Facebook live. “But again, we still have 15 days from receipt of the resolution upang tayo ay maghain ng motion for reconsideration.”

(Here, the controversy is already ripe. Why? Because the Constitution has been amended – illegally and unconstitutionally. The Supreme Court must not let that happen. But again, we still have 15 days from receipt of the resolution to file a motion for reconsideration.)
Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution states that a person may “be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the Members of the Senate.”

When the Senate impeachment court adjusted this threshold, it stated that it will count only the vote of senator-judges who are “legally and factually capable” of participating in the proceedings at the time of the vote.

blocks.caption: Why Sara Duterte ally is taking impeachment vote threshold fight to SC

blocks.text: In his appeal, Rodriguez said he will reiterate his “intergenerational sovereignty” argument. This is his locus standi, according to him.

“Ibig sabihin po nito, ang bawat henerasyon ay may karapatan at kalayaang magpasya, magdesisyon para sa kanilang sarili sa kasalukuyang panahon, at hindi dapat igapos o limitahan ng mga desisyon no’ng mga naunang henerasyon,” the lawyer explained.
(This means that every generation has a right and freedom to decide for themselves at present, and cannot be bound by the decisions of the previous generations.)
“And this is precisely the locus stand or our legal personality when we filed the petition for certiorari,” he added.
Having locus standi was really the challenge in Rodriguez’s fight against the threshold. He had to prove, after all, that he has a personal interest in the case or is directly affected by it.

With respect to the camp of the Vice President, the party that may be affected by the adjusted threshold, it’s still uncertain when they will file a petition. But it’s still on the table, according to defense lawyer and spokesperson Michael Poa.
“Now, if you’re asking what about the defense if whether we will file, definitely that’s still on the table,” Poa said in a mix of Filipino and English on Thursday, October 1.

“We’re just talking if we really need to file and if we need to file, what would be the main arguments that we will raise. Because of course, we want that when we file with the Supreme Court, we also don’t want to waste the court’s time,” he added. – Rappler.com
