articles.title: ‘We just want to be listened to’: student protests shut schools across France
articles.summary: Lack of investment, overcrowded classrooms, crumbling buildings and poor teacher pay among reasons for protests by school students

blocks.text: As dozens of school pupils sat on top of a pile of wheelie bins blocking a high school entrance in north-eastern Paris, Sophia, 17, was on the frontline of the barricade, when she would normally have been attending Spanish class.

“We hope this grows into a massive youth protest movement,” said the final year baccalaureate student at Paris’s Lycée Voltaire, who did not want her real name published. She was on her second day of blocking the school entrance along with hundreds of others, ensuring all lessons were cancelled. “We just want to be listened to by the government. We’d rather stand here doing this than have to learn in poor conditions. It’s the only way to make ourselves heard.”

“School is a right, not a privilege,” read a cardboard sign as Sophia listed the grievances of teenagers across France: a lack of state investment in education, overcrowded classes of up to 40 children in crumbling buildings, poor teacher pay, staff absences and an unequal system in which social background determined success. Other reasons for the protest included the opaque and difficult online system for university applications as well as the unbearable temperatures in classrooms during the heatwaves in May and June.

“The education budget is being cut to shreds while so much extra funding is being put into the army,” said Sophia, who wanted to go on to study art and work in animation. She said she hoped the demonstrations and blockades would continue into next week. Several teachers stood by the barricades in support.

blocks.caption: Students block the entrance of the Voltaire high school in Paris. Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/AP

blocks.text: The French government is struggling to deal with its worst crisis in months after it was taken by surprise by the thousands of teenagers demonstrating outside schools across the country this week. Students’ unions say the education system is underfunded and neglected. Hundreds of high schools were closed or barricaded on Friday, and hundreds of young people have been arrested as the movement threatens to roll on into next week.

Many school students protesting have accused the state of disengaging from secondary education, describing difficult conditions in classrooms with ceilings partially collapsing during class, leaks, cockroaches and buildings in disrepair. Others have spoken of excessively long school days and a lack of teaching staff.

The government said the grievances were legitimate but condemned what it called “urban violence”. Students have accused police of using excessive force and causing injuries by regularly firing teargas canisters to disperse the protests. In Paris on Friday morning, fire damaged the entrances of two high schools – Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the south-east.

blocks.caption: Students face policemen during a protest in Paris. Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/AP

blocks.text: Several students have been injured in the protests, while the education ministry said 65 education staff were injured, including 40 school principals. An investigation is under way after a 14-year-old boy in Val d’Oise suffered serious injuries to his mouth and jaw after police allegedly beat him and fired a form of rubber-bullet launcher. The family’s lawyer said the boy had thought he was “going to die”.

Outside Lycée Voltaire, riot police stood guard on Friday amid the quiet demonstration by hundreds of children. “We’re totally pacifist,” said Yves, a 17-year-old final-year pupil who did not want his name published. He would normally have been in history class but said he had the full support of his parents to be on the barricade. He wanted to study catering next year.

“The atmosphere on this barricade is generally very calm,” he said. “But there have been other people from outside school who have come past and tried to set fire to things, so we’ve tried to move the bins to stop that.”

On Friday morning, loud bangs rang out as some people further away from the school, let off firework mortars. Yves said: “Yesterday I heard bangs going off every two minutes, it’s loud and scary when things are being fired horizontally and not up into the air. There were people provoking running battles with police but it wasn’t pupils from our school.”

blocks.caption: High school students gather outside the Lycee Voltaire high school. Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters

blocks.text: Camille, 18, who said she wanted to become a teacher, said pupils were also protesting over the French government’s lack of engagement over poor results in international education rankings. “France has disastrous results and yet we’re one of the countries with the longest school days,” she said. “The government refuses to see that it’s about quality, not the number of teaching hours.”

Farther east, on the barricade outside the Lycée Hélène Boucher, students were singing and holding cardboard signs of support for people in Gaza, as well as banners against the far-right presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, who is riding high in the polls.

Sofiane, 19, who was studying literature, said students feared the government would scrap its special one euro meals for struggling students and reduce welfare aid for housing. “We’re also protesting about the conditions in the heatwave,” he said. “It was unbearable sitting exams in 35C – 40C heat, even the teachers said those were impossible conditions.”

He said the demonstrations were likely to continue. “Young people just want to study and learn in decent conditions. The French state seems surprised about worsening school results, but they’re do nothing to remedy that.”

articles.title: 'Prepared ourselves for the worst': FlyDubai passenger recounts moments during cockpit attack
articles.summary: Almog Italie and his family were on the final leg of their trip home following a vacation in Japan when they felt FlyDubai flight FZ1073 plummet. Italie was one of 174 people on board the plane…

image.caption: A plane, carrying passengers who were on the FlyDubai aircraft bound for Israel from the U.A.E. that was diverted to Saudi Arabia following an emergency signal, arrives at Ben Gurion International Airport in Lod, Israel, earlier this week. (Ammar Awad/Reuters)

blocks.text: World

Almog Italie and his family were on the final leg of their trip home following a vacation in Japan when they felt FlyDubai flight FZ1073 plummet. Italie was one of 174 people on board the plane earlier this week when one of the pilots stabbed the other in an attempt to crash the plane. The flight plunged 30,000 feet in under 30 seconds.
Amog Italie was on his way home to Israel following family trip to Japan during foiled attack
Almog Italie and his family were on the final leg of their trip home following a vacation in Japan when they felt FlyDubai flight FZ1073 plummet.

"Suddenly we were moving like a roller-coaster without any notice ... I thought it was turbulence," Italie said, adding that after several seconds, the plane stabilized before it started diving again.
He quickly realized something was amiss.
"We understood something is wrong and something is going on in the cockpit, because that wasn't normal at all," he told CBC News.
How a FlyDubai flight survived a hijacking attempt against impossible odds | About That
Italie was one of 174 people on board the plane earlier this week when one of the pilots stabbed the other in an attempt to crash the plane. The flight plunged 30,000 feet in under 30 seconds.
"It was very fast," Italie said of the situation.
He recounted how crew and passengers ran to the cockpit to foil the attempt.

A spokesperson for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu later revealed how the stabbed pilot, Indian national Smit Machchhar, was covered with blood and on the floor when he managed to open the cockpit door, allowing others to rush in, subdue the perpetrator and let a second pair of FlyDubai pilots take over the flight.

items: 'I was fighting for my life': Indian pilot hailed as hero recalls FlyDubai cockpit attack

blocks.text: Those involved resurfaced several minutes later to update the other passengers and confirm that they were looking for a safe place to land.

"So, what needed to be done was to maintain calm, stay in the seats and do nothing else that would cause chaos," Italie said. "And this is exactly what saved our lives. Nobody panicked and we controlled the situation."
"We didn't know how the landing was going to go, so we prepared ourselves for the worst," he added.
Ultimately, the plane landed safely in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, where Italie said authorities warmly welcomed passengers and crew, even providing food.
"They were very, very nice," Italie said. "Much appreciated."
'Unity' saved everyone's life: passenger
Hours later, passengers were on board a different flight and made it to Tel Aviv. But passengers continue to recount those terrifying minutes.

"I just can say that it was a miracle. It was awful, crazy, and we thank God that we survived it. We didn't think we will make it, but thank God we are in Israel. We are back home. And we are happy to see everyone here," said another passenger, Lital Shachaf.
For Italie, the "unity" on board saved everyone's life.

items: Passengers foil bid to crash Dubai-Tel Aviv flight after co-pilot stabbed pilot, Israel says

blocks.text: Yaniv Hayun, 50, was one of four passengers who rushed to the cockpit during the chaos to overpower the unidentified co-pilot behind the attack. He said he learned what to do thanks to an aircrash television show. Another, a dentist, treated Machchhar's wounds.
"The people united. We helped each other," Italie said. "That's a message I want to share."

articles.title: Police divers find body of person missing after helicopter crash near LA
articles.summary:
Death toll of medical helicopter crash is now three people as two others continue to recover from injuries, authorities say

Police divers have found the body of a patient who went missing…

blocks.text: Police divers have found the body of a patient who went missing after a medical helicopter crashed into the Pacific Ocean off Catalina Island near Los Angeles, bringing the death toll to three while two other people were recovering from their injuries, the authorities said on Friday.

Divers with the Los Angeles county sheriff’s department found the victim’s body Thursday in the wreckage of the helicopter after searching more than 156 sq miles (404 sq km) over 23 hours, the Coast Guard said in a statement.

Relatives of the missing person told local TV network ABC7 that the woman was being transported from Catalina Island to the mainland for medical care after having an allergic reaction. They also said her 20-year-old son went with her in the helicopter to help as a language interpreter.

The helicopter with five people onboard went down shortly after takeoff and hit the water not far from the island, officials said. The cause is not clear and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) is investigating. First responders pulled four people from the water on Wednesday night.

Robert Luna, the Los Angeles county sheriff, said authorities were not yet identifying the victims by name. But he described two of the people who died as the male pilot and a female nurse. He also said another medic and a fourth person, a man, were hospitalized. Luna said the helicopter wreckage was about 200ft (60m) deep in the water.

The helicopter’s operator, Reach Air Medical Services of Sacramento, confirmed that two of its crew members died and a third was recovering at a hospital. The company declined to provide more details.
A memorial service was held on the island to honor the victims.

The helicopter had landed on the island shortly after 7pm after a 24-minute flight from an airport in Oceanside, on the California coast between Los Angeles and San Diego, according to the flight tracking service Flightradar24.
Janice Hahn, the Los Angeles county supervisor, said it was a terrible tragedy, adding: “The people who were on board dedicated their careers to saving lives. They are heroes.”

articles.title: School protests send shivers down French government's spine
articles.summary: A movement that started nearly two weeks ago has spread, and in France young people on the streets spells trouble, writes Hugh Schofield.

blocks.text: It is a piece of wisdom that all French leaders take care to heed: young people on the street equals trouble.
Since the student protests of May 1968 – memorably described by President De Gaulle as chienlit (bed defecation, in other words chaos) – every government has run scared of angry French youth.
Why? Because youth movements are unpredictable and shapeless, often with no clear structure to negotiate with. Because when they protest, other groups join in.

Also: because as they're young, the public tends to sympathise. And because if the police mess up and cause injury or worse, then the consequences are incalculable. And presidential elections are only months away.
For all these reasons, when la jeunesse en colère (angry youth) is at the barricades governments tread very carefully indeed.

Right now, French teenagers are at the barricades and if they are not visibly angry (the mood is more excitement), they certainly have the government of President Emmanuel Macron in what Le Monde called on Friday "the cold sweats".
A movement that started nearly two weeks ago in the low-income Seine-Saint-Denis area of northern Paris has in the last few days spread across the country.

An internal report prepared for the Paris police department which was leaked to the media analysed the opening of the movement in Seine-Saint-Denis. It concluded that students were being "egged on by far-left elements from students unions… and political groups such as… LFI."
It said the tensions "could be part of a flame-kindling strategy… aimed at imposing their ideas ahead of the national elections".

In support of its conclusion, the report's writers cited the presence of protesters who are not themselves lycéens, the vagueness of the demands, the flying of Palestinian and Algerian flags, and the use of tactics – like calling for supplementary protests at police-stations - that come from the radical-left playbook.

The LFI strongly denies doing anything more than lending its natural support to a movement it regards as legitimate. On Thursday Mélenchon called on students to avoid violence "which only serves our enemies' interests".

But his opponents believe that the 75-year-old veteran – who stands a good chance of making it to the second round of the presidential elections in May, probably against the hard-right's Marine Le Pen – knows exactly what he is doing.

Polls show he has massive support – some 40% -- among 18-24 year-olds in France, and that this is concentrated in the populous, high-immigration city suburbs where his talk of a "new France" and "creolisation", to reflect France's changing language and population, are highly appreciated.

But young people are also the biggest abstainers in French elections, so the strategy – as the elections approach – will be to give constant reminders to this part of the population that the LFI is at their side, and that their vote can count.
Whether this will be enough to ensure victory for Mélenchon is another matter. He must surely take seriously the polls which all show him losing massively in a run-off against Le Pen.
If that happens, France will be in very unstable territory - for which the young people's protests of recent days will indeed have been a harbinger.

articles.title: Napolis provides silver lining with jiu-jitsu bronze after Ramirez, Custodio heartbreaks in Asian Games
articles.summary: Kaila Napolis breaks through for the Philippine jiu-jitsu team in the 2026 Asian Games with a bronze medal after world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered surprise early exits

blocks.text: WIN. Jiu-jitsu athlete Kaila Napolis in action for the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Kaila Napolis breaks through for the Philippine jiu-jitsu team in the 2026 Asian Games with a bronze medal after world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio suffered surprise early exits

items: Kaila Napolis won a bronze medal in jiu-jitsu at the 2026 Asian Games, marking the Philippines' only jiu-jitsu medal in the event.
Napolis secured her medal after defeating Mongolia's Tsagaanbileg Altangerel 2-0, following a loss in the quarterfinals.
Her victory came after the disappointing exits of fellow competitors Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio, who were expected to perform well.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Kaila Napolis somehow made up for the heartbreaking defeats of world champions Annie Ramirez and Kimberly Custodio as she salvaged a jiu-jitsu bronze medal in the 2026 Asian Games.

Napolis clinched what is so far the Philippines’ only jiu-jitsu medal in the continental meet in Nagoya, Japan, after a 2-0 win over Mongolia’s Tsagaanbileg Altangerel in the battle for the women’s 52kg bronze at the Aichi Prefectural Martial Arts Hall on Friday, October 2.

A Southeast Asian Games champion, Napolis crashed out of gold-medal contention after a 3-2 loss to to Mongolia’s Mongoljin Ganbaatar in the quarterfinals, but she found her way to the podium by coming out triumphant in the repechage against Singapore’s Sofia Anabel Rivas and toppling Altangerel for the bronze.
“I really wanted to bounce back [and end] with the bronze medal. I wanna give it all. And thankfully, I pulled it off,” said Napolis in a mix of Filipino and English.
Napolis replicated her campaign in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, where she also won bronze after losing in the semifinals.

Her podium finish came after the surprise exits of Ramirez and Custodio, who were tipped as strong gold-medal contenders following their triumphs in the Ju-Jitsu International Federation World Championships in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in August.

Eyeing a second Asian Games gold after ruling the women’s 57kg class in 2023, Ramirez lost her opening match as she competed in the lighter 52kg division, falling to Thailand’s Nuchanat Singchalad in the round of 16 on Friday.
The match ended in a scoreless tie, but Singchalad advanced by virtue of her two advantage points.

Meanwhile, Custodio — a four-time world champion in the women’s 45kg category — saw action in the heavier 48kg class, where she exited the round of 16 against UAE’s Balqees Abdulla on Thursday, October 1.
Similar to the fate Ramirez suffered, Custodio lost via advantage.
“We’re a bit sad, of course, for those who did not medal. But I’m still super thankful for the support,” said Napolis. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Man shot by ICE in Texas has surgery to remove bullet lodged in his back
articles.summary:
Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez remains in custody after surgery to remove bullet supporters say was stuck close to his spine

The Venezuelan delivery driver who was

blocks.text: The Venezuelan delivery driver who was shot and wounded by a federal immigration agent in Texas last month had surgery on Thursday to remove the bullet that had been lodged in his back for nearly two weeks.

Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez, 28, had appeared in court in a wheelchair on Wednesday, wearing a sling on his arm. He remains in custody on charges that he assaulted an officer while trying to evade arrest.

Supporters and representatives had been lobbying for him to be given the chance of surgery, asserting that there was a risk he would lose feeling on the left side of his body because of the bullet being stuck so close to his spine.

He had been taken from a hospital where he was being treated after being shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin and put in detention at a facility about 140 miles away the same day.

The authorities said Garcés Pérez struck an officer with his side mirror on 20 September while trying to drive away after a traffic stop and questioning. The federal officer who shot Garcés Pérez, and who allegedly was hit by the side mirror of the car, wasn’t wearing a body camera.

Garcés Pérez faces up to 20 years in prison if convicted on the assault charge. He was also facing deportation when he was stopped while driving on a DoorDash delivery in Austin last month, with some of the incident caught on bystander footage, including how ICE officers called an ambulance and then stood by as the wounded man sat in his car and then was given first aid by local police when they arrived.
The bullet was successfully removed during surgery, and Garcés Pérez is recovering in the custody of the US Marshalls, said Fabiana Meléndez Ruiz, a spokesperson for his legal team.
His case has sparked outrage and protests in the Texas capital city against Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, including federal officers’ conduct. It was the latest shooting by ICE officers.

Garcés Pérez said he was struck by a law enforcement SUV and his car spun around before he was shot. Federal officers told investigators, however, that Garcés Pérez attempted to strike an officer with his car at the end of the chase before the officer fired his weapon.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: VP Sara Duterte, Mans Carpio accepted money from China --Trillanes
articles.summary: Former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV accused Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio, of respectively accepting P150 million and P319 million through their separate…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 8:19pm

Former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV accused Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband, lawyer Maneses Carpio, of respectively accepting P150 million and P319 million through their separate organizations.
In a "24 Oras" report from Sandra Aguinaldo on Friday, Trillanes presented the evidence he was supposed to show the impeachment court before the prosecution removed him as a witness.
“Tumanggap sila ng P150 million from the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China, itong foundation ni Sara Duterte,” Trillanes said.
(Sara Duterte’s foundation accepted P150 million from the Embassy of the People’s Republic of China.)
Trillanes also alleged that Carpio received P319 million from the Chinese government through his company.

“Ito na ang paraan ng China ng pagsuporta sa mag-asawang Duterte, maliwanag po ito. Kaya dapat kikilabutan po tayo rito, kasi vice president po siya, may national security implications, bawal po yan,” Trillanes said.
(This is how China is supporting the Duterte couple; it is clear. So we should be afraid, because she is the vice president; there is a national security concern, this is not allowed.)
GMA News has sought the reaction of the Vice President's camp and will update the story once it is available.
Duterte also allegedly failed to declare in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth her peso and dollar time deposit and insurance, the former lawmaker said.

Trillanes said that he himself initiated his removal as a witness in Duterte’s impeachment trial to remove pressure from the prosecution panel, however, he did not disclose further details about this.
“Sa akin naman kasi the signal is clear. Hindi ako welcome,” Trillanes said. (For me, the signal is clear. I am not welcome.)
He also criticized impeachment presiding officer Chiz Escudero for his handling of the proceedings, saying that he should be more liberal.
“Bantayan niyo yung presiding officer. That's what I'm saying. Tignan nyo,” Trillanes said. (Guard the presiding officer. That's what I'm saying. Look at him.)
Impeachment court spokesperson Regie Tongol dismissed the claim that Trillanes was not welcome, as he was treated like a guest when he attended the trial. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Mangin, Barbosa fall short of more PH taekwondo golds in Asian Games
articles.summary: World junior champion Tachiana Mangin and three-time Southeast Asian Games titlist Kurt Barbosa lose their respective title bouts as they add a pair of taekwondo silvers to the Philippines' haul in…

Andy Chua/REUTERS

World junior champion Tachiana Mangin and three-time Southeast Asian Games titlist Kurt Barbosa lose their respective title bouts as they add a pair of taekwondo silvers to the Philippines' haul in the 2026 Asian Games

items: The Philippines missed out on two gold medals in taekwondo at the 2026 Asian Games, with Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa winning silver instead.
Mangin lost to China's Ma Jingyue in the women's -49kg final, while Barbosa was defeated by Kazakhstan's Tamirlan Tleules in the men's -58kg final.
Despite the losses, both athletes had strong performances, with Mangin making her Asian Games debut and Barbosa improving from his previous competition results.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines missed out on two additional gold medals in the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, after taekwondo jins Tachiana Mangin and Kurt Barbosa settled for a pair of silvers on Friday, October 2.

Barbosa and Mangin lost their respective title bouts at the Toyohashi Gymnasium as they fell short of delivering another gold in the sport after Jeus Gabriel Derick Yape ruled in the mixed individual virtual taekwondo earlier in the day.
Mangin saw her superb run come to a disappointing end at the hands of China’s Ma Jingyue, who pulled off a 2-0 victory in the women’s -49kg finale.
The two rounds each ended in a scoreless tie, but the Chinese won both by superiority to claim the gold medal.
Still, it was a promising campaign for Mangin as she won a medal on her Asian Games debut at just 18 years old.

A former world junior champion and a Southeast Asian Games titlist, Mangin beat Kazakhstan’s Rita Bakisheva in the round of 16, Chinese Taipei’s Wang Chieh-ling in the quarterfinals, and Japan’s Ruka Okamoto in the semifinals to get a crack at the crown.
Meanwhile, Barbosa absorbed a 16-14, 15-2 loss to Kazakhstan’s Tamirlan Tleules in the men’s -58kg final.
After losing a nip-and-tuck opening frame, Barbosa sought to pull level in the second round, but Tleules landed two straight head kicks to seal his golden victory.

Despite the defeat, the pride of Abra redeemed himself from his campaign in the 2023 edition in Hangzhou, China, where he lost his opening match in the round of 32. The Tokyo Olympian also bounced back from his failed four-peat bid in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games in Bangkok, Thailand.

Barbosa reached the final by stunning Asian champion Jafar Aldaoud of Jordan in the semifinals, following up on his victories over Saudi Arabia’s Abdullah Essa Almushraf in the round of 16 and Japan’s Hidetaka Maeda in the quarterfinals.
A win by either Mangin and Barbosa would have marked the first time the Philippines won at least five golds in an Asian Games edition since its seven-gold haul in 1962.
The country currently has four golds courtesy of Yape, gymnastics star Carlos Yulo (with two golds), and pole vault ace EJ Obiena. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Does Philadelphia’s ‘house of horrors’ hold the key to seven missing women?
articles.summary:
City on edge as police comb home of Raymond Horsch, pornographer who died last year, in grisly case involving disturbing pictures and film

A dilapidated house, burned out above the second…

blocks.text: A dilapidated house, burned out above the second story, may hold clues to dark tales and – potentially – the darkest of endings as the FBI and police in Philadelphia try to unpick what took place at 417 West Chew Avenue for more than three decades.

Last week, homicide investigators shifted their focus from examining an archive of a million photographs and film recovered from what is known locally as the “house of horrors” to excavating what is in or under the home of Raymond “RC” Horsch, a career criminal, local artist, author and snuff photographer who died last year aged 82, and his son Eugene, 44.

So far, at least seven missing women have been linked to the home in the Olney section of the city, originally a German American neighborhood but now largely African American, Hispanic and Asian. Investigators believe five are dead.

Fifty-eight women seen on film and in photographs recovered from the trash-strewn property have been identified. Of those, 25 have been located but not yet interviewed; 19 have spoken with detectives but declined to cooperate.

Investigators are faced with a difficult task: how to discern from images whether Horsch’s subjects are posing, and what is real and what is staged. Such is the grim nature of snuff photography and the murky exchanges that lie beneath. Investigators have said that the five women appear unconscious, lifeless or injured, but with no bodies the medical examiner cannot issue death certificates.

“We’re going slow and methodical,” a police source said. “Do we think people were killed in the house? Sure. It’s a tough investigation because the guy who had the house was a violent pornographer. Is it art or is it reality?”

blocks.caption: Raymond Horsch, pictured in about 1999. Photograph: Raymond ‘RC’ Horsch

blocks.text: Deputy police commissioner Frank Vanore said at a news conference on 10 September: “Some of this is play-acting. Some of it we believe could be real, but we’re not there yet.”

The five women who police believed to be dead are Blair Tonzelli, 35, missing since 2023; Nicole Fusaro and Maribel Fresses, both 27, who disappeared in 2018; Amy McHale, who disappeared in June 2016 and had been married to Horsch; and Gabrielle Amarando, 22, who disappeared in 2012.

Four miles from the Olney home lies Philadelphia’s Kensington neighborhood, an area notorious for its open-air drug use, prostitution and homelessness, and as a place where people simply disappear from life.

Many women in the community last week recalled some of those identified by investigators. One had connections to the Olney house – her driver’s license was registered there – but declined to discuss the case. Others said they recalled Horsch’s son, Eugene, currently in custody pending federal gun and drug charges, cruising the block in a black BMW. One remembered Fresses as an “Italian princess – sweet and kind”.

Ashley, making her way from a woman’s shelter with a plastic bag of candies, syringes, and a glass bowl for smoking fentanyl or meth, said bleakly: “A lot of girls go missing here. You get dope sick, it makes you crazy, and then you make bad decisions.”

Not all the women who passed through the Olney home were connected to Kensington. Media reports suggest that some met Horsch in Camden, New Jersey, 20 miles away. A woman from the area told ABC Philadelphia she had gone to the Olney home, blacked out from the drugs Raymond Horsch gave her, and woke up with him standing over her, taking pictures.

Police first raided the home in June after Eugene Horsch was stopped in a car in Philadelphia’s Old City neighborhood. Horsch was carrying fake ID indicating he was federal law enforcement and DEA agent. A female passenger was carrying Tonzelli’s identification.

blocks.caption: A million photographs and film were recovered from what is known locally as the ‘house of horrors’. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Two handguns and approximately $8,000 worth of illegal drugs were found in the vehicle. According to court documents, Eugene Horsch allegedly said Tonzelli would “never be seen again”. A search of the home turned up an additional illegal firearm, a marijuana grow operation, a fake FBI badge and five urns containing cremated remains.

The arrest of the younger Horsch, who had not been charged in connection with the missing women, shone a spotlight on his father, who was never charged in connection with the disappearances of any of the five identified women. The city’s medical examiner’s office has advised that if images of at least three women recovered from the home “are authentic and have not been altered, the women depicted appear to be deceased”.

Court records show that Raymond Horsch was convicted in 2009 for attempting to lure a nine-year-old girl into his car in Kensington. “Come here, in my car, sexy girl,” Horsch said to her, according to an arrest report. Horsch was found guilty, sentenced to two and a half to five years in prison, and required to register as a sex offender.

But his lawyers sought a new trial and the case collapsed because the girl was too afraid to testify a second time, according to the Philadelphia Inquirer. Horsch’s conviction was expunged and the records placed under seal. A judge has ordered them to be preserved.

According to a 1985 psychological examination obtained by the Inquirer, Horsch was a manipulative criminal who was “consumed by anger … grandiose, mistrustful, suspicious, and excessively controlling”.

The profile was commissioned as part of a federal drug manufacturing case. Horsch fled the US with his second wife, Myroslawa Anna Ferkuniak. He was arrested in New Zealand, where he’d been living under the name of Stanley Stokowski, a real California chemist who had a Stanford doctorate.

blocks.caption: Eugene Horsch. Photograph: Philadelphia police

blocks.text: According to the profile, he spoke in the third person, as if describing “events from someone else’s life”. Michael Yoder, a retired FBI special agent, told the outlet that, judging from the report, “I would say you have a potential serial killer on your hands.”

For a time, Horsch and his young son lived in Pennsylvania’s Berks county, where he opened a barbecue restaurant while also pursuing a career as a fetishistic or “snuff” photographer. In 2009, he was arrested after a marijuana grow operation was discovered in his basement, and he was sentenced to five years in prison.

Raymond Horsch had been offering cash and drugs to women in Kensington in exchange for participating in his violent pornographic films since the early 2000s. He also had access to to a crematorium connected to Kensington’s Garzone funeral home to photograph corpses. In 2007, the business was shut down for selling body parts on the black market.

Horsch wasn’t hiding his access to the morgue – a video exhibited at a “Transgressions” art show in 2014 featured a body being loaded into an incinerator. The exhibition asked visitors to consider if Horsch’s “often transgressive images can possibly be art? Or, as many critics and philosophers claim, are art and pornography completely and forever mutually exclusive?”

Horsch was not reticent about his obsession with women in addiction. He uploaded photos of his subjects to his website featuring women “imagining and acting their own deaths” juxtaposed with real photos of overdose victims. A handwritten note found in the home describes hurting people and makes reference to serial killer Ted Bundy.

blocks.caption: Agents carry out an investigation in June. Photograph: Kyle Mazza/Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Horsch’s films included a documentary, Whore!, and films including Deleted Scenes: A Serial Killer’s Video Journal and Slaves. He starred in and directed Lovers, which was produced by a feminist porn studio. He produced The Erotic Memoirs of a Male Chauvinist Pig, featuring Georgina Spelvin, the star of The Devil in Miss Jones.

He published a two-volume photo book called Eroto~ To the Prurient Interest, showing a woman he referred to as “Anna” in staged “deaths”. 2014’s Empathy included a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman’s body with chemicals.

The home is already a tourist attraction even as investigators still search for evidence. “It was creepy vibes. He’d be out front staring at women, or he’d be in his yard doing some kind of chemist stuff,” recalled Jessica Diaz, 37. A neighbor living opposite the home said he recalled young women coming and going from the home. On occasion, ambulances were called. “They need to tear that house down,” he opined.

With Raymond Horsch dead, and his son Eugene under investigation, it remains possible that no charges will be brought and the best the families of the missing can hope for is a police report. “We have a duty to those families who are all concerned about whether their loved one lost their lives in that house or maybe somewhere else,” said the Philadelphia police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.

But the story of Raymond Horsch is already entering the annals of Philadelphia horror lore. Edgar Allan Poe and Bram Stoker both wrote in the city, and it’s had serial murderers in the past. In the 1980s, Gary Heidnik, an inspiration for the fictional character Buffalo Bill in The Silence of the Lambs, imprisoned six vulnerable women in a pit in his basement with the goal of creating a “baby farm”.

Josh Hitchens, a writer and historian known locally as a prominent “purveyor of the macabre”, said that in each case, it was people preying on the vulnerable. “These are often not the people that law enforcement pays much attention to. That’s one of the horrifying things about what’s unfolding now – what Raymond Horsch was doing was apparently known and talked about within the community.”
Hitchens said Horsch is likely to become a point on the horror map of Philadelphia, achieving a measure of recognition in death that his films and writings failed to secure in his life.
“I hope that within that we’re not just talking about Raymond and Eugene Horsch, but the lives of the women are also remembered and given the respect they deserve.”

articles.title: Mayors, First Nations chiefs in Alberta's oilsands region react tentatively to West Coast pipeline designation
articles.summary: Political leaders in Alberta’s oilsands region say they hope the potential one million barrels of oil per day that could flow through a new West Coast oil pipeline will also bring jobs and economic…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney shakes hands with Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo Mayor Sandy Bowman at a news conference at SMS Equipment north of Fort McMurray, Alta., announcing next steps to accelerate the West Coast pipeline project. (Vincent McDermott/CBC)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New

Political leaders in Alberta’s oilsands region say they hope the potential one million barrels of oil per day that could flow through a new West Coast oil pipeline will also bring jobs and economic spinoffs.
PM and Alberta premier announced next steps for Pacific Link project Thursday

Prime Minister Mark Carney and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced during a Thursday visit to Fort McMurray, Alta., that the proposed pipeline – which is now called the Pacific Link – is the first project designated as being in the national interest under the Building Canada Act.
Now the federal government will fast-track the project by finding ways to consolidate the approval process.

“What we’re seeing today overall is a strong provincial government working with the federal government, and that’s something we haven’t seen in a long time,” Regional Municipality of Wood Buffalo Mayor Sandy Bowman said following the news conference.

“It’s one of probably the biggest announcements we’ve had in a long time, and to have a prime minister here when it’s not a natural disaster is a huge thing. That’s usually when we have a prime minister in the community.”

The proposed 1,200-kilometre pipeline would start roughly 47 kilometres northeast of Edmonton in the town of Bruderheim. The pipeline would run towards the Roberts Bank deepwater port near Delta, B.C., and the oil it carries would be loaded onto tankers bound mostly for Asian markets.

The estimated cost of the pipeline is between $35.2 billion and $43.7 billion. The federal government and Alberta’s government aim to have the project completed by 2032-33. Smith has said she also wants the oilsands to double production to eight million barrels of oil per day by 2035.

The province and the federally-owned Trans Mountain Corporation will each own a 45 per cent stake in the pipeline. Calgary-based Pembina Pipeline, whose CEO Scott Burrows also attended Thursday’s announcement, will own a 10 per cent stake.

Pembina Pipeline will have an opportunity to purchase another 10 per cent stake in the project once it’s been completed. Carney said Indigenous communities will also be offered a minimum 10 per cent ownership stake.
Project will get ‘Indigenous buy-in’: Powder

Chief Raymond Powder of the Fort McKay First Nation, which is roughly 60 kilometres north of Fort McMurray, said he is interested in a potential partnership. He said he is also optimistic that the pipeline “will get Indigenous buy-in" as long as environmental concerns are addressed during consultation.

“I believe that today’s announcement actually brings benefits to the nation because when we think about it, where do we want to go and what do we want to do? We want to continue to sustain the growth of our nations,” Powder told reporters after the announcement.
"But within that support, of course, we're going to have to address some of the challenges."

items: AFN chief warns Carney against 'abusing' majority to pass new major projects bill
‘Environmental racism’: Fort Chipewyan residents protest proposed treat-and-release plan for tailings water

blocks.text: Mikisew Cree First Nation Chief Melody Lepine said she is not ready to endorse the pipeline. At the same time, Lepine said she is also not yet prepared to oppose the project.

Lepine, who leads an Indigenous community downstream from the oilsands in the Fort Chipewyan area, said local First Nation leaders met with Carney on Wednesday evening. She said they raised their concerns with equity stakes and environmental impacts.

“I’d say it’s too early to tell, but we’ve got the commitment that we’re going to work on these things, and I can say I’m committed to do that work,” Lepine said in an interview with CBC News. “If this pipeline is the opportunity to address a number of these concerns, then we’re going to take advantage of that.”

The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation (ACFN), which is also based in the Fort Chipewyan area, issued a statement Thursday evening that said economic opportunities “do not diminish our responsibility” to address the First Nation’s ongoing health and environmental concerns stemming from industrial development in the oilsands.
“We want to emphasize that participation in these discussions does not constitute ACFN’s consent to the proposed pipeline,” the statement said.
“This is the beginning of a process and its outcome is not predetermined.”
Fort McMurray prepares for economic boom ahead of new pipeline
Steady growth, not a boom: Bowman

In Edson, Alta., which sits on the pipeline’s path, Mayor Kevin Zahara said the community is going through a “mini-boom” thanks to two unrelated pipeline projects being built by TC Energy and Atco. He said he is ready to prepare for an influx of new construction workers for Pacific Link.
“I’m heartened to see the positive relationship between the province and the federal government, but it takes action,” he told CBC News Network’s Power and Politics on Wednesday.
“When you actually see shovels in the ground and things moving forward, I think that will have a bigger impact on residents.”

Bowman said he doubts the pipeline’s construction will signal a return to the lucrative days of the last oilsands boom, a period that saw record population growth and tax revenues rise across the oilsands region.
However, Bowman said he believes the region will experience “steady growth.” He pointed to the 2025 census, which reported a slight population bump for Wood Buffalo for the first time in a decade.
Bowman also said there is plenty of land ready for developers if new housing is needed.
“This community has gone from being a small town to a boomtown, which is now kind of a hometown,” he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Vincent McDermott covers Fort McMurray and the Wood Buffalo region for CBC News. He was previously the editor of Fort McMurray Today, where he was part of a team that won a National Newspaper Award for coverage of the 2016 Horse River Wildfire. He is also a former contributor to the official magazine of the Royal Astronomical Society of Canada. He can be reached at vincent.mcdermott@cbc.ca
With files from Peter Zimonjic

articles.summary: Niagara Falls Tourism has placed a full-page open letter in a Buffalo newspaper, inviting Americans to cross the bridge and celebrate with Canadians on Saturday, including witnessing Niagara Falls…

The playing earlier this month of the Canadian and U.S. anthems at the new stadium, shown in the background, is among the latest cross-border friendly gestures amid t

blocks.text: Hamilton

Niagara Falls Tourism has placed a full-page open letter in a Buffalo newspaper, inviting Americans to cross the bridge and celebrate with Canadians on Saturday, including witnessing Niagara Falls light up in the Bills' red, white and blue colours. The latest gesture in the face of the trade war comes after the NFL team played Canada's anthem at the recent home opener.
Niagara Falls Tourism's open letter in Buffalo paper comes after anthem tribute by NFL's Bills
Amid a heated trade war, there's been lots of love between Ontario's Niagara region and Buffalo, N.Y.

In the latest show of camaraderie, Niagara Falls Tourism placed a full-page open letter in the Buffalo News on Friday, inviting Americans to cross the bridge and celebrate with border neighbours Ontario on Saturday night.
That's when Niagara Falls will be lit up in the red, white and blue colours associated with the NFL's Buffalo Bills, accompanied by matching-coloured fireworks.

items: Buffalo Bills to 'celebrate' O Canada at home opener amid more Trump threats during trade war

blocks.text: The open letter in the newspaper notes that when the Bills played O Canada at the Sept. 17 home opener at the new Highmark Stadium, "Canadians sang along from the stadium, in sports bars and on couches across the country." The highly anticipated event featured the Barenaked Ladies singing O Canada and actress Auliʻi Cravalho's rendition of The Star-Spangled Banner.
Visit Buffalo also posted billboards across southern Ontario with the message, "O Canada, We're Still Singing it, Love Buffalo."

On Sept. 16, the team posted a video on social media showing retired Bills quarterback Ryan Fitzpatrick and former wide receiver Stevie Johnson completing some cross-border football catches along the Niagara River, tossing to each other from aboard distant ferries.
'We just want to say thank you'
Adam Stiles, interim president and CEO of Niagara Falls Tourism, noted the anthem tribute and other kind gestures coming from Buffalo.
Stiles said Canadians want to return some of that love and spread a message of coming together at a time tariffs and other political issues are dominating the news.

items: As Canada-U.S. relations sour, border towns of upstate New York fear damage will be permanent

blocks.text: "When you get down to that human level, people want to rally around that idea and those gestures," he told CBC News.
"We just want to say thank you for doing something nice for us."
Why the Buffalo Bills played O Canada at their home opener

In a news release, Stiles said “Buffalo’s welcome [at the NFL game] meant a great deal to Canadians, and we wanted to return that warmth. Our communities share much more than a border: we share friendships, families and a love of the Bills.
"Saturday is our way of saying thank you and reminding our American neighbours that they are always welcome in Niagara Falls, Canada.”
The special illumination lighting is set to take place between 10 p.m. and 10:15 p.m. ET, with fireworks from 10 p.m. to 10:05 p.m.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Manchester City Premier League charges: What do they mean?
articles.summary: Since being bought by the UAE in 2008, Manchester City have become one of the world's most successful football clubs. A raft of serious financial charges threatens to undermine this and bring chaos…

image.caption: Sheikh Mansour, as he is widely known, fronted the deal to buy City for the UAE nearly 20 years agoImage: Martin Rickett/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Manchester City has won the English Premier League eight times over the last 14 years. Whether those titles will remain is one of a plethora of issues at stake after England's top division charged one of its most high-profile clubs with more than 100 breaches of its financial regulations.

On Tuesday, the Premier League announced that an independent commission had found City had drawn up "sham contracts" as well as "relying on sham agreements to artificially inflate the club's revenues and reduce its costs." These contracts, dubious sponsorships and a number of other methods were, according to the commission's report, used to inflate the club's revenue to the tune of about £900 million (€1.05 billion) over the period between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.
The case has been ongoing for eight years after initial revelations from Der Spiegel, a German magazine, and Rui Pinto of the 'Football Leaks' website. City continues to deny any wrongdoing.

"The Club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," read a club statement. "Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe."
On Friday, the club issued a further statement saying it had lodged a "comprehensive Appeal."
What was the Premier League verdict on the Manchester City charges?

The 750-page report was damning, accusing City of inflating contracts and sponsorship deals, running secondary contracts off the books, making "concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the Premier League investigation" and signing off inflated image rights deals to artificially boost their earnings. The report says all this enabled them to pass both Premier League and UEFA financial spending limits.

The Premier League's chief ­executive, Richard Masters, described the case "as the most significant in Premier League history," adding that the club "systematically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade."

Although the Premier League, the world's most commercially successful football league, has drawn some praise for its actions, others point out that it took Pinto leaking emails and media reports to take action. The report shows that Manchester City, which had won the league once in 71 years before being taken over by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in 2008, were consistently posting revenues way higher than any of their more established and successful rivals.
Who are the key figures at Manchester City?

In this context, its the owners. The Abu Dhabi United Group, essentially an investment vehicle for the UAE royal family, bought the club in 2008. Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, know simply as Sheikh Mansour, fronted the takeover. He is a member of the ruling Al Nahyan family and the UAE's vice president and deputy prime minister. Khaldoon Al Mubarak, who also holds several government positions in the UAE, was brought in as chairman.

Nation-state ownership of this type is controversial in European football. Manchester City's owners have long been criticized for the country's human rights record and using the club for sportswashing. Similar criticisms have been made of European champions Paris Saint-Germain, which Qatar owned and City's Premier League rivals Newcastle United, which is owned 85% by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund.

blocks.caption: As well as huge domestic success, City won the Champions League under Pep Guardiola in 2022-23Image: Jose Breton/NurPhoto/IMAGO

blocks.text: City's CEO, Ferran Soriano, joined in 2012 as City expanded their ownership into foreign leagues, buying up clubs in the US, Japan and Australia. He replaced former head coach Roberto Mancini with fellow Spaniard Manuel Pellegrini before former Bayern Munich and Barcelona coach Pep Guardiola took over in 2016, ushering in the club's most successful period.
How did Manchester City's system work?

The club immediately started splashing out on big-money transfers after the UAE investment arrived. At the time, neither UEFA nor the Premier League had the tight financial rules they now have. UEFA introduced its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules for the 2011-12 season, while the Premier League followed with its Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) in 2013-14.

City's free spending and relatively low commercial income meant they were likely to fall foul of such rules. The club was handed a conditional €60 million UEFA fine for losses in the 2011-12 and 2012-13 seasons. They would later be banned from the Champions League on similar grounds in 2020 before being reinstated on appeal.

In an attempt to try and comply with these financial rules, City set up a system they called "Project Longbow" in 2012. The commission said much of this was genuine, but one arm of it was an agreement with a third party called Fordham that was, according to the ruling, "little more than a front." Essentially, it reads, the club's UAE owners "would be used (and were used) to enable Fordham to acquire from the club (at a sizeable, artificially inflated price) the club's entitlement to benefit financially from its players' image rights."

In other words, City's owners were pumping money into their own club through vastly inflated sponsorship and image rights deals so their income looked higher and they could spend more, particularly on player transfers and wages. The report also claims that City paid three individuals, whose names are redacted, through a third party to keep them off the books.
What happens next?

That's the question on everyone's lips. So far, no sanctions have been imposed on City, and the appeal will likely drag proceedings out even longer. Meanwhile, the club, which is top of the Premier League, faces Liverpool on October 11, after the international break.

While there is no precedent for such a tranche of charges, clubs have previously fallen foul of the Premier League's PSR regulations. Everton were handed a 10-point penalty for a £19.5 million breach over a period ending with the 2021-22 season. This was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach, plus an additional point for every £5 million the club overspent. Given that City's overspending is close to a billion pounds, applying that would certainly relegate them, though the Premier League does not operate England's second-tier league, the Championship.

For now, it looks like City and the league will play on under a cloud. But if the verdict remains after appeal, clubs and individuals whose careers and honors stand to be impacted will likely come forward and litigate. City themselves could be relegated, docked points over successive seasons, face transfer bans or any combination of those things. The titles won in the relevant period could also be stripped.
This article was originally published on September 30, 2026. It was updated on October 2, 20206 with Manchester City's statement confirming that it had lodged an appeal.

articles.title: Fictitious name? The curious case of ‘Ang Hai Peng,’ Sara Duterte’s biz partner
articles.summary: Ask former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, and he will tell you it's a person who doesn't exist.

blocks.text: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV alleges on October 2, 2026 that the name Ang Hai Peng in the corporate records of a company tied to Vice President Sara Duterte belongs to a person who does not exist.
Rappler screenshot
Ask former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, and he will tell you it's a person who doesn't exist.
Who is behind the Chinese name that had appeared — but later disappeared — in the corporate records of Vice President Sara Duterte’s company?
Ask former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, and he will tell you it’s a person who doesn’t exist.

During his press conference on Friday, October 2, Trillanes put the spotlight on Ang Hai Peng, which Trillanes said appeared in the records of Timesquare Bee Foods, a company incorporated by Duterte, as per her assets list over the years.
Trillanes said the company’s corporate documents showed that Ang owned 60% of the company from 2013 to 2013. The company was later renamed Gencorp.
Gencorp’s records with the Securities and Exchange Commission didn’t bear Ang’s name beginning 2022. The top shareholder has become the JTC Group of Companies, owned by Jaime T. Cruz.
Cruz is a business partner of the Dutertes. His name appears in numerous corporate documents co-owned by the Vice President, her husband Mans Carpio, and her siblings Paolo and Sebastian Duterte.
Central to Trillanes’ allegation is that Peng does not have government records.
“They have no birth certificate, they have no passport, their TIN is fake, and, incidentally, their birthday is the same as Jaime T. Cruz’s,” Trillanes claimed.
“They are one person. I am one hundred percent person that [Ang Hai Peng] is nonexistent,” he added.

blocks.caption: Fictitious name? The curious case of ‘Ang Hai Peng,’ Sara Duterte’s biz partner

blocks.text: We have emailed JTC Group of Companies’ email address for Cruz’s side of the story. We will update this story once we receive a reply.

Rappler first reported about Jaime T. Cruz in mid-September as part of our exposé on Gencorp and how it has bagged millions of pesos in contracts with Davao City Hall led by Mayor Sebastian since 2022. The arrangement raises conflict of interest and constitutional violation issues against the Vice President.
The prosecution’s team has zeroed in on Gencorp at the impeachment court, but it has yet to say whether it will actually call Cruz a witness.
With Trillanes no longer in prosecution’s witness lineup, it remains to be seen whether the issue he has raised will find their way somehow into the impeachment court. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Half of Europe witnessed record heat stress this summer — EU
articles.summary: The EU's climate monitor said this summer was third-warmest for the continent on record. European rivers also registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992.

image.caption: Europeans across the continent had to cool themselves off during repeated heat waves [FILE: July 30, 2026]Image: Volodymyr Sindieiev/picture alliance

blocks.text: A record 52% of Europe witnessed "very strong" heat stress by the end of this summer, the EU's Copernicus Climate Service (C3S) said in new research published on Friday.
What did Copernicus say in its findings?
According to Copernicus, "very strong" heat stress is characterized by temperatures which feel higher than 38 degrees Celsius (100.4 degrees Fahrenheit).
Around 80% of Europe witnessed "strong" heat stress by the end of the summer. "Strong" heat stress is when temperatures feel like more than 32 degrees Celsius (89.6 degrees Fahrenheit).
Heat stress is when temperatures and humidity are so high that the body cannot cool itself through perspiration.
This summer was the third-warmest on record on the European continent and the hottest on record in Western Europe.
"One of the things that stands out for 2026 is that the heat was not only remarkable for its intensity, but also for its geographical extent," Samantha Burgess, the deputy director of the C3S, said.

blocks.caption: The Rhine River in western Germany saw record lows during the heat waves this summer Image: Hesham Elsherif/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Copernicus also said that European rivers registered their lowest average flows since records began in 1992. In addition, the service said that "56% of the European ocean was much warmer than average, with 22% experiencing record-high summer sea surface temperatures."
Burgess said that drought impacted almost half of Europe by the end of this summer.
"That's one of the defining characteristics of summer this year, that it was not a single record. It was the way that multiple records appeared together across the climate system," she said.
What was the impact of the European heat waves this summer?
Tens of thousands of people died in heat waves in Europe this summer, which also impacted economic activity and agricultural harvests.
Some cities such as Paris even temporarily restricted alcohol sales as temperatures frequently spiked above 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit) on parts of the continent.
Air conditioning is uncommon in some parts of Europe, with many Europeans staying home or going out to the pool to cool off.
France's firefighters on the wildfire frontline
In addition, the frequent heat waves and dry conditions this summer also led to wildfires in southern France and the southern Spanish region of Andalusia, among other locations.
The biggest wildfire in history in Germany's most populous state, North Rhine-Westphalia, triggered evacuations in August before it was brought under control.
Wildfires not only damage buildings but also create harmful air pollution in the environment.

articles.title: P5B budget sought for sugar industry, restricted importation in new bill
articles.summary: A bill seeking a P5 billion budget for the sugar industry and restrictions on sugar importation was filed in the House of Representatives.

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 7:49pm
A bill seeking a P5 billion budget for the sugar industry and restrictions on sugar importation was filed in the House of Representatives.

Negros Occidental 3rd District Rep. Javier Miguel “Javi” Benitez made the proposal under House Bill 9088, or Tunay na Ugnayan, Buhay, at Oportunidad sa Asukal (TUBO) Act, a measure which he announced during a LegisHear public consultation in Victorias City in his home province.

Benitez said the measure seeks to address problems exposed by previous sugar importation, strengthen support for farmers, and make government decisions affecting the industry more transparent and firmly anchored on production, inventory, and consumption data.

Benitez said the measure provides that, of the said P5 billion annual budget starting 2027, 30 percent will go to farm-to-mill roads and irrigation while 20 percent will be earmarked for climate adaptation and resilience.
“The bill fixes where it goes, so nobody can quietly move it,” Benitez said.

“This increased funding has become more urgent because of the spread of the red-striped soft scale insect (RSSI), which, as of September 1, had affected 134,000 hectares nationwide, including 95,000 hectares in Negros Occidental,” he added.
Likewise, Benitez said the measure provides for an 18-month pause on commercial sugar imports upon effectivity, subject to an exception for verified shortages.
After the said pause, imports would be permitted only when warranted by supply data and would be prohibited during the first three months of the milling season.
Further, the measure sets a trigger allowing imports when verified raw sugar stocks fall below 200,000 tons.
This way, Benitez said importation will only be merit-based instead of a whimsical decision.
“[Because] when an import decision is made by order, without data and without the people who grow the cane, the farmer carries the cost,” Benitez said.
Benitez’s proposal would also require random and unannounced audits of mill laboratories, with penalties including fines, suspension or loss of license for tampering.

In addition, the bill requires sugar orders to be published within 15 days together with votes and dissents, establish a public dashboard tracking the use and beneficiaries of industry funds, and provide for twice-yearly consultations with farmers, workers, agrarian reform beneficiaries, millers and refiners.

Other assistance provided in the measure includes block farming, socialized credit, discounts of up to 30 percent on fertilizer and machinery, emergency cash assistance during pest outbreaks or calamities, temporary relief from loan penalties, price-support purchases, auditable mill measurements, and farm-to-mill infrastructure.
Benitez, however, said the bill is still subject to the feedback of sugar farmers and other stakeholders.

“This bill remains under consideration, and the inputs gathered from sugar farmers and other stakeholders during LegisHear would feed into the work of the technical working group,” he said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Man City lodges 'comprehensive' appeal after being found guilty of financial rule-breaking
articles.summary: Manchester City has lodged a "comprehensive" appeal, the club confirmed Friday, following the publication of a report by an independent commission detailing large-scale financial rule-breaking by the…

image.caption: A exterior shot of the Etihad stadium, home of Manchester City football club in Manchester, England, on Thursday. The team has filed an appeal against an independent commission ruling that found the club guilty of serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, seeking to overturn the verd

blocks.text: Soccer

Manchester City has lodged a "comprehensive" appeal, the club confirmed Friday, following the publication of a report by an independent commission detailing large-scale financial rule-breaking by the Premier League giant.
Club has yet to receive a punishment for the violations found
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Oct 02, 2026 7:47 AM EDT | Last Updated: 7 minutes ago
"The club's firm position," read a short statement from City, "is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe."

City has protested its innocence throughout the long-running case, which dates back to 2018, and reached a milestone Tuesday when the Premier League published a verdict saying the Abu Dhabi-controlled club was "guilty of all charges related to serious breaches" of the competition's financial rules from 2009-18.
Officials said they would lodge an appeal and that was filed on Thursday evening, the club said, ahead of Friday's deadline.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case," City said, using language from previous statements on the case.

items: Manchester City guilty of almost all 115 financial charges, Premier League says in explosive verdict

blocks.text: According to the Premier League handbook, the chair of the three-person disciplinary commission that found against City now has to appoint a new appeal board. That also will consist of three people, one of whom "shall have held judicial office," the league's rules state.
The appeal board will then schedule a hearing that should finish within 12 weeks after the appeal is filed, and cannot exceed five consecutive days.

City has yet to receive a punishment for the violations found. That will be addressed in a separate, confidential hearing with the commission and there has been no word whether sanctions can be imposed before the decision of the appeal is reached.
The Premier League has only said its intention is that the process is concluded "as soon as possible."

According to the Premier League, potential sanctions against City could be a reprimand, a fine, a suspension, points deduction or, in the worst case, expulsion from the competition. No team has ever been expelled from English soccer's top flight.
Rule-breaking used 'sham' commercial deals, according to commission

City was found to have systematically broken the Premier League's financial rules for nearly a decade in what the competition's chief executive, Richard Masters, described as the most significant disciplinary case in the league's history.

The investigatory panel found that City artificially inflated its revenue — using what the league has called "sham" commercial deals — by more than $1 billion US from 2009-18 to circumvent financial fair-play rules that restricted rival clubs, and allowing City to buy some of the best players in the world.

items: More soccer coverage

blocks.text: That was the foundation of a long and unprecedented period of success in which City changed the landscape of the world's most popular soccer league, with the northwest club winning eight league titles from 2012-24.

City committed almost all of the 115-plus violations, the commission found: 80 from 2009-18 for alleged financial misdeeds and another 35 from 2018-23 for allegedly not cooperating with the investigation.

articles.title: This island in Kiribati could be the key to solve the Amelia Earhart mystery
articles.summary: Nearly 90 years after US aviator Amelia Earhart vanished over the Pacific, a new expedition to the remote island of Nikumaroro hopes a lagoon anomaly could finally reveal the fate of her missing…

image.caption: Amelia Earhart disappeared in the South Pacific in 1937 while on an around-the-world flightImage: picture alliance / Courtesy Everett Collection

blocks.text: Amelia Earhart's attempt to become the first woman to fly around the globe at the equator ended in mystery when she and her navigator, Fred Noonan, disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in July 1937.

With the 90th anniversary of her disappearance on the horizon, a new expedition is setting out to finally determine what happened over the vast Pacific. This expedition has what it believes is crucial new evidence.

The team from Purdue University in Indiana and the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI) is scheduled to depart for the uninhabited island of Nikumaroro on Saturday to determine if an anomaly in the island's lagoon is Earhart's missing plane.
Part of the low-lying Pacific island nation of Kiribati, Nikumaroro has long been considered the place where Earhart and Noonan died.
The pair took off from New Guinea on July 2, 1937, on the leg to the island of Howland, where they were to refuel before continuing on to Hawaii and completing the circumnavigation in California.

blocks.caption: Amelia Earhart, left, and navigator Fred Noonan hold a map of the Pacific Ocean showing the planned route of their flightImage: picture alliance / AP Photo

blocks.text: Something went amiss en route, however, and even though a US Coast Guard ship could hear Earhart's radio transmissions and her Lockheed Electra must have been tantalizingly close, she was never found.
One of the last messages said she was running on a north-south navigational line that gave her the best chance of finding land before her fuel ran out. That line went through Nikumaroro.
Landing on a coral reef
In 1988, researchers from the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery (TIGHAR) were the first to suggest that Earhart could have reached Nikumaroro and landed on its fringing coral reef.
TIGHAR's first visit to the island was in 1989, and the group has returned seven more times, turning up compelling artifacts, including lengths of aircraft aluminum and plexiglass from a windscreen.
The group found a scent bottle, a zip made in Pennsylvania in the mid-1930s, parts of a pocket knife of the same brand listed in the aircraft inventory, and the heel of a woman's shoe.
Archive research discovered that human remains discovered on the island in 1940 were initially believed to be of Earhart or Noonan — but were lost in the chaos of the Pacific war.
Despite the searches, no one has yet found the "smoking gun" artifact, an item that could only have come from the doomed flight.
Satellite images offer fresh hope
Expedition leader Rick Pettigrew, executive director of the Archaeological Legacy Institute (ALI), believes the elements may have uncovered incontrovertible evidence.

A powerful tropical cyclone tore through the central Pacific in 2015, shifting geographical features on the island and in its lagoon. Satellite images taken over the following years showed what might be the outline of an aircraft fuselage and wings in shallow water off the Taraia promontory.

"This object in the satellite images is exactly the right size to represent the fuselage and tail of the Electra," the ALI website states. "It also appears to be very reflective and is likely to be metallic. It lies in very shallow water, largely covered by sediment, in a place where the current would bring an object floating into the lagoon through Tatiman Passage, the opening to the ocean and the reef."

Pettigrew's 17-strong team intends to focus all its efforts on the place where the images indicate debris may be located, using drone photography, remote sensing with magnetometers and sonar units. If the initial results are positive, a hydraulic dredge will excavate sediment.

"Once we have a sufficient portion of the object exposed, we should be able to identify it," according to the ALI's expedition plan. "If it is made of aircraft aluminum and has the specific shape and rivet patterns of the Electra, we will know that we have found the remains of Earhart's aircraft."
In search of a 'smoking gun'
Much of the ALI's theory is based on the research and fieldwork carried out by TIGHAR, but its executive director, Ric Gillespie, is not convinced the researchers will find the "smoking gun."

blocks.caption: The expedition to Nikumaroro could finally resolve a mystery that has endured for nearly 90 yearsImage: Google Earth

blocks.text: "The object visible in old satellite imagery that Pettigrew believes is aircraft wreckage does not look like aircraft wreckage," Gillespie told DW. "It looks like a dead pandanus tree that was uprooted in a storm and washed up on Taraia."

"Pettigrew thinks the wreckage is no longer visible because it is buried in silt," Gillespie noted. "He has never been to that location and does not understand that the silt there is only a few inches deep."
Teams from TIGHAR searched the same location in 2001 and 2007 with metal detectors and drew blanks, he said. Yet Gillespie remains convinced that Earhart was on Nikumaroro.

"I think the aircraft sank immediately after being washed over the reef edge and was smashed to pieces in the surf," he said. "Major components were eventually buried in underwater landslides … or grown over with coral. We have found what there is to find."

Dorothy Cochrane, who has monitored progress in the search for Earhart for more than 35 years as curator at the Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum in Washington, DC, and continues to do so since her recent retirement, says Earhart still holds fascination for so many people "because it is 'the greatest unsolved mystery of the 20th and continuing into the 21st centuries.'"
An alternative scenario

She has a different view of what happened in 1937. She argues that if Earhart was nearly out of fuel while still close to Howland, it would have been impossible to fly another 640 kilometers (400 miles) to Nikumaroro. Cochrane also says that items cited as evidence of a castaway on the island can be explained by other visitors and by a small settlement that existed there for several years.
"I believe that Earhart and Noonan were in the general vicinity of Howland Island, based on the facts of the flight, but just could not find it before they ran out of fuel," she said.
"Howland Island was a tiny speck in the morning light of a vast sea," she said, suggesting Earhart could not establish radio contact to guide her the last few miles to her destination.
Cochrane believes the Electra lies on the seabed near Howland. Others have advanced this theory, and several searches of the area have been carried out in recent years.
If Pettigrew's lead pays off, however, it will conclude aviation's nearly 90-year puzzle.
