articles.title: Activists plan legal action against police ban on entering security zone near Perth weapons expo
articles.summary:
Under new WA laws anyone who defies an exclusion order could face a maximum $36,000 fine and three years in prison

  • Get our

blocks.text: Activists and a Greens MP have threatened legal action after the Western Australia police banned at least 12 people entering a designated security area where the Land Forces weapons expo will be held in Perth from 6 October.
The police used special powers given to them by the WA government last month to ban the activists from entering the area surrounding the Perth Convention and Exhibition Centre.

Two of the activists, 18-year-old Will Shanahan and 22-year-old Matilda Lane-Rose said in a media conference held with the Greens MP Sophie McNeill on Friday they would take legal action if police and the police minister, Reece Whitby, did not revise the ban.
“We’ve sought legal advice, and we think that we have standing to pursue a judicial review into this decision,” said Lane-Rose, who works as a staffer for McNeill.

Rose told reporters the police called her on Thursday saying she had been placed on the exclusion list, despite having no plans to attend the protest against the expo, which is being organised by the WA Anti-War Collective.

The legislation used to ban her and 11 others, called the Land Forces (Special Powers) Bill 2026 was passed last month. It gives police expanded stop-and-search powers and the ability to ban people from entering a security zone that extends from the Elizabeth Quay bus port to the convention centre for 10 days.
Anyone who defies an exclusion order could face a maximum $36,000 fine and three years in prison.

Whitby said at the time the legislation was “about making sure WA Police have the powers they need to keep people safe and effectively manage Land Forces, while respecting the right to peacefully protest”.

The Land Forces International Land Defence Exposition event is held every two years and is Australia’s biggest weapons expo. The last event was held in 2024 in Melbourne, and attracted a large protest where police were accused of using excessive force.
Melbourne activists Violet Coco and Brad Homewood are among the 12 people issued an exclusion order by WA police.

The companies expected to exhibit at the expo are not listed on the Landforces website. Last month McNeill made public the list, which included an Australian subsidiary of Israel’s largest weapons company, Elbit Systems, and the state-owned company Rafael Advanced Defense Systems.

The two companies have been criticised by a former member of the UN commission of inquiry, Chris Sidoti, for being “key enablers of the Israel Defense Forces in its commission of war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide against the Palestinian people in Gaza over the last two years”.
Shanahan, who recently moved to Newcastle from Perth, said he had not intended to attend the protest given he no longer lived in Western Australia, but now planned to do so, to defy the ban.
after newsletter promotion
“I cannot sit and watch my home state be captured by global militarisation and be turned into an all-out police state,” he said.
On Friday, McNeill accused the government of using the legislation to target peaceful climate activists.
“They said that these powers were for people who had the propensity to commit violence, people who are a threat to the community,” she said.
“Instead, what we’ve seen is peaceful activists targeted … who didn’t even have any plans to be here in Perth next week. It’s outrageous.”

Lane-Rose was fined $2,000 last year after pleading guilty with other Disrupt Burrup Hub activists to attempted trespass and criminal damage at the home of the then Woodside boss, Meg O’Neill, in 2023.
Whitby and the WA police were approached for comment.

articles.title: Verdict on Sara Duterte may be out December 16 — Senate court spokesman
articles.summary: Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol says the prosecution's dropping of witnesses fast-tracked Vice President Duterte's impeachment trial

blocks.text: NOT ENEMY. Senate impeachment court spokesman Reginald Tongol urges House prosecutors to focus their energy on building up their case.
SENATE YOUTUBE SCREENSHOT
Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol says the prosecution's dropping of witnesses fast-tracked Vice President Duterte's impeachment trial

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court may issue its verdict in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte as early as December 16, spokesperson Reginald Tongol said Friday, October 2.

In a virtual press briefing, Tongol said the trial remains “aggressively” ahead of schedule despite the suspension of proceedings, and that the court could finish the case before the Senate goes on its holiday recess.

The court cut short the hearing on Thursday, October 1, and suspended the proceedings slated for October 2, after granting the defense counsel’s request to defer the testimony of Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura over confidentiality issues.
The trial resumes on Monday, October 5, with Buenaventura taking the witness stand.

According to Tongol, the prosecution’s decision to drop some of its witnesses has expedited the proceedings, saving the court 27 trial days. He also said the House prosecution panel is expected to finish presenting its witnesses on Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth by next week.

If the prosecution formally drops the bribery charges against Duterte, it may proceed with its formal offer of exhibits. The defense will then be asked to comment on the prosecution’s formal offer before presenting its own witnesses.
The defense has been allocated 30 trial days for its presentation of witnesses. Tongol said that if the defense uses all 30 days, the senator-judges could issue their verdict by December 16.
“If the defense consumes all 30 days they requested, then the verdict may come by December 16,” Tongol said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Under the pre-trial order, the prosecution listed 57 witnesses to be presented in 62 trial days. The defense panel said it will present 45 witnesses in 30 trial days. – Rappler.com

articles.title: 'Like an episode of Breaking Bad': Man caught in N.L.'s largest fentanyl bust pleads guilty
articles.summary: Martin Marks has pleaded guilty to four dozen charges after being caught twice with copious amounts of fentanyl and cocaine.

image.caption: Martin Marks appeared by video from Her Majesty's Penitentiary on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. He pleaded guilty to dozens of charges stemming from a fentanyl and cocaine operation he ran in St. John's. (Ryan Cooke/CBC)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New
Martin Marks has pleaded guilty to four dozen charges after being caught twice with copious amounts of fentanyl and cocaine.
Martin Marks caught with 1.4 kg of fentanyl mixtures in 2024 bust
It started with a blizzard.
A snowplow operator came across a grey Honda CRV parked on Ridge Road in St. John's. The driver was slumped over the steering wheel with the engine still running.

By the time police arrived 10 minutes later, Martin Marks was emerging from a zombified state to realize he was in a world of trouble. A urine sample later showed cocaine, methamphetamine, fentanyl, hydromorphone and oxycodone in his system.
A search of his vehicle turned up a BB gun tucked under the driver's seat, along with nearly 100 grams of cocaine, 44 grams of crystal meth, 33 hydromorphone pills and 124 oxycodone pills.
“A mobile pharmacy,” provincial court Judge Paul Noble remarked as he heard the facts read aloud in his courtroom on Thursday.
“You haven’t heard anything yet,” prosecutor Trevor Bridger replied.
The traffic stop was just the beginning of a Royal Newfoundland Constabulary operation to surveil Marks and his girlfriend, Emma Murphy, from February to September of 2024.

Police watched the couple on 47 different occasions as they made 84 interactions that were believed to be drug deals. Most instances were quick hand-to-hand transactions, according to an agreed statement of facts read into the record in Marks's case on Thursday.

The officers soon discovered the couple wasn't just using their house in St. John's for their operation, but also a camper in Cochrane Pond — a campground that sits on Crown land about 25 kilometres from the centre of St. John's.

An undercover officer — who goes by the pseudonym UC Vic — made two buys from Marks and Murphy in the summer of 2024. On one occasion, he bought 8.7 grams of cocaine with a purity of 90 per cent. The second time, it was 16 grams of cocaine that tested at 95 per cent pure.

items: Fentanyl seized in N.L.'s largest-ever bust enough to kill half the province, police say

blocks.text: On Sept. 22, 2024, police believed they had probable grounds to make an arrest. They secured warrants to search the couple's home, as well as the camper at Cochrane Pond.
They found a whopping 521 grams of fentanyl, along with 846 grams of fentanyl mixtures — including carfentanil, acetylfentanyl, methylfentanyl and fluorofentanyl.
It was the largest fentanyl bust in the province's history.
"It sounds like an episode of Breaking Bad," Noble said in response to the facts.
Marks and Murphy were released as charges were still pending. The facts in the case against Marks show police watched as the pair continued to sell drugs.
They were surveilled again between July 9 to July 17, 2025, again making a series of quick hand-to-hand transactions.
When their home was raided again, police found another 33.5 grams of fentanyl mixtures along with 110 grams of cocaine and 98 grams of methamphetamine.
Marks pleads guilty
The two were charged with a long list of drug and weapons offences, along with a third person who police believe acted as a courier for the couple.
Marks entered guilty pleas to 48 charges on Thursday. Murphy has yet to go to trial and is next due in court on Oct. 29 for a status update.

Marks was being held at the West Coast Correctional Centre in Stephenville until he was moved to Her Majesty's Penitentiary in St. John's last week. The move caused some confusion on Thursday, as staff at the prison were unaware Marks was supposed to be in court.
After a brief delay, he appeared by video.
Marks will have a sentencing hearing on Oct. 16, where lawyers for the Crown and defence will make submissions on how long Marks should serve behind bars.
Bridger and defence lawyer Stephen Orr told the court they're not far apart on their suggestions.

articles.title: Progella, Pagara turn back China for PH’s maiden Asian Games beach volleyball medal
articles.summary: Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara complete a thrilling come-from-behind win over China to give the Philippines its first-ever beach volleyball medal in the Asian Games

blocks.text: DUO. Beach volleyball players Khylem Progella and Sofiah Pagara of the Philippines in the 2026 Asian Games.
PSC-POC Media Pool
Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara complete a thrilling come-from-behind win over China to give the Philippines its first-ever beach volleyball medal in the Asian Games

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines captured a breakthrough Asian Games medal in beach volleyball as the duo of Khylem Harl Progella and Sofiah Shanine Pagara escaped with a bronze on Friday, October 2.
Progella and Pagara completed a thrilling come-from-behind 13-21, 23-21, 15-13 win over China’s Cao Shuting and Don Jie in the battle for bronze at the Hekinan Ryokuchi Beach Court in Japan.

Only in their early 20s, the Alas Pilipinas duo displayed steely resolve against their older Chinese foes, bouncing back from a first-set blowout and saving match point en route to giving the country its first medal in the sport, which debuted in the Asian Games in 1998.

The Philippines teetered on the brink of defeat when China grabbed a 20-19 lead in the second set, but Pagara scored on a drop shot that knotted the score and sparked a 4-1 run that sent the match into a decider.
China once again led 12-11 in the third set, only to fall short again as Progella and Pagara clinched four of the next five points to nail the bronze.
Progella, 20, and Pagara, 20, redeemed themselves after kissing their golden aspirations goodbye following a straight-sets defeat to Thailand in the semifinals.
That marked the Filipinas’ only loss as they went unbeaten in the preliminary round with a 3-0 record, swept Hong Kong in the round of 16, and edged top seed Japan in the semifinals.
Earlier in the tournament, Alas Pilipinas’ other beach volleyball tandem of Sisi Rondina and Bernadeth Pons crashed out of the quarterfinals.

Rondina and Pons, the reigning Southeast Asian Games champion, absorbed a narrow 21-17, 12-21, 15-13 loss to Thailand’s Taravadee Naraphornrapat and Worapeerachayakorn Kongphopsarutawadee on Wednesday, September 30. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Trillanes claims Sara Duterte has undeclared millions in time deposits
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte did not declare millions in time deposit assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth from 2007 to 2010 when she was Davao City vice mayor, former senator…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 4:12pm

Vice President Sara Duterte did not declare millions in time deposit assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth from 2007 to 2010 when she was Davao City vice mayor, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday.
Trillanes issued the claim a day after he asked the prosecution panel to drop him from the list of witnesses for the impeachment trial of Duterte.
The former lawmaker said that based on the research of his team, the Vice President had undeclared dollar and peso time deposits from 2007 until 2010.
He said the Vice President also did not declare a million dollars worth of life insurance in her 2010 SALN.
“Siguro naman, iyong senator-judges, hindi na mababaryahan rito (Maybe the senator-judges won’t see this as a pittance),” Trillanes said at a press conference.
“Iyan po ang mga milagro ni Sara Duterte (That is the miracle of Sara Duterte),” he added.

During the same press conference, Trillanes also said that Cale 88 Foods Corporation as well as Tapang at Malasakit Alliance for the Philippines, Inc., which are declared assets of Duterte in her joint SALN with husband Manases Carpio, also received P319 million and P150 million, respectively, from the Chinese government and firms.

He also reiterated the allegation he made before the House justice panel in April 2026 that a certain Sammy Uy, an alleged drug lord, transferred P181 million worth of money to the Duterte family, including the Vice President.
On Friday, Trillanes said that the Vice President knew Uy when she was 21 years old, because Uy sold land to her in 1999. The former senator presented a copy of a Deed of Sale between Uy and Duterte.
"When she was 21 years old, Uy sold two lots to her. It is a total of 900 square meters. Uy was their family friend," Trillanes said.

During the House justice panel hearing on the impeachment complaints against the Vice President, Anti-Money Laundering Council Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura said that at least 18 bank transactions linked to Duterte and her family members, as cited in the affidavit of Trillanes, match the AMLC records of covered and suspicious transaction reports.

Buenaventura told the House committee on justice that 18 of the randomly selected transactions cited in Trillanes’ affidavit and testimony correspond to entries in AMLC records, including three transactions allegedly involving Uy.
Asked for the source of his findings, Trillanes said that these are based on official documents from government agencies and are all verifiable.

“Lahat po ‘yan ay backed up by official documents. SEC, PSA, and AMLC documents posted on the Senate impeachment court website. Maliwanag po 'yan. Hindi tayo gumagawa ng mga kathang-isip na allegations,” he said.
SEC is the Securities and Exchange Commission, while PSA is the Philippine Statistics Authority. AMLC is the Anti-Money Laundering Council.

“Subok na 'yan. Our research team will eventually share this with the prosecution, and they would ask the same question to the impeachment trial witnesses, kung papayagan pa. Baka iyong pro-China senators, mag-protesta naman,” Trillanes added.
GMA News Online reached out to Duterte's legal counsel, Atty. Paolo Panelo, for comment and will publish it once available.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President, alleging unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. —AOL/RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: 400 French schools closed on Friday as protests escalate into ‘urban violence’ – Europe live
articles.summary:
Dozens of schools have been damaged and nearly 3,000 teenagers have been detained since the start of the tensions

Some 100 schools have been severely damaged during French high…

blocks.text: Morning opening: French protests continue to escalate with 400 schools closed on Friday

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa

Some 100 schools have been severely damaged during French high school protests that escalated this week into “urban violence,” with 40 headteachers injured, according to the latest figures from the French education ministry.

The pupils’ grievances range from overloaded timetables and overcrowded classes to insufficient teachers and unbearable temperatures during heatwaves earlier this year. Riot police have been deployed to confront the increasingly violent protests.
Nearly 3,000 lycée students – aged between 15 and 18 – have been detained since the start of the protests, including 1,949 on Thursday alone, the interior ministry said.

During a call with local prosecutors last night, the justice minister Gérald Darmanin urged them to pursue civil liability claims so that parents are made financially responsible for damage caused by their children.
Meanwhile, education minister Édouard Geffray asked parents for help, warning that “children are in danger on the streets.”

But there are no signs of tensions going down, with first incidents reported near the Jean-Rostand high school in Strasbourg and the Simone-Veil high school in Marseille. Some 400 schools remain closed today.

blocks.caption: A student walks in a cloud of tear gas smoke as part of a student blockading protest near the Couffignal secondary school, in Strasbourg. Photograph: Romeo Boetzle/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Damages from this week’s protests are likely to go into hundreds of millions euros, with the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region reporting 25 million in damages.
I will keep an eye on that for you, and bring you all the latest from Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, too.
It’s Friday, 2 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.
Key events

items: 20m agoMorning opening: French protests continue to escalate with 400 schools closed on Friday

blocks.text: The prefect of Bouches-du-Rhône in southern France told BFMTV that the situation on the ground was “incomparable” to the riots on Thursday, with “far fewer demonstrators” joining the protests today.
11 schools in the region are affected, while 55 switched to e-learning, Jacques Witkowski told the broadcaster.

articles.title: Hidden cameras show some stores unlocking speed limits on e-bikes, selling e-scooters that go up to 120 km/h
articles.summary: A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages…
articles.byline: Bobby Hristova, Madeline McNair, Asha Tomlinson

image.caption: Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area with hidden cameras rolling to test how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario laws. (CBC)

blocks.text: Whether it's children cruising down a suburban street, drivers delivering food downtown or a daredevil taking their need for speed to the highway, electric bikes and electric scooters are becoming more common across Canada.

A new hidden camera investigation by Marketplace shows how some stores are selling e-scooters and e-bikes with top speeds much higher than provincial speed limits and with recommended rider ages younger than provincial regulations allow.

Most provincial traffic laws limit e-bikes and e-scooters to 32 kilometres per hour or less. Age restrictions, meanwhile, vary across the country, ranging from 12 to 18. The territories and some provinces have no minimum age to ride.

That means it is mostly up to local police services to enforce these rules at a time when the number of injuries caused by these vehicles is climbing yearly, and public calls are growing for stronger, consistent rules nationwide and better enforcement.

Marketplace visited some of Canada's most well-known big box and specialty shops in the Greater Toronto Area — Amego, Emmo, EZbike, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Costco — that sell popular brands. The undercover journalists tested how easy it is to find an e-bike or e-scooter that either had a maximum speed or age recommendation contravening Ontario limits.

In Ontario, e-scooter and e-bike riders must be at least 16. E-scooters cannot travel faster than 24 km/h on a flat surface, and e-bikes cannot travel faster than 32 km/h, according to provincial laws.
10 of 12 stores exceeded Ontario limits
Of the 12 stores journalists visited undercover, salespeople at six stores told us or showed us how to bypass built-in speed limits.
While most stores reminded us of Ontario rules, 10 stores sold e-bikes or e-scooters with maximum speeds beyond Ontario limits.
Stores are allowed to sell the e-bikes no matter how fast they go, but Michael Pasquali, founder of the Canadian Electric Bicycle Association (CEBA), says it's "heartbreaking."
"Shops that are selling products that are way beyond the legal limit, they're putting a lot of people in danger."
Seven stores also had e-scooters for sale with manufacturer-recommended rider ages under 16, though some medical experts say e-bikes and e-scooters are too unsafe for anyone under 16.

items: Watch the full Marketplace investigation on Friday, Oct. 2, on CBC-TV and YouTube.

blocks.text: "It's not just a toy; it's a motorized vehicle," said April Kam, an emergency physician at McMaster Children's Hospital in Hamilton.
"We're seeing kids who are presenting with brain bleeds, with abdominal injuries, solid organ injuries."

Recently released data from the Canadian Institute for Health Information shows 150 people ages 15 and under were hospitalized for falls involving an e-scooter in the 2025-2026 fiscal year across Canada, compared to 54 the year prior. That's an increase of roughly 178 per cent — and reflects a steady year-over-year increase for the last three years.

The number of head injuries related to e-scooters has also increased, from 50 in the 2022-2023 fiscal year to 157 in the 2025-2026 fiscal year. Fractures, dislocations and or muscle and tendon injuries have more than doubled in that same period, with 544 last fiscal year.
The Canadian Paediatric Surveillance Program released its own survey in August and found 10 children have died from using devices like e-scooters and e-bikes in 2025.
Meanwhile, sales for the electric rides have more than quadrupled in Canada since 2019, with roughly 372,000 e-bikes and 76,000 e-scooters sold so far this year, according to Statista.
Marketing to kids 'deceiving' parents, doctor says
The youngest age recommendation the Marketplace journalists found was at Canadian Tire — a Razor e-scooter that hits a maximum speed of 16 km/h and is recommended for children who are eight or older.

"That just boggles my mind. Kids at this age don't necessarily have the developmental ability to maneuver these motorized vehicles," said Kam, who is also president of the Canadian Paediatric Society's emergency medicine section.
"It's very concerning that there's this huge market for selling children these motorized vehicles, essentially, and deceiving the parents and family, marketing them as toys."
Doctor says kids 16 and under shouldn't ride e-bikes, e-scooters
Razor, the manufacturer of that particular e-scooter at Canadian Tire, said in a statement its device meets U.S. safety guidelines that say eight-year-olds can operate slow-moving motorized vehicles.
The company said its e-scooter is safe when properly used, isn't meant to be on public roads and that riders should follow local laws.

In statements to Marketplace, Best Buy, Canadian Tire and Emmo said customers should follow local laws. Best Buy said rules for e-bikes and e-scooters are evolving and that it tries to keep product information updated.
Costco didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.
E-bike stores can modify speed controls
At an EZbike location in Richmond Hill, a salesperson told undercover journalists it sells e-scooters that can reach 120 km/h — a speed that could get you a ticket on most highways.

At other stores, some e-bikes have their speed limited to 32 kilometres, adhering to Ontario's rules. But when asked if they modify vehicles, a salesperson at an Emmo location in Toronto said yes, they could modify a bike to go up to 150 km/h for off-road use.
"That's horrible," said Pasquali, of CEBA, who owns his own e-bike store in Hamilton.
Emmo and the company that operates the Emmo stores Marketplace visited said in a statement that a product's technical capabilities should not be confused with what's allowed on the roads.
But as an employee at an Emmo in Vaughan, Ont., described it: bypassing the speed limiter is "just like a toggle switch."
E-bike stores can modify speed control
Passing on that kind of advice is "extremely unethical," Pasquali said.

"If you're showing consumers how to push a button and make it faster or offering to modify it to go faster with the caveat that you keep it off road, well, that's technically right. But most consumers aren't doing that, right?"

A salesperson at an Amego store in North York, Ont., went a step further, unlocking the 32 km/h speed limit in front of undercover journalists and revving the motor, showing the e-bike exceeding the speed limit and saying it could hit a top speed of roughly 50 km/h.
Amego said in a statement it does not offer or perform modifications, and its salesperson likely exaggerated the top speed.
EZbike didn't comment on Marketplace's findings.
Mom wants change after son's devastating injury
Amy Richards, of St. John's, became one of those parents pleading for change after watching her son spend 102 days in the hospital after losing control of his e-scooter.
Jayden King, 14, was riding his e-scooter on a quiet street in May when he hit a speed bump and lost control.

King's mom says he was wearing a helmet at the time of the accident but suffered a traumatic brain injury. He spent 21 days in a coma and had to have part of his skull surgically removed due to brain swelling. Once he's healthier, King will have to undergo another surgery to get the rest of his skull put back in place, Richards said.
Mom wants change after son's devastating e-scooter injury
He learned to walk, talk and eat again but still lives with a long list of issues, including memory loss.
"I can't remember nothing in my whole life," King said. He says there's not a chance he'll ride an e-scooter again.

Newfoundland and Labrador has no rules governing e-bikes or e-scooters, but a spokesperson for Government Services said in a statement that it has consulted the public and is looking at changes to the Highway Traffic Act to include micro-mobility devices.
Richards said it should have happened a long time ago, and no one under 16 should be able to ride one.
"We need to protect our children. That should come first and foremost," she said.
Pasquali says the federal government needs to step in and stop the sale and importation of e-bikes and e-scooters that can be modified with the flick of a switch.
Safety is top priority, federal minister says

Canada's Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon told Marketplace in an interview in late September that he has heard stories of people being injured riding e-bikes and e-scooters, and he wants to talk to his provincial counterparts about how to respond.
Most of the legislation governing e-bikes and e-scooters is provincial, he said, and there is "impetus" for provinces and municipalities to act.
But, MacKinon also said the federal government needs "to absolutely consider what we will do in terms of regulating the safety of those devices."
"We'll always work with safety in mind. Safety is our principal priority."

articles.title: Why your Habs tickets cost more than any other NHL team's this season
articles.summary: Montreal Canadiens fans wanting to see their team play at home this season will have to pay a premium for tickets, with average prices at the Bell Centre higher than anywhere else across the NHL.

image.caption: Montreal Canadiens fans pack the area outside of the Bell Centre during the 2026 playoffs. (Ivanoh Demers/CBC/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal
Montreal Canadiens fans wanting to see their team play at home this season will have to pay a premium for tickets, with average prices at the Bell Centre higher than anywhere else across the NHL.
Canadiens claim title for priciest tickets, with average home ticket cost over $220
Move over, Toronto.

Following a successful year that saw the Montreal Canadiens reach the Eastern Conference final, tickets to see the Habs play at home this season will be the most expensive in the NHL — a new feat for the historic franchise.

According to sports betting and online casino research firm Bookies.com and TicketData.com, a website devoted to tracking resale ticket prices, Canadiens fans will pay an average of over $220 for cheapest tickets — more than double the league average — to see their team in action this season.

Montreal is one of the biggest markets in the NHL, and the Canadiens consistently rank in the top five among priciest tickets in the league, with the Toronto Maple Leafs leading the pack most seasons over the past decade.
Moshe Lander, a sports economist and associate professor at Concordia University, says although Habs fans might not be happy about the high ticket costs, they shouldn’t be surprised.
“Unfortunately for Montreal Canadiens fans, a little bit of success is the type of thing that reawakens a lot of dormant fans.”
3 things fans should know about the Montreal Canadiens this NHL season

After starting a rebuild in 2021 that saw the Canadiens finish at or near the bottom of the standings three years in a row, Montreal reached the playoffs in each of its last two seasons, and a skilled young core is driving a renewed sense of excitement around the team.
Lander says it is also driving ticket prices up.
“It’s in demand like anything else,” he said.
'It used to be more accessible,' fan says

Habs fan Melissa Plett has been attending games at the Bell Centre since she moved from Manitoba to Montreal 15 years ago, but current prices are making her think twice about buying a ticket this season.
Plett says she understands why ticket prices are going up, but as the team continues to improve, she worries die-hard fans will be priced out of the rink.

“I feel like it used to be more accessible,” Plett said. “Even when you go down [to the boards] for warm-up and then you have to leave because the ticket owners come down. It definitely feels like it’s the elites or whatever you want to call them that can afford that down there.”
Plett says playoff tickets are even more inaccessible.
“You keep wondering which game you should pay for because these tickets are so expensive,” Plett said. “It’s become such a gamble on your money.”
Is it cheaper for Montreal Habs fans to make the trip to Buffalo than the Bell Centre?
For other fans, like Sunil Peetush, it’s worth the gamble.
“It is the hottest ticket in town. It is the big show in Montreal, so you’re expected to pay a premium,” he said.
Peetush, who is a season ticket holder, says he maintains that it is a good deal to see the Habs play in Montreal — if you can get tickets before they hit the resale market.
His season tickets come out to less than $200 per game. “I see them selling on the aftermarket sometimes $600 to $1,000 a seat where I am sitting,” Peetush said.

items: Quebec is tightening rules around reselling tickets. But changes won't address soaring prices

blocks.text: While the team doesn’t have any say in resale prices, Canadiens owner Geoff Molson wrote in a statement to CBC News that the organization aims to make games accessible to as many fans as possible.

At the start of each season, it releases thousands of tickets to the public, including discounted options for families and students. A limited number of tickets for upcoming games are also released on the 15th of each month.

The same seats sold directly by the organization are consistently cheaper than those on the resale market, but Plett says they go so quickly, she doesn’t even bother trying to get into online ticket queues.
“Even if I tried to get on that… chances are I'm not going to be the one to buy them and then I forget about it and I miss out,” she said.
Secondary market booming
Earlier this year, Quebec cracked down on resale markets when it passed a law requiring platforms to disclose when tickets are being resold.
But critics say it still comes up short in lowering prices for consumers on the secondary market.
Unlike similar legislation in Ontario, the Quebec law doesn’t include a price cap on resale tickets, which allows resellers to charge inflated prices much like an unregulated market.

When faced with criticism, Justice Minister Simon Jolin-Barrette defended his government’s decision to stop short of introducing a price cap on resale tickets, arguing that it would create an illegal market.

items: Ontario starts crackdown on ticket resale above face value

blocks.text: In the Canadiens’ case, the law, which came into effect Sept. 12, has so far done little to limit illegal resale markets.

Although the organization’s terms and conditions state holders must resell their tickets exclusively through Ticketmaster, the team’s official marketplace, fans looking for seats can still find them on a number of other ticketing sites or through social media groups dedicated to reselling and buying Canadiens tickets.
High interest paired with a healthy resale market means the price to see the Habs play at home likely won’t decrease any time soon.
Still, Peetush says this season’s high get-in price at the Bell Centre will be worth it most nights.
“The team is so dynamic, it’s so young, the building is just topping… I guarantee you if they win, you’ll be hyped for a week."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Boshko Maric is a journalist with CBC Montreal. He loves to report on arts and culture and is also a jazz musician. You can send him an email at boshko.maric@cbc.ca

articles.title: Why are B.C. firefighters still using wildfire data from the 1990s?
articles.summary: Prolonged drought in B.C.'s Southern Interior has led to explosive wildfires that current modelling software struggles to predict. It's partly because the data that informs these computer models was…

image.caption: Neal McLoughlin, superintendent of predictive services at the B.C. Wildfire Services, surveys the burn scar of the Pear Lake wildfire, near Clinton, B.C. The fire was the largest in the province this season and experienced several pyrocumulus cloud events. (Georgie Smyth/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada

Prolonged drought in B.C.'s Southern Interior has led to explosive wildfires that current modelling software struggles to predict. It's partly because the data that informs these computer models was collected at least 30 years ago, when extreme fire behaviour, driven by events like prolonged drought — a feature of climate change — was less common.
Forecasters say prediction models are underperforming during province's extreme fires

Neal McLoughlin, superintendent of predictive services with the B.C. Wildfire Service (BCWS), is trying to get one of B.C.'s most challenging fires, the Bald Range wildfire, to behave in his modelling software the way it did on the ground in the Okanagan Valley on Aug. 7.

On his computer, he's turning up the dials for extreme fire behaviour, replacing the forest fuels with more flammable types, programming a stronger wind from the west and swapping local topography of a downward sloping hill with a flat landscape.

Only with those interventions do his simulations get close to what actually happened on the ground that night in Summerland, when more than 12,000 people were forced to flee as flames rushed toward the town in mere hours. One woman died in the chaos.
"Observed fire behaviour is doubling what our models would otherwise predict," said McLoughlin.

It's partly because the data that informs these computer models was collected at least 30 years ago, when extreme fire behaviour, driven by events like prolonged drought — a feature of climate change — was less common.

The challenge is especially pronounced in B.C.'s Southern Interior region, officially the driest place in Canada, according to the Canadian Drought Monitor, in a wildfire season that saw less area burned than average, yet was one of the most devastating seasons on record for property destruction.

BCWS specialists look to their model predictions the way most of us consider a weather forecast. In their case, they're co-ordinating a response to a wildfire, thinking about how quickly it might spread and how their tactics and safety plan should change around that. It's part of the larger toolbox, on top of human resources, BCWS uses to evaluate and dedicate resources to wildfires.
While it's a conceptually robust prediction system, based on more than 100 years of data collection and analysis, even its website states it "was last updated in the early 1990s."
Trusting the models

In practice, McLoughlin says, his team have learned to become more skeptical of the model's predictions on those exceptionally hot and dry days, when even decades of high-grade data cannot overcome their own instincts that a wildfire could be significantly worse than the models say.

Ultimately it's people that make decisions about how to respond to a wildfire, not models, and on those fire-prone days McLoughlin has begun training his team to really apply their lived experience of past extreme fires. On some days, he says: "I don’t trust the models on this day. I expect it's going to do something very different."

"Black swan events" is what Chelene Hanes, a research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service (CFS), calls those unpredictable fires, which fall outside what years of fire science has taught practitioners like her.
The basis of the prediction software is the Canadian Forest Fire Danger Rating System (CFFDRS), which forms the foundation of how agencies across the country evaluate the potential of wildland fires.

Hanes says updates to the Fire Behaviour Prediction System, part of the modelling that forecasters use, could be rolled out by 2029, but including new data from these more aggressively burning fires is unlikely because it's both very expensive and dangerous to collect.

"A lot of it is reanalysis of data that was collected over numerous decades because it is really good data," she said. "But we do need to collect more information because we are trying to stretch our capabilities with the models with our knowledge of physics and math in the fire environment."
Deeper and hotter

McLoughlin took us close to the ignition point of B.C.'s largest wildfire this summer, the Pear Lake Wildfire, near Clinton — a fire that had the hallmarks of behaviour that needs to be more accurately modelled.

The fire, which eventually scorched an area larger than Greater London, burned through more than 100 structures and, from where we stood, seemingly all the pines on the hill across from us, leaving a strange landscape of thousands of blackened stumps, standing like tiny spent matchsticks.

There's a lot of evidence of the impacts of drought, McLoughlin said as he walked through some of the burn scar. He pointed to 30-metre-tall trees that had burned from the top right down to the root plates, leaving huge holes in the ground, and other trees spotted black and yellow — so-called "leopard or cheetah trees," a phenomenon also observed in the Jasper wildfire — when a fire burns so hot bark explodes off the trunk in patches.
Persistent drought means fires burn deeper and hotter, he said.

These are the kinds of conditions that can lead to a convective or column-driven fire, best known by their distinctive tall pyrocumulonimbus clouds that can look and act like huge thunderstorms as superheated gases and debris are pushed skyward, sometimes mixing in air from the upper atmosphere.
It used to be something you'd see once in your career, said McLoughlin. B.C.'s 2023 season had close to 100.
The fire ground we were standing in had multiple pyrocumulus events, one of them with lightning, which started a new fire that eventually merged together.
"Those were not the conditions we collected data for," says McLoughlin.
Predicting the behaviour of a column-driven fire is simply "not part of our old systems," he said, as opposed to a more horizontal wind-driven fire where the models "do a great job."
Lack of data on extreme conditions
The last time that modelling software had a major update was 1992, but it's not as straightforward as putting some newer numbers in a spreadsheet said Hanes, from the CFS.

The capacity to do the kind of science where a timer could be put in the ground to measure the spread of a fire or infrared cameras could be used to look at the intensity of a fire is hard to imagine occurring in a life-threatening situation like the Bald Range or Pear Lake wildfire.

Even experimental burns — which is how scientists studied fires that informed the prediction systems used today — are too dangerous under the extreme conditions they're experiencing, according to Hanes.
"We don't have a lot of data on the extreme end," Hanes said, because the risk of an experimental blaze getting out of control during extreme conditions is just too high.

So, Hanes says they're often "piggybacking" their research on prescribed burns, though she admits many didn't happen this year because the season got too busy. They're also collaborating with some research groups like NASA whose planes can fly through fire storms to collect data.

McLoughlin says he's been asked multiple times about BCWS using artificial intelligence to help predict these new, seemingly unpredictable wildfires, but for him it still comes back to collecting more contemporary data.
"If we're not making an effort to collect that data on the ground to inform these models, they're not going to make good predictions," he said. "It's as simple as that."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Georgie Smyth is a CBC Network Reporter and Producer in Vancouver. She's worked for BBC World News in London and for Nine News in Australia. She's focused on local, national and international stories that affect all Canadians. Got an idea or story tip? Email: georgina.smyth@cbc.ca

articles.title: In Gaza, a UN cash-for-work program gives Palestinians some income — and hope
articles.summary: The UN World Food Program's cash-for-work program helps provide stable work and income for Palestinians in Gaza, who have with little to no other options.

image.caption: The UN World Food Programme has been running a cash-for-work program in Gaza since April, offering people the opportunity to work for three months at a factory, repurposing aid materials into tote bags and furniture. (Mohamed El Saife/CBC)

blocks.text: World·New
The UN World Food Program's cash-for-work program helps provide stable work and income for Palestinians in Gaza, who have with little to no other options.
Participants spend 3 months with program repurposing aid materials

In a factory in Gaza City, dozens of women sit in chairs lining the back room, picking at the stitches on bags of flour. Periodically, two of them will huddle together around a small wood table, holding both ends of one bag as a third woman cuts it in half with a pair of scissors.
There’s some chatter in the air, but the women mostly work in silence. They are turning the sacks into tote bags, folding, cutting and sewing them into the final product.
At another part of the factory, other women oversee the last step. They sit in pairs at each sewing machine, and one folds the handles of the bag together while the other sews them on.

They are part of what's known as a cash-for-work program, meant to give displaced people temporary employment. This one has been run by the UN World Food Programme (WFP) since April, and offers people in Gaza the opportunity to work for three months at a factory, repurposing supplies originally given as aid, like bags of flour and wood pallets. Participants are paid 1,000 shekels a month, the equivalent of about $462 Cdn.
Palestinians in Gaza find jobs — and support — through World Food Program initiative

The money doesn't go very far, covering about a week's worth of groceries and living essentials for some families. Still, for participants, it's a source of income as well as purpose in a territory that has been ravaged by war.
“I really wanted to have a job; I really wanted to have money to spend because my husband is sick,” Warda Aliwa, 38, told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife.
“These bags of flour come to us as support from outside.... After they are emptied, why should we throw them away?” said Aliwa. “We make them into a bag and we put food in them.”

items: Palestinian death toll in Gaza war rises above 74,000 since war began
UN rights chief says uncovered remains in Gaza raise concerns of war crimes

blocks.text: 'I can stand on my own two feet'
For some, the job means they’ll be able to feed their families for a while. Nisreen Abbas, 54, cares for her 12 grandchildren and her 87-year-old husband, who is on a wheelchair.
“Thank God, I can stand on my own two feet,” she said. “I bring food for my grandchildren; I bring medicine for my husband.”

Though temporary, the work is a welcome opportunity for many. Israel and Hamas have been under a ceasefire agreement since October 2025, but the impact of the war has decimated Gaza's economy. About 78 per cent of Palestinians in the enclave were unemployed last year, according to United Nations Trade and Development, with that figure shooting up to more than 90 per cent for the working-age population.

At the same time, it has become challenging for people to obtain everyday goods. Despite more commercial and aid trucks arriving over the summer, three-quarters of households reported difficulties accessing markets, largely due to cash shortages and high costs, according to the UN WFP's August report.

items: This 11-year-old does gymnastics atop the rubble of Gaza as the war rages on

blocks.text: Faten Abu Sharkh, the project’s co-ordinator, says there are approximately 113 women and 20 men involved in the program, which will be renewed annually. The products they create are given to people and schools for free.
She said the women have seen a positive change in their lives because of the program.
“They worked on this project in order to change their mentality and give them financial, social and mental support,” she said.
“They had depression and they were given medication but thank God, the work changed their mentality.”
Some normalcy after tremendous loss
Nearby in a different part of the factory, men work on wood pallets that once carried aid, carefully taking them apart with crowbars.
They sort and throw out the broken pieces, working with the ones still intact. They sand the wood down, cutting and putting it together to create small tables and shelving units for those in need.
Khaled al-Kurd, 50, lost his wife, his daughter, his home and his sewing business in the war.
“It was a total collapse for me,” he said. “Total destruction.”
But he said this job helped bring him back to some semblance of normalcy.
“There is a small amount of resources, but it helps us in life."

items: At least 21 killed in Gaza, including many children, as unstable building collapses
Is Israel erasing evidence of alleged war crimes in Gaza? A visual investigation

blocks.text: Once participants' time with the WFP is over, they will have to find their way on their own. Many already wish they can get another chance with the program.
“I would like for this to be renewed, for us to keep working and for the income to keep coming to us,” said Aliwa. “We are doing something beneficial.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yasmine Hassan is a producer in CBC's Ottawa bureau. From there, she covers developments inside Gaza and the West Bank related to the Israel-Hamas war. If you have a story idea, send news tips in English or Arabic to yasmine.hassan@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Amid the push to build Canadian, a Quebec train factory is booming
articles.summary: A Quebec train factory battered by years of layoffs is expanding as governments push to buy Canadian. Alstom's La Pocatière plant is hiring and scaling up for major domestic rail contracts, including…

image.caption: A worker at Alstom's factory in La Pocatière, Que., works on a door panel for Vancouver's SkyTrain. The plant is seeing more work as contracts for Canadian transit projects increase. (Alexandre Silberman/CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

A Quebec train factory battered by years of layoffs is expanding as governments push to buy Canadian. Alstom's La Pocatière plant is hiring and scaling up for major domestic rail contracts, including a $4.7-billion VIA Rail project.
Once on the brink of possible closure, Alstom's plant in La Pocatière, Que., is now growing
For Claude Michaud, the increasingly loud buzz of machinery, welding and ringing steel is a source of optimism at the train factory where he has worked for much of the past 34 years.

The Alstom plant in La Pocatière, Que., a community of about 6,000 people, has endured waves of layoffs and uneven production over the past two decades. But amid a wave of new Canadian projects, the plant is expanding its factory floor and preparing to hire more staff.
"There's pride in building trains at home for people here in Canada," Michaud said in French. "It's a positive change."

Alstom, a French company whose Americas headquarters is in Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville, Que., is seeing a rise in orders amid a push by all levels of government to buy Canadian. The company completed its acquisition of Bombardier's rail-building division in 2021.

The company is building rail cars for Vancouver's SkyTrain, subway trains for the Toronto Transit Commission and vehicles for a new Quebec City tramway. It will soon begin work on a $4.7-billion contract to build long-distance passenger cars for VIA Rail.

In La Pocatière, 140 kilometres northeast of Quebec City, the plant has long been one of the region's largest employers and an economic driver. But it became heavily dependent on export projects, often for the United States.

The number of employees at the plant — more than 1,000 in the 1990s — fell to about 150 in 2021, according to Alstom and the union. The decline threatened the economic viability of keeping the facility in operation. Now, there are about 550 employees and the company is preparing to grow.
A shift toward buying Canadian
Olivier Marcil, Alstom's vice-president of public affairs for Canada, said increasingly protectionist manufacturing policies in the U.S. effectively closed the door to the market south of the border.

The U.S. Federal Transit Administration Buy America policy requires projects receiving federal funding to use materials and final products, including buses, trains and ferries, manufactured in the United States. The threshold of percentage of domestic components was raised between 2016 and 2021.

"When you look at the megatrend that we've experienced over the last decades — the United States were asking a lot from manufacturers to build local, right? While Canada was not asking anything," he said.
"If everybody's protecting their industry, everybody's nurturing their industry — Canada must come at par with those and do the same."
Rebuilding manufacturing capacity
Dan Breznitz, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, said there are challenges to restoring manufacturing in sectors such as rail.
He said Canada needs to be more strategic about which industries it chooses to invest in as part of a return to manufacturing.

"We have to find the people, we have to find the manufacturing, we have to find the other factories that produce everything that you need to make rail," said Breznitz, who studies how innovation and government policy affect industries.
"The problem is, if you don't do it for 20 to 30 years you lose the skills."
Nearly a decade of work
For Alstom, the VIA Rail project will generate manufacturing work for nearly a decade, with additional employment supported by a 15-year agreement for technical support and spare parts.
The new long-distance train cars will be built in La Pocatière, with final assembly in Thunder Bay.
Frédéric Platteeuw, Alstom's site manager in La Pocatière, said the facility will have to scale up and adapt to focus entirely on the contract for the Crown corporation.
"It's a real challenge, such a project, because it will push us to rethink all the layout," he said. "To optimize our surface, to optimize our work, to develop new technology."

For employees like Michaud, the new contract signals a long-awaited shift from the federal government. As a union leader, he pushed for years for the federal government to introduce Canadian-content requirements for trains.
A major blow came in 2018, when a $989-million contract for VIA Rail's Quebec City-Windsor corridor fleet was awarded to German company Siemens, which built the train cars in California.

Michaud followed in the footsteps of his father, who built the first cars to roll out of the plant for the Montreal Metro. He said it's refreshing to see the plant, where other members of his family work, come back to life with Canadian projects.
"We see that the government is finally listening," he said. "A dollar invested in Quebec and in Canada is money that stays in our country."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandre Silberman is a national reporter for CBC News, based in Montreal. He's worked in CBC bureaus across Canada, including stops in Saskatchewan and New Brunswick. You can reach him by email at: alexandre.silberman@cbc.ca

articles.title: It's the biggest Alberta separatist account on the internet. It has links to a movement leader
articles.summary: The account Rise of Alberta is anonymous and drives four times as much engagement as the next most popular account.

image.caption: The most influential social media account on Alberta separatism is called Rise of Alberta, and it has ties to independence leader Keith Wilson. (CBC News Graphics)

blocks.text: One of the most influential voices on Alberta separatism is not a politician or even a clearly-identified person at all, but a combination social media account and merchandise line that is among the independence movement’s breakout stars.

The RiseOfAlberta account was created in the spring of 2025 and describes itself as “accelerating Alberta’s journey towards independence.” Since then it has amassed almost 100,000 X followers with a firehose of shareable clips and AI-generated memes about Alberta.

“They’ll depict, for example, eastern Canadians as very bureaucratic, government loving people, whereas Albertans are these Wild West people that hate government and love building,” says Chris Ross, a senior analyst at the Media Ecosystem Observatory, a research initiative that studies Canada’s online world and recently released a report into the dominance of separatist influencers.
“It’s a very idealistic, utopian perspective of what their idea of an Albertan is.”

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: In between separatist talking points, the account dabbles in the conspiratorial side of the movement, posting images of Alberta workers standing up to “globohomo,” derogatory online slang for the 2SLGBTQ+ movement, echoes Donald Trump’s call to see “mass immigration” as an “existential threat to Western civilization" and refers to climate change as “fake and gay.”
Many points are punctuated by an ad for an Alberta-branded blanket or hat.

Distrustful of mainstream institutions, some in Alberta’s separatism movement have constructed their own online world populated by independence-minded influencers. Within that, Rise of Alberta is a behemoth, driving four times the engagement of the second-most popular account, according to the report. (The account is aware of this, based on a response to a curious American back in January: “I’m the biggest Alberta Independence account on X,” it wrote. “Happy to chat.”)

But as the account has grown its influence, the person behind the curtain has remained a mystery. The account has not responded to curious social media users, nor did it respond to direct messages sent by CBC News and Radio-Canada asking about the account’s identity.

It’s also not clear where the money from the premium camo hoodies and charcuterie boards is going, though the account has said that the proceeds help cover the costs of the “tools” used to make its graphics.
Now, CBC News has found that the account has links to another heavyweight figure in the separatist movement, Keith Wilson, a lawyer who leads the Alberta Transition Council.

According to an analysis by CBC News and Radio-Canada, the same email address was used to set up the Rise of Alberta website, the site where merchandise is sold, and the website for one of Wilson’s companies and the site for the Alberta Transition Council.

When asked by CBC News, Wilson said that he was pleased that the account was so successful, and that it had come up with some “incredible, interesting and funny ads.” But he was clear he was not the one behind the account: “Not everybody’s interested in being famous, right?” he said.
“I can tell you, it’s not me.”

In a followup call and email, Wilson acknowledged that he knows the person behind the account, explaining that it was run by the person who had set up his websites — “a website designer and webmaster” — which was why the same email had been used.
He “clearly” had a relationship with the person, he said, but he declined to provide more detail or to identify the person.
“The individual has chosen to engage in political commentary anonymously,” he wrote. “I respect that choice.”
Wilson stressed he had no say over the content Rise of Alberta posted and had "nothing to do with" the money the store was making.
He does provide some assistance to the person running the Rise of Alberta account, he said, including listing its merchandise on the “store” tab of his personal YouTube channel.
“I let him do that,” he said. “It doesn’t cost me anything and helps him.”

Returns of unwanted Rise of Alberta merchandise are also sent to the mailing address for his law firm, he said, though he added there weren’t many. (“Those blankets are amazing,” he said. “I have three.”)

While the person posting on the Rise of Alberta account remains unclear, they frequently share video clips of Wilson, and comment positively on his activities in the separatist movement. With the launch of Let Alberta Decide in June, the account posted that it was “incredibly encouraging” that Wilson was helping lead a “serious campaign.”

Wilson, who has publicly debated former premier Jason Kenney on the topic of independence, is also very active online, but strikes a different tone. He tweets clips of his own commentary and links to articles from the news sites dismissed by Rise of Alberta as “fake news.” The post pinned to the top of his page quotes the French Enlightenment philosopher Voltaire.

Rise of Alberta “constantly amplifies Keith Wilson’s posts, essentially acting as a campaign tool, but without any of the normal consequences,” says Ross, who was the lead author of the Media Ecosystem Observatory’s recent report on separatism influencers.

This is particularly notable because Rise of Alberta is “by far” the most influential account driving the conversation about separation, Ross said. The recent report found the account is single-handedly driving 11.8 per cent of all online engagement about the upcoming referendum, he said.
One in five of the images posted by the account is an ad for merchandise, according to an analysis by researchers from Common Ground at the University of Alberta.

The second most influential account, according to the report, is Keith’s personal X account, meaning the two accounts get almost 15 per cent of the online shares, likes and comments on separatism-related content.

In a normal election, party leaders would be scrutinized over their online campaign materials, Ross said. But because there are no elected politicians championing the separatist side, that vacuum has been filled by highly active, anonymous social media accounts, he said.

“The movement is structurally revolving around the Rise of Alberta account online, but no democratic form of scrutiny can interface with it,” he said. “It is bizarre, but the result of a modern campaign organized outside of party politics.”

(Wilson disagrees with this characterization, pointing out that he has more than 80,000 followers and many other big accounts interact with his posts. Besides which, he says, the separatism movement predates the Rise of Alberta account.)
‘Slopaganda’: University researchers study AI videos promoting Alberta separatism
Last November, a social media user pointed out the similarities between something Wilson and Rise of Alberta posted, and questioned whether they were the same person. Both accounts denied it.
“It’s not, but I am flattered,” Rise of Alberta posted with a cowboy emoji.
“I am too,” Wilson responded.

CBC News and Radio-Canada were able to link the Rise of Alberta website and Keith Wilson via the emails used to set up their respective websites by using DomainTools, a web analytics tool. An archived version of the Rise of Alberta website also listed the same mailing address as Wilson’s law firm in St. Albert, Alta.

While Rise of Alberta’s website was registered anonymously, meaning the identity of the owner is not publicly displayed, the company hosting it provides an anonymized email address to contact the website’s owner.

That same email address was first used a decade ago to register the website for Veritas Litigation Support, a company founded by Wilson. Starting last year, it has since been used for 16 other websites, most of which are related to Alberta independence.
It was also used for the websites for the Alberta Transition Council, an independence group led by Wilson, and Let Alberta Decide, a registered third-party advertiser co-chaired by Wilson.
The email has also been used to register a site called Rise of Saskatchewan, which is not active.

items: Experts warn betting on Alberta separatism could influence results

blocks.text: Wilson said the person behind Rise of Alberta sets up all of his websites, and he’s not sure why the sites all list the same email.

“I have been using the services of the person who runs that account for my websites for many years, and I don’t track all of the other stuff that they do,” he said. “I just know the stuff they do for me and they’re very good at it.”

The origin story on the Rise of Alberta website says the account began in the spring of 2025 because the person behind the account “had become convinced that Alberta would be better off as an independent country, and [they] wanted somewhere to say it.”

Things really took off after Prime Minister Mark Carney was elected last year, and soon posts were reaching millions of people, the site says. A few months later, followers started asking for merchandise and the store was born. (CBC News sent messages to the Rise of Alberta website and Facebook page, asking about the person running the account, and did not receive a response.)

Wilson says the person behind Rise of Alberta is “highly skilled” and “very creative.” Wilson also said he hadn’t seen the posts in which Rise of Alberta referred to climate change as “fake and gay” or referenced “globohomo,” and reiterated that he had nothing to do with what that account posted.
There’s a cost to being a public separatist in Alberta, Wilson says. There’s the risk to your career, to say nothing of the physical risk, he says. He gets hate mail and death threats, he adds.

“There’s a logical explanation as to why someone would want to remain anonymous, and I’m going to go as far as to suggest it’s almost admirable that the person’s not seeking personal fame, unlike every other social media influencer.”

articles.title: Marcos on school shootings: Everyone has a role to protect kids
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said that protecting children amid the spate of school shootings is everyone's responsibility.

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 3:48pm
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. on Friday said that protecting children amid the spate of school shootings is everyone's responsibility.
Since June, there have been three high-profile school shootings that saw the deaths of students. Marcos spoke about the matter during a visit to Patul Elementary School in Santiago City, Isabela.

“Ngayon po ay nakakalungkot na mayroon tayong nakikita na mga pangyayari sa ilang eskuwelahan. Nangyari po ito, tiyak ako na nabalitaan na ninyo ang nangyari sa Tacloban, nangyari sa South Cotabato, at sa Zamboanga. Ito po ay kailangan po nating bantayan nang mabuti,” Marcos said.
(It is saddening that we are seeing these in several schools. This happened, I am sure you have heard about it, in Tacloban, it happened in South Cotabato, and in Zamboanga.)

“Kailangan po magkasama tayong lahat. Hindi po lamang ang pulis, hindi lamang ang mga teacher, hindi lamang po ang mga magulang, hindi lamang po ang pamahalaan. Kailangan po lahat tayo ay magkaisa at magsama-sama tayo. Bantayan po natin nang mabuti ang ating mga kabataan,” he added.
(We need to be united. Not just the police, not just the teachers, not just the parents, not just the government. We all need to be united, and we need to be together. Let us protect our children.)
Marcos said that the government is doing everything it could to keep kids safe.

During his visit to the elementary school, Marcos also witnessed the rollout of the Kaagapay Program in the Cagayan Valley, which aims to help enable parents to recognize signs of bullying, abuse, and online risks in their children.

Authorities have suspected that the school shooters were influenced by malicious online actors. Debates over regulating social media and online games have ignited, but many experts urged proper and healthy communication between parents and children as a preventive measure.
“Bantayan po natin nang mabuti ang ating mga bata, ang ating mga anak. Bantayan po natin na hindi sila nasasama sa mga ganyang klaseng kagagawan,” Marcos said.
(Let us take care of the kids, our children. Let us guard them so that they are not involved in these things.)

The Tacloban shooting saw the deaths of three children, while the Zamboanga school shooting saw two—including the shooter himself. The latest school shooting, which occurred in South Cotabato, also resulted in three deaths, again with the shooter included. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Polish president to make first-ever visit to PH
articles.summary: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will host Polish President Karol Nawrocki for a state visit from October 5 to 8, the first visit to the Philippines by a Polish head of state, as Manila moves to deepen…

blocks.text: Poland's President Karol Nawrocki speaks during a press conference following a session of the parliament, where the Polish Minister of Foreign Afairs presented the main points of the Polish government's foreign policy in Warsaw on February 26, 2026.
AFP / Wojtek Radwanski

MANILA, Philippines — President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. will host Polish President Karol Nawrocki for a state visit from October 5 to 8, the first visit to the Philippines by a Polish head of state, as Manila moves to deepen its ties with Warsaw.

The visit is "expected to open more opportunities for cooperation" in a wide range of interests, including defense and security, trade and investment, and agriculture, among others, the Presidential Communications Office (PCO) said on Friday, October 2.
Marcos and Nawrocki are also expected to discuss regional and international issues of common interest, the PCO said.

The visit comes after two rounds of high-level talks between the two countries this year: the first meeting of the Philippines-Poland Defense Cooperation Committee in Warsaw in July, and the 7th Philippines-Poland Political Consultations in Manila in September.
25,000 Filipinos in Poland
The Philippines and Poland established diplomatic relations on September 22, 1973.

According to the PCO, ties have grown over the past decade, with Poland becoming an important economic partner of the Philippines. In 2025, Poland ranked as the country's 28th largest trading partner.
Poland is also home to an estimated 25,000 Filipinos.
In July, Poland signed on to the ASEAN Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (TAC), along with Lithuania, Romania, and Sweden.
The four countries acceded to the treaty during its 50th anniversary commemoration in Manila, held under the Philippines' chairship of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

articles.title: Taiwan: first new F-16V fighters arrive amid China threat
articles.summary: The US-made jets, part of an order made in 2019, touched down as concerns grow in Taiwan that support from the United States could be wavering. Washington insists its policy towards Taiwan and China…

image.caption: Concerns are growing in Taiwan that support from Washington could be waveringImage: Ann Wang/REUTERS

blocks.text: Two new F-16V Block 70 fighter jets landed in Taiwan on Friday, the first of a batch of 66 US-made planes ordered back in 2019 as the island nation looks to bolster its defenses in the face of threats posed by neighboring China.
The aircraft, which flew via Hawaii and Guam, touched down at Chihhang Air Base near Taitung on Taiwan's mountainous east coast at midday local time (0400 GMT).
The arrival of the fighter jets was delayed by several months due to reported software issues, and Taiwanese Defense Minister Wellington Koo said more were on the way.
"Of course we won't only have delivered these two by year-end," he told reporters in the capital, Taipei, without providing further details.
"At present, I think aircraft are gradually moving through the production line, and there are also aircraft that have passed tests," he said.
Taiwan fears drop in US support

The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan regarding the United States' commitment to arming Taiwan – and ​a week after US President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

The US insists that there has been no change in policy towards China and Taiwan but Trump has stalled signing off on a new $14 billion package for Taipei. In May, he called it a "very good negotiating chip" in dealings with Beijing, raising fears that Taiwan's security could be traded away.

"We continue standing with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values — that includes Taiwan," said a US State Department spokesperson when asked about the new F-16Vs.

The jets, made by US defense contractor Lockheed Martin as part of an $8 billion sale agreed seven years ago, are equipped with advanced avionics, and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters — but Washington has been unwilling to provide its most advanced fighters like the F-22 or F-35.
Trump floats arms sales to China
The Taiwanese air force, which scrambles on an almost daily basis in response to aggressive Chinese maneuvers, is expected to have over 200 F-16Vs once deliveries are completed.
"China's intention to annex Taiwan by force has never changed," said Defense Minister ​Koo, referring to Beijing's claims that the democratically governed island belongs to China.

The Chinese foreign ministry has not commented on the arrival of the F-16s but US officials told the Reuters news agency that a Chinese invasion before 2028 is considered increasingly ​unlikely in Washington.
Taiwan: locals welcome arrival of F-16Vs

That assessment didn't stop dozens of locals – some equipped with binoculars and long-lensed cameras – gathering near the air base's perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.

"The threat from the CCP has always been there so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities," Eric Chan, a 57-year-old former air force servicemen, told the AFP news agency, referring to the Chinese Communist Party and stating that the F-16Vs will "play a very important defensive role."

"In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement," added Kimi Chi, a 37-year-old salesman from the central city of Taichung who had travelled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft.
"But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots."
As China threat looms, US pausing arms sales to Taiwan

articles.title: I opened cockpit door of plane while being attacked, Indian pilot tells Modi
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar, who was stabbed on the Israel-bound flight, has been hailed as a hero.

blocks.text: Indian pilot Smit Machchhar has said he opened the cockpit door of the Israel-bound Flydubai plane to allow passengers to come in and halt its rapid descent.

In a video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Capt Machchhar said he was on the ground and still being attacked by his co-pilot when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to do something.
"I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he said.
"Others came in and also played a role [in controlling the situation]. I was of course fighting for my own life but at the same time I knew I was not going to let others die," he added.
Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a flight bound for Tel Aviv from Dubai, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
Modi told the captain that "his courage, patience and quick decision-making saved the lives of so many people" and the whole country was proud of him.
The captain, who has also been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken initially to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia.
He was later airlifted to Abu Dhabi where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The Indian embassy in the UAE on Thursday said Machchhar was "in good health and recovering well". Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him.
