articles.title: TIMELINE: How TBS 'evolved' through the years
articles.summary: TIMELINE: How TBS 'evolved' through the years

blocks.text: Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla recently announced the government’s crackdown against members of True Brown Style (TBS) who were allegedly involved in illegal activities, including grooming minors into crimes.
According to him, TBS is entrenched in all local government units (LGUs) in Metro Manila as well as in 78 provinces.

Remulla said the group originated in California 35 years ago and reached the Philippines about 25 years ago as a small group before developing into what authorities now describe as a criminal syndicate.

But TBS Worldwide urged authorities to not generalize all members as criminals, pointing out that many of them are “professionals, workers, parents, business owners, and ordinary law-abiding citizens.” It added that some members have been engaging in charitable works.
According to TBS Worldwide, this is how its group evolved through the years:
1991 - True Blunt Systah emerges

True Blunt Systah (TBS) was formed in 1991 and became rooted in the local hip-hop and street culture of the time. The group developed a strong presence in urban communities and established its own identity and network of members.
1993 - Original Hiphop Posse Brotherhood is formed

The Original Hiphop Posse Brotherhood (OHPB) emerged in 1993 as another street group with links to the local hip-hop scene. Like TBS, OHPB developed its own membership, identity and reputation in different communities.
1994 - TBS and OHPB merge

In 1994, OG Hoodaz of Tandang Sora Hood introduced TBS leader Don Lucas to OHPB’s Joseph Ceñidoza AKA Joseph Saitan and Maynard AKA Dorobo. The meeting eventually led to an agreement between members of TBS and OHPB to join forces.
The collaboration resulted in the formation of True Brown Style 13.
1995 - TBS 13 leadership is formalized
Before Don Lucas moved to West Covina, Los Angeles, California, Saitan and Dorobo visited him to formalize the collaboration and leadership structure of the newly formed group.
Saitan was designated as president.
During this period, Saitan also decided to stop accepting women into the TBS, “believing that their presence caused conflict and strife among the members.”
1995 to 1996 - Internal differences
The merger and name change initially created misunderstandings among some longtime TBS members, particularly those in the North, including Manila and Tondo.
Some members had helped expand TBS in those areas but were initially not included in discussions about the collaboration.
Differences in membership and the greater presence of women in the Galleria area also contributed to misunderstandings between members.
By 1996, the members were eventually informed about the changes and accepted the new structure.
Late 1990s - TBS gains notoriety
True Brown Style 13 continued to expand its presence while also becoming associated with criminal activities, violence, and legal problems, according to the account of TBS Worldwide.
The group's activities resulted in confrontations and strained relationships with some communities.
Early 2000s - Members begin reconsidering their direction
By the early 2000s, some TBS key members began reflecting on the consequences of their involvement in crime and violence.
Increasing incarcerations, violent incidents, and personal losses prompted members to consider changing the group's direction.
2000s - True Brown Style 13 rebrands
The group eventually adopted the name True Brown Style Worldwide.
The rebranding was presented as a break from its previous criminal identity and a commitment to positive change, both in the Philippines and among members abroad.
TBS said its new direction focused on community service, empathy, personal development, and respect for the law.
2026 - Government crackdown

Philippine authorities are now gathering intelligence and hunting down TBS members who were allegedly involved in illegal activities following reports of minors getting involved in criminal activities and school shootings due to bad influences online. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: DFA rejects China's claim over Batanes waters
articles.summary: The Department of Foreign Affairs on Friday, October 2, "firmly and strongly" rejected China's claim that it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in waters off Batanes, affirming that Manila never…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Foreign Affairs on Friday, October 2, "firmly and strongly" rejected China's claim that it has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in waters off Batanes, affirming that Manila never allowed a Chinese research ship to carry out studies there.
The survey vessel Jia Hai Ke 7 was recently spotted about 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, "well within" the Philippines' exclusive economic zone (EEZ), the DFA said.
"The Philippines did not receive any request from the Chinese side and no consent has been given to any Chinese vessel to conduct MSR (marine scientific research)," the department said.
Under Article 246 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), research in a coastal state's EEZ and continental shelf requires that state's consent.
The DFA said the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) was conducting "lawful and routine law enforcement operations" when it responded to the presence of the Chinese vessel.
The department urged China to meet its obligations under international law and to "avoid actions that are counter-productive and undermine efforts to rebuild mutual trust."
Embassy accuses PCG of harassment

The DFA was responding to an October 1 statement by the Chinese Embassy in Manila Deputy Spokesperson Guo Wei, who said the ship was conducting "normal operations in waters under China's jurisdiction" in line with international law, including UNCLOS.
Guo accused the PCG of harassing the vessel and said that doing so had infringed on China's sovereign rights and jurisdiction and endangered Chinese ships and crew.
China "has taken, and will continue to take, resolute measures to safeguard its legitimate rights and interests," he said.

Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, urged Guo to stop meddling and vowed that the coast guard would keep driving away Chinese research ships that conduct research activities in Philippine waters without permission.
The PCG said it had monitored Jia Hai Ke 7 inside the country's EEZ since Monday, September 28.
Among others, Tarriela accused the ship of transmitting false location data, an action called "spoofing," as it lingered near an undersea cable corridor.
In response, on Thursday, October 1, the PCG deployed its flagship 97-meter BRP Teresa Magbanua and a patrol aircraft to the area.

The Teresa Magbanua approached within less than 100 yards of the Chinese research ship and launched a rigid-hull inflatable boat to drive it away, while its personnel repeatedly issued radio challenges.
The Chinese vessel repeatedly maneuvered to evade the Philippine boats, the PCG said.
China Coast Guard vessel 2503 then arrived and issued its own radio challenges.
"The involvement of a China Coast Guard vessel is significant because JIA HAI KE 7 is privately owned," the PCG said in a statement yesterday.

"A government law enforcement ship moving to shield a supposedly private research vessel conducting illegal MSR in another country's EEZ raises serious questions about who JIA HAI KE 7 is really working for," it added.
According to the PCG, the Jia Hai Ke 7 left at around noon, heading north with the Chinese coast guard ship, while the Teresa Magbanua shadowed it to make sure it exited the EEZ.
Rising tension up north
The standoff is the latest friction over the waters around Batanes, the Philippines' northernmost province, which sits between Luzon and Taiwan.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi announced in May that Manila and Tokyo would begin talks to fix the maritime boundary where their EEZs and continental shelves overlap.
China's foreign ministry reacted to these talks and described them as "illegal, null and void," as it argues the area lies east of Taiwan, which it claims as part of its territory.
In June, Chinese scholars at a symposium in Guangzhou claimed Batanes is a natural geographical extension of Taiwan and therefore falls under China's sovereignty.
Beijing did not formally echo the scholars' claim at the time.

blocks.text: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Friday threatened Ukraine with "further measures" if Kyiv does not issue a public apology for revealing that North Korean POWs were sent to South Korea.

What has led to the rift between Seoul and Kyiv?

Prisoner swap: From North to South Korea via Ukraine

South Korea claims that Kyiv violated an agreement to keep the transfer of the two soldiers to Seoul confidential to protect them. However, Ukrainian officials have denied that such an agreement existed.
Ukrainian media on Thursday cited Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as saying that Kyiv is trying to mend ties with Seoul.
"I would not like to call this an incident. Let's say, it's a diplomatic misunderstanding," Sybiha told ⁠journalists ​at an event, according to Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine.
"South Korea is an important country for us. And I very much hope for momentum, continued cooperation, and concrete results that we are indeed achieving with them," he said.

articles.title: Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
articles.summary: Shoko Kawata's maternity leave drew mixed reactions in Japan, a country struggling to lift birth rates.

blocks.text: Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine.
The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September.
Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth.
Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates.

Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics.

But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign".
Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave.

In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family.

"If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said.

While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could.

On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X, external, thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide.
"As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote.
"I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together."

articles.title: Who was Cesar Virata?
articles.summary: Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines" longest-serving finance chief and prime minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., passed away on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
articles.byline: JON VIKTOR D. CABUENAS, GMA News

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:48pm
Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines’ longest-serving finance chief and prime minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., passed away on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
Virata served as finance secretary from 1970 to 1978 and finance minister from 1978 to 1986.
He was the Philippines’ prime minister from 1981 to 1986. He also served as the country’s governor at the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.
As a key figure in economic policymaking, Virata was recognized by the Department of Finance (DOF), among other former secretaries, for his leadership during major crises.
He was at the helm of the DOF when Super Typhoon Yoling and the Great Central Luzon Flood struck the country in 1970.
His death was announced by the Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC), where he served as a director since 1995 and as corporate vice chairperson for 26 years.

Virata was also a longtime educator at the University of the Philippines (UP), where he served as dean of the UP College of Business Administration from 1960 to 1967 and is credited with introducing the Master of Business Administration program.

He graduated cum laude from UP with degrees in Mechanical Engineering and Business Administration before earning a Master of Business Administration in Industrial Management from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

A biography of Virata, “Cesar Virata: Life and Times Through Four Decades of Philippine Economic History,“ was launched in 2014 by economist and educator Gerardo Sicat after 12 years of research and writing.

“He covered all aspects of the tax system – national and local, and also international taxation. His contributions are beyond tax changes. Many of these were in the nature of administrative decisions as well as the infusion of delicate rules and protocols of tax reviews and investigations,” Sicat said in a paper released in 2011.
Virata’s career in government and academe spanned several decades, making him one of the Philippines’ most prominent economic managers of the postwar era. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Friday briefing: How we covered the flydubai incident as it unfolded
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: When a passenger plane plunges 17,000ft amid claims of terrorism, hijacking and geopolitical intrigue, Guardian journalists have to try and separate fact from fiction in…

blocks.text: Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers.

This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more.
This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world.

So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories

items: UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.

Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.
US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night.
AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.
Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned.

blocks.text: In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’

blocks.caption: Assaf Regavim filmed the first widely circulated video from inside the cabin. Photograph: Erik Marmor/Getty Images

blocks.text: International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury.

Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.

Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.”
‘The story changed moment to moment’

William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots.
“I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.”

Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation.

Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.”

Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing.

Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story.

“It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.)
‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’

But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.”

The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that.

This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals.

Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William.

Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu was personally alerted to the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”.
‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’

It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, says Taz Ali, who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.”

Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.”

A woman convicted of murdering a schoolmate 30 years ago has been taken to hospital after surviving two rounds of lethal injections in Tennessee. Christa Pike would have been the first woman to be executed in the state in 200 years. blocks.text: Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become the youngest ever ‘woman grandmaster’ at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board.

Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster.

She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
articles.summary: The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian forces battle rebel fighters across northern region.

blocks.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.

On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.
Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.

It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Addis Ababa accusing Eritrea of supporting an alliance of armed groups fighting the Ethiopian government – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.
Ethiopia said it was expelling 10 Eritrean diplomats who "pose a direct threat to Ethiopia's national security" and would shut its embassy in Asmara.
In response, Eritrea announced on late Thursday that it was severing diplomatic ties with Ethiopia, describing Addis Ababa's decision as "astounding".
"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.
The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people died during that two-year conflict.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of helping the alliance.
A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray also told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines. The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.
But in a rare interview with the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected the accusations.
He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.
The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea. Asmara accuses Ethiopia of pursuing what it describes as an increasingly hostile policy over the Red Sea.
Landlocked Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.
The latest diplomatic confrontation came hours after loud explosions were heard on Wednesday night in Addis Ababa, close to the headquarters of the intelligence service.

A source linked to the opposition alliance told Reuters news agency that its forces had carried out drone attacks in the capital. Ethiopian authorities have not confirmed what caused the explosions, and there have been no official reports of casualties or significant damage.

Residents in two areas of Addis Ababa separately told the BBC that they heard powerful explosions during the night. One resident near the intelligence headquarters said the blast was loud enough to trigger car alarms.

The explosions came hours after Ethiopia's National Intelligence and Security Service imposed an indefinite ban on drone flights over Addis Ababa and surrounding areas, citing the need to protect senior officials, important infrastructure and public events.
Meanwhile, fighting continues across northern Ethiopia.

Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.

The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.

Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.
Independent verification remains difficult because journalists have limited access to the conflict areas and communications across much of Tigray have been disrupted.

The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.

The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.
The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Trillanes: I am not welcome at Senate impeachment court
articles.summary: Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday the impeachment court should be asked why a subpoena was not issued for him to testify for the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:29pm

Former senator Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday the impeachment court should be asked why a subpoena was not issued for him to testify for the prosecution in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In a press conference, Trillanes said he was ready with his testimony.

"Nag-request ang prosecution ng mga isu-subpoena, my name was there last week. Bumalik 'yung mga subpoena ako lang ang wala. Meron bang power na ganyan ang iimpeachment court? May power ba ang presiding officer? They don't have that power kasi diskarte ng prosecution ito. Do not second guess kung ano ba ang itetestify niyan, pakinggan mo muna," he said.

(The prosecution requested for the subpoenas, I was included there last week. But when the subpeona returned, he was the only one left out. Does the impeachment court has that power. Does the presiding officer has that power? They don't have that power because it is a strategy of the prosecution. Do not second guess what will be testified, they should listen first.)
He added the issuance of a subpoena is ministerial.

"Again, bakit hindi mo inisyuhan ng subpoena si Trillanes? Kung ordinary witness ako, hindi niya ako kilala, 'di ba dapat, ano ba, sasabihin n'yo, o sige, gusto nung prosecution, eh di sige. Bakit hindi niya ini-issue? Huwag na tayo umikot pa," Trillanes said.

(Why was a subpoena not issued to me. If I am an ordinary witness whom they do not know, they would say the prosecution wants him to testify so okay, we will issue the subpoena. Why was the subpoena not issued?)

"Sa akin kasi the signal is clear, hindi ako welcome. And by the way, hindi ito collective na parang sinasabi kasi ayaw daw ako ng mga senador. Inisa-isa natin 'yung mga naabutan natin doon. Hindi naman sila nakonsulta kaya next time na may magsabi na kasi may mga ano yung mga senador, don't swallow it right away,” he added.

(For me, the signal is clear, I was not welcome, but this is not a collective sentiment. There were comments that senators do not like me. I asked my former colleagues, and they said they weren’t consulted. So next time someone says senators don’t like me, don’t swallow it right away.)
Trillanes then said that journalists could ask the senator-judges one by one to confirm his account.

“Tanungin ninyo, sino, kasi sabi nung iba hindi naman o kaya better yet, isa-isahin ninyo, Sir, ikaw ba'y kumukontra? Isa-isa ninyo. Ngayon makikita ninyo kung sino talaga ang kumukontra, di ba?,” he added.
(You should ask the senators one by one if they are the ones who are against me testifying for the prosecution.)
It can be recalled that Escudero did not issue a subpoena for Trillanes but said that such decision does not prevent the prosecution from presenting him as a voluntary witness.
The House prosecution panel then dropped Trillanes as one of its witnesses.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President alleging unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a Constitutional provision. —AOL, GMA News

blocks.text: Filtered By: Topstories
News
Published October 2, 2026 1:21pm
Cesar Virata/File photo
Cesar E.A. Virata, the Philippines’ longest-serving finance chief and former Prime Minister under President Ferdinand Marcos Sr., died on Friday, October 2, at the age of 95.
His death was announced by the Rizal Commercial Banking Corp. (RCBC), where he served as a director since 1995 and as corporate vice chairperson for 26 years. No further details were given.

Virata served as finance secretary from 1970 to 1978 and finance minister from 1978 to 1986. He was the Philippines’ prime minister from 1981 to 1986. He also served as the country’s governor to the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

He was also a longtime educator at the University of the Philippines (UP), where he served as dean of the UP College of Business Administration from 1960 to 1967 and is credited with introducing the Master of Business Administration program at the institution. — Jon Viktor D. articles.title: UP scientist on Super El Niño: Prepare for heavy rains, too
articles.summary: Heavy rains and storms remain possible even during generally dry El Niño conditions.

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — A University of the Philippines scientist urged the public to prepare not only for drier conditions expected during a Very Strong El Niño, but also for possible episodes of heavy rain.

Rafaela Jane Delfino of the UP Institute of Environmental Science and Meteorology said the public cannot control when El Niño and La Niña occur or how intense they become, but can take steps to reduce their impacts.

"So naturally occurring itong El Niño and La Niña, and essentially parang hindi natin mako-control kung kailan siya bumabalik, kung gaano siya kalakas. Ang kaya lang natin sigurong maikontrol is kung paano natin mababawasan 'yung impact niya," Delfino said in a video from the University of the Philippines on Thursday, October 1.
("El Niño and La Niña are naturally occurring, and essentially, we cannot control when they return or how strong they become. What we can control is how we reduce their impacts.")

PAGASA said a Strong El Niño is already active in the tropical Pacific and is expected to intensify into a Very Strong El Niño between September and December 2026, then persist through the first half of 2027.
Climate Change Commissioner Albert Dela Cruz has described the developing event as potentially the most severe the Philippines may experience on record.
Heavy rains still possible
While El Niño generally increases the likelihood of below-normal rainfall, dry spells, droughts and water supply stress in parts of the Philippines, it does not mean rain and storms will disappear.

PAGASA's September 23 climate advisory said above-normal rainfall may still occur over the western parts of the country due to the southwest monsoon and tropical cyclones even as generally drier conditions prevail elsewhere.
The Climate Change Commission has likewise warned that intense tropical cyclones, including those reaching super typhoon strength, may still occur during El Niño conditions.

"Maaaring umabot sa kategoryang super typhoon ang mga bagyong ito at magdulot ng malawakang pagbaha," the agency warned. ("These cyclones could reach super typhoon strength and cause widespread flooding.")
Warmer Pacific
Delfino explained that El Niño is characterized by warmer-than-usual sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific.

Under normal conditions, easterly trade winds push warm surface water toward the western Pacific. During El Niño, these winds weaken, allowing unusually warm water to spread eastward across the tropical Pacific.

For the Philippines, this shift generally favors drier-than-normal conditions. PAGASA likewise defines El Niño as the abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific, accompanied by cooler-than-average waters over the Philippine Sea.
"Kaya inaasahan natin, during El Niño conditions, relatively drier sa Pilipinas," Delfino said. ("That is why we expect relatively drier conditions in the Philippines during El Niño.")
Delfino said scientists monitor sea surface temperature anomalies, among other indicators, to characterize the strength of an El Niño event.
She noted that current anomalies in parts of the monitored Pacific are already more than 2 degrees Celsius above normal, a level associated by some scientists with the informal term "Super El Niño."

"Papunta pa lang tayo sa peak. Developing pa lang siya. So kaya siya tinatawag na Super El Niño kasi literally, off the charts," Delfino said. ("We are still heading toward the peak. It is still developing. That is why it is being called a Super El Niño because it is literally off the charts.")
PAGASA, however, officially uses the classification "Very Strong El Niño" and expects the phenomenon to peak toward the end of 2026.
Preparing for both extremes
Delfino said reducing El Niño's impacts begins with understanding the hazards it may bring and preparing accordingly.
For agriculture, she suggested establishing rainwater harvesting systems, particularly in rain-fed areas, and planting drought-tolerant crops.
Water management preparations could include early planning for dam operations and reducing household water consumption.
But preparations should not focus exclusively on drought.
"Pero huwag din nating kalimutan na kailangan pa rin nating maghanda sa malalakas na ulan," Delfino said. ("But let us not forget that we still need to prepare for heavy rains.")

articles.title: UP Rural High School condemns red-tagging following Martial Law remembrance activity
articles.summary: The University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS) in Los Baños, Laguna has condemned the alleged red-tagging of the school and its constituents on social media following its observance of…

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 1:13pm

The University of the Philippines Rural High School (UPRHS) in Los Baños, Laguna has condemned the alleged red-tagging of the school and its constituents on social media following its observance of an institutional activity remembering Martial Law.

In a statement late Thursday evening, UPRHS called out social media posts by Facebook accounts identified as "Emjay Chico" and "Lorraine Baddie" or Lorraine Badoy, former National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC).

The two accounts raised questions about the school activity, which was reported by UPRHS' official student publication, The Ruralite, regarding the University of the Philippines (UP) Day of Remembrance held on September 21.
UPRHS said the annual activity is an institutionalized UP event commemorating the declaration of Martial Law and reflecting on a significant period in Philippine history.
The school said its program was "student-initiated and student-led," properly communicated to parents, and conducted with the necessary permits and institutional approval.
Participation was also voluntary, UPRHS said.
The program included a resource person who discussed the role of the media in addressing historical distortion about Martial Law.
"We categorically reject the use of red-tagging as a means of intimidating, silencing, or casting suspicion upon our students, faculty, and staff," UPRHS said.
The school also rejected insinuations that students were being exploited, saying that keeping learning safe does not mean shielding young people from difficult questions and realities.
"We will continue to nurture students who respect human rights and uphold the fundamental values of truth, justice, and freedom," it said.
As of posting time, The Ruralite disabled comments to its posts on UP Day of Remembrance activities in UPRHS.
In his post, Chico questioned why the high school students were allegedly involved in a political activity inside school premises.
He stressed that while political participation is a right, children must also be protected from exploitation, manipulation, and undue political influence.

"A school should be a safe space for learning, not a venue for using minors to advance political interests. The responsibility of school officials is not merely to facilitate activities, but to protect the welfare, dignity, and rights of every learner," he said.
Badoy reposted Chico's post and said, "UP Rural School in Bay, Laguna HANDS OFF OUR CHILDREN!"
GMA News Online has sought comment from Chico and Badoy but they have yet to provide statements as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Ukraine, South Korea clash over transfer of 2 North Korean prisoners
articles.summary: A diplomatic scandal has erupted over two North Korean prisoners of war, with South Korea demanding an apology from Ukraine. What's been the reaction in Kyiv?

image.caption: The North Korean soldiers, seen here in photos taken at a POW camp in Ukraine last February, had expressed a wish to resettle in South KoreaImage: Kim Hong-Ji/REUTERS

blocks.text: Speaking at the UN General Assembly on September 23, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy sparked a diplomatic dust-up with South Korea.

In his speech, Zelenskyy mentioned that Ukraine had recently "sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea" — men who had been captured by Ukrainian forces during fighting in Russia's Kursk region in January 2025. Both had expressed a wish to resettle in South Korea, he said.

The reaction from Seoul was swift: South Korea's Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador to Seoul, Andrii Vieshkin, and demanded an explanation for what it described as Kyiv's "unilateral disclosure" of the prisoners' transfer, despite a prior agreement to keep the matter confidential, along with an official apology.

blocks.caption: Russia's war in Ukraine has given North Korea the opportunity to strengthen ties with Moscow, in part by sending soldiers to the battlefieldImage: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: Responding to Zelenskyy's speech, South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war was a sensitive topic with wide-ranging consequences for diplomacy and national security on the Korean Peninsula.
Did Kyiv and Seoul have a secret agreement?

Dmytro Lytvyn, Zelenskyy's spokesperson, wrote on Facebook that no such confidentiality agreement existed between the two countries, adding that it was wrong to keep secret where such prisoners were being transferred.

Soon after, South Korean presidential spokesperson Kim Sung-wan called Lytvyn's denials false, according to news agency Reuters. Kim said Ukraine had asked for confidentiality — allegedly over concerns there might be criticism at home if the North Korean prisoners weren't swapped for Ukrainian prisoners being held in Russia.
Seoul had agreed to the secrecy for diplomatic reasons, he added, but also to protect the prisoners and their families who were still living in North Korea.
Missed opportunity to 'improve bilateral relations'

Nataliya Butyrska, an Asia-Pacific expert at the New Europe Center in Kyiv, told DW that Ukraine and South Korea lacked a continuous, trust-based dialogue, especially under the current government in Seoul.
"We should actually be natural partners — we should be standing shoulder to shoulder, with North Korea fighting against Ukraine," she said. "But that's not the case, due to a lack of trust."
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

The prisoner transfer has been a hotly debated topic in South Korean media in the last week — not least because, according to South Korea's constitution, North Koreans are considered citizens of South Korea. It's also been instrumentalized by opposition lawmakers, while President Lee, aiming to ease tensions with the North, has taken a more measured approach.

"The prisoners could have been used by Ukraine to improve bilateral relations between Kyiv and Seoul," said Butyrska, adding that no one in South Korea was now thinking of thanking Ukraine for transferring the prisoners.

Butyrska pointed out that Russia, which usually doesn't express any interest in foreign prisoners, had actually demanded the return of these two North Koreans. "There was even a period of six months when the Russians refused to release any Ukrainian prisoners of war," she said. "They were not prepared to undertake any swap, because they wanted the North Koreans."
Is Ukraine being held hostage by South Korea's domestic politics?

For some observers, the diplomatic crisis can be linked back to domestic conflicts in South Korea. The opposition wants to know why the president agreed to keep the prisoner transfer secret, and have accused Lee of trying to gain favor with the North.

"President Lee Jae Myung was surprised by the incident, and now wants to shift the blame in part on Ukraine," said Mykola Polishchuk, a Korea expert based in Ukraine. He believes the transfer would have become public knowledge sooner or later, and that Seoul knew that Kyiv was going to comment on it. Reports that Ukraine had asked for secrecy were, he added, a way for a frantic politicians in Seoul to come up with an explanation.
"Ukraine has ended up mired in a scandal which it neither wanted nor planned for," said Polishchuk.
North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine

"South Korea has been pursuing the transfer of the prisoners for a long time. And now everybody seems to be happy that those Korean prisoners are in custody," said Shim Sangmin from the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul. "But what really complicates the matter is the fact that the South Korean government is trying to make new ways to reconcile with the North Korean regime." He said Seoul was now worried that this transfer of North Korean prisoners could hamper efforts to reestablish communication between the North and the South.

In his view, the Lee government is "more open to the idea of reestablishing ties" with Russia, rather than continuing to cooperate with Ukraine. "That's possibly one of the reasons why this government is skeptical about containing military cooperation with Ukrainian military forces, even though there would be a definite military advantage for South Korean military forces," he added.
Ukraine shouldn't expect military support from South Korea
Butyrska said the latest developments indicate a likely further cooling of ties between Kyiv and Seoul.

"The South Korean government wasn't particularly friendly toward us to begin with, and will now likely keep its distance," she said, adding that it would have been better for Kyiv to have stayed quiet.

In return for a gesture of goodwill and "quiet diplomacy," she added, Ukraine might have seen support from South Korea in another form — technology, for example, especially via third countries. While South Korea isn't directly selling weapons to Ukraine, it does deliver to Poland, Finland, the Czech Republic and Romania, and it's pursuing further integration with the European military equipment supply chain.

For Polishchuk, any cooperation on military technology between Ukraine and South Korea is out of the question, now and in the future. He believes trade and humanitarian help would continue, however. South Korea, he said, is highly unlikely to side with Russia, especially given Seoul's many obligations toward the United States.
This article was originally written in Ukrainian.

articles.title: Turkey: Stock market scandal hits half a million investors
articles.summary: Asset managers are alleged to have artificially inflated the value of their funds. Turkish authorities have made multiple arrests, and a leading AKP lawmakers has resigned.

image.caption: Turkey's stock market crisis affects almost half a million Turkish investors and has already caused the resignation of a female politician of the AKPImage: Yasin Aras/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Investors in Turkey want one thing above all else: for their money to retain its value. Given inflation of around 30%, that is not exactly easy. As a result, many people are buying gold, foreign currency or stocks and increasingly, mutual fund shares that promise high returns.

But the stock market has become a trap for around half a million Turkish investors. In mid-September, the benchmark BIST 100 index plummeted by 6% in a single day and lost about 12% within just a few trading days.

This sharp drop in stock prices was triggered by a major market manipulation scandal. Approximately 455,000 investors have been affected, more than 45 people have been arrested and a high-ranking politician from the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has resigned.
What happened?

Everything started when some investment fund providers had trouble making timely repayments to investors. Among those affected were funds managed by the companies Pusula Portfoy and Tera. Two Tera funds alone held assets totaling around €6.5 billion ($6.37 billion).

In response, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) intervened and shut down the funds of seven asset managers, including Tera, Pusula and Atlas. According to the state-run news agency Anadolu, a total of 131 funds are set to be liquidated.

The Istanbul Public Prosecutor's Office is now investigating charges of fraud, violations of the capital markets law and the formation of a criminal organization, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek announced.
The suspicion: The fund companies are alleged to have artificially inflated the value of their funds, while in reality their funds contained worthless "junk stocks."
Among the 45 people arrested so far are executives from investment firms. In addition, the assets of 42 individuals and 46 legal entities have been frozen, according to Gurlek on X.
The Istanbul Stock Exchange has also taken action: it excluded 27 stocks from the BIST 100 benchmark index as of October 1.
Will investors get their money back?

The funds are being liquidated: Their assets will be sold and the proceeds distributed to investors in proportion to their fund shares. The deadline for this has been extended from three to six months. According to Aysel Gundogdu, an independent financial advisor in Istanbul, this is intended to reduce selling pressure so that stocks are not sold at fire-sale prices. However, this does not mean that the liquidation of each fund will take six months. Depending on market conditions, it may be completed more quickly.

Only, there is no guarantee. An investment fund is not a savings account and any loss in value affects the investor. Gundogdu expects that money market funds will largely be redeemed. With hedge funds and equity funds holding "junk stocks" that are virtually untradeable, however, the situation could prove more difficult.
It is important to distinguish between market losses and damages resulting from potential irregularities.

Economist and columnist Guldem Atabay emphasized that a distinction must be made between price losses and manipulation: Investors bear the market risk, but they do not have to accept false information, artificially inflated prices, or a lack of oversight.
Are the fund company and managers liable for the damages?
If funds are closed or liquidated, the shares and other securities in the portfolio can be sold. The question is how much they are worth and how easily they can be sold.

Financial expert Gundogdu believes that the fund's assets will not cover investors' claims. Furthermore, she says there have been structural failures. "The crisis is far greater than a simple liquidity crisis. There are flaws in management and oversight."
She therefore considers it possible that the assets of the fund founders and managers could also be tapped to make up for the shortfall.

Economist Atabay calls for those responsible to be identified and for the damages to be recovered from them. Following the liquidation of the funds, it must be clarified who is responsible for any legal violations. "Liquidation is no substitute for accountability," Atabay said.

blocks.caption: Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya of the ruling AKP asked Turkish President Erdogan to resignImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What are the political costs of the crisis?

The crisis has already led to the resignation of a high-ranking female politician in the ruling AKP party. Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, deputy party chair and former minister of family affairs, asked Turkish President and AKP leader Recep Tayyip Erdogan to "relieve her of all her posts." This has been a phrase frequently used within the AKP for years when someone is forced to resign.

She was facing allegations regarding stock transactions by her and her husband, Ilyas Kaya, in connection with the fund crisis. Political responsibility, she wrote on social media, goes beyond legal responsibility. She said her position should not hinder the investigation.

The opposition now intends to bring the issue before Parliament. Selcuk Ozdag, deputy leader of the Yeni Yol parliamentary group, announced that as soon as Parliament reconvenes, he will submit a motion for a parliamentary investigation. The investigation is intended to determine whether politicians are involved in the manipulation scandal.
This article was originally published in German.

articles.title: Trillanes: Firm of VP Sara's husband got P319M from China
articles.summary: Former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV said Friday, October 2, that a food company partly owned by Vice President Sara Duterte's husband took in more than P319 million from China while reporting no…

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 12:26pm
Composite image shows Vice President Sara Duterte as seen in June 2026 and her husband, Mans Carpio, in April 2026.
Duterte office; The STAR / Miguel de Guzman; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — A food company partly owned by Vice President Sara Duterte's husband, took in more than P319 million from China while reporting no rank-and-file employees, Former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV alleged on Friday, October 2.

Trillanes made the claim at a press conference a day after House prosecutors withdrew their bid to present him as a witness in Duterte's impeachment trial. The former senator said he had asked to be dropped to relieve the prosecution of any more pressure and promised to disclose today everything he would have shared during the trial.

The former senator argued the flow of Chinese funds to companies with ties to the vice president had severe national security implications and on its own was enough to impeach and disqualify her from public office.

"Dapat kilabutan po tayo dito... Bawal po iyan. Bawal tumanggap from a foreign government, especially high-ranking official ang vice president," Trillanes said. "Kapag hindi pa ba impeachable iyan, ewan ko nalang. Nagbubulag-bulagan tayo."
Duterte has denied all allegations of possessing unexplained wealth and in April accused Trillanes of repeating the same allegations he has made since 2016, this time with a "machinery backing him."
Cale88's 'red flags'
Trillanes' presentation claims the funds flowed from the Chinese government and Chinese corporations, to Cale88 Foods Corp., a company with ties to Duterte's husband Mans Carpio.

Securities and Exchange Commission Director Gerardo Del Rosario previously testified during the impeachment trial that Carpio was an incorporator, director and shareholder of Cale88 from 2021 to 2024, and that his stake rose to 47.5% in 2024, before disappearing in 2025.

articles.title: DFA strongly rejects China's claim over Batanes waters
articles.summary: DFA strongly rejects China's claim over Batanes waters

blocks.text: Published October 2, 2026 12:15pm
The Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) on Friday rejected the Chinese Embassy’s claim of sovereignty and jurisdiction over the waters off Batanes.
“The Department firmly and strongly rejects the Chinese Embassy’s assertion that China has sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the waters off Batanes,” the DFA said in a statement.
This comes after the Philippine Coast Guard recently warded off a Chinese Coast Guard near Cabra Island in Mindoro.

“... The Department affirms that the Philippine Coast Guard was conducting lawful and routine law enforcement operations in response to a suspected unauthorized Marine Scientific Research (MSR) activity in the waters off Batanes,” it added.
DFA said authorities detected the Chinese research and vessel JIA HAI KE 7 approximately 37 nautical miles northwest of Itbayat, Batanes, well within the Philippines’ Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ).
'No consent'
It emphasized that the Chinese research was conducted without the consent of the Philippines, which is required under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).

“Under Article 246 of UNCLOS, marine scientific research in the EEZ and on the continental shelf shall be conducted with the consent of the coastal State. The Philippines did not receive any request from the Chinese side and no consent has been given to any Chinese vessel to conduct MSR,” DFA said.

In a Facebook post on Thursday, the Chinese Embassy responded to a statement by Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea rear admiral Jay Tarriela, who called on Ambassador Jing Quan to cease asserting claims over Batanes and urged the public not to give in to harassment.
The Chinese Embassy addressed Tarriela, describing his statement as a “baseless accusation” and “nothing but political theater.”
The embassy said that under international law, including UNCLOS, China holds sovereign rights and jurisdiction in the area due to overlapping maritime claims with the Philippines.

“Under international law, including [UNCLOS], China has sovereign rights and jurisdiction over the relevant waters. China and the Philippines have overlapping maritime claims there, and in accordance with international law and the consensus between the two sides, this should be resolved through negotiation,” Deputy Spokesperson of the Chinese Embassy Guo Wei said.

“China firmly opposes the Philippines' illegal actions in waters under China's jurisdiction based on unilateral claims, and will continue to take resolute measures to safeguard its own rights and interests,” he added.

In response, the DFA called on China to abide by its international obligations and refrain from counterproductive actions that hinder efforts to restore mutual trust, adding that it will continue to defend the Philippines’ claim in its EEZ.
“The Philippines will continue to uphold the country’s sovereign rights and jurisdiction in its EEZ peacefully and responsibly in accordance with international law,” the DFA said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: ‘No one disrespects Our Lady’: fears for Brazil’s patron saint grip country ahead of election
articles.summary:
Speculation that Flávio Bolsonaro will try to strip Our Lady of Aparecida of position could become deciding factor in run-up to Sunday

A row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: A row of Biblical proportions has erupted in the run-up to Brazil’s presidential election, with the country’s patron saint, Our Lady of Aparecida, emerging as an unlikely kingmaker in the deadlocked race.
Ahead of Sunday’s vote, the two frontrunners – the leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro – are level in the polls.

But in recent days, speculation that Bolsonaro – son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro – might strip the widely cherished patroness of her position have caused a nationwide outcry, leaving some to question if it could tip the knife-edge election in favour of Lula, who is Catholic.
“It could sway things one way or the other,” said Thomas Traumann, a political analyst who has been tracking the unusual election row.

It remains unclear precisely how the commotion began, but debate over the issue exploded last week when a remark by Bolsonaro, whose movement includes many evangelical Christians, went viral online. In a recent broadcast, the former senator said one of his first acts as president would be to “decree that Brazil belongs to the Lord Jesus Christ”.

Some Catholics took that as a sign that the Protestant politician planned to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida, although only the Vatican – which declared her Brazil’s patroness in 1930 – has the authority to do so.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s rightwing senator and presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro of the Liberal party during a campaign rally in São Paulo. Photograph: Nelson Almeida/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Those suspicions were reinforced by Bolsonaro’s reported links to JB Carvalho, an evangelical leader who has previously called for the patroness’s removal. In 2007, another Bolsonaro ally tried to introduce legislation to the same effect, although the bill was dropped.

Bolsonaro has called claims he plans to unseat Our Lady of Aparecida “fake news”. He alleged the rumours were being spread by Lula supporters, as well as members of the Episcopal Conference of Brazil, a Catholic bishops’ organisation. The conference rejected the charge.

Lula’s leftwing movement has taken advantage of the furore, keenly aware it could hurt the far-right candidate’s chances in a country where nearly 57% of the population is Catholic. With the result expected to be even tighter than the last one – when Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by less than 2% – even a small number of votes could mean the difference between victory and defeat.

Lula has appeared on the campaign trail holding statuettes of the Virgin Mary while his wife, Janja da Silva, has worn a pendant honouring Our Lady of Aparecida. “As long as I’m president, no one will disrespect Our Lady of Aparecida. No one. People need to learn to respect all religions,” Lula told a rally in the Amazon. Lula’s vice-president and running mate, a devout Catholic called Geraldo Alckmin, published a video describing how he had received messages from Catholics “worried about the direction of the country and the terrible news that has been circulating”. Alckmin assured voters he and Lula would preserve and protect “religious traditions, so sacred to Brazilian families”.
The row speaks to the rivalry and tensions between Brazil’s once dominant Catholic church and the evangelical movement, which has grown rapidly since the 80s.

Traumann said: “It touched a raw nerve, which is the growing power of the evangelicals. Evangelicals make up about 30% of the population, but their political power is much greater than 30% – and within Bolsonarismo it is even more significant”.

Traumann believed that, irrespective of whether Bolsonaro really did intend to remove the patroness, the furore had tapped into “a genuine fear among Catholics of being pushed outside the system”. “I have no doubt that this is going to be important [in the election]. [Flávio Bolsonaro] knows it has landed badly,” he added.

Luiz Antônio Simas, a historian and author of the book So Many Marys: Our Lady in Popular Culture, said the outcry “was a symptom of the popularity that Aparecida and the Virgin Mary in general have in the formation of our culture”.

blocks.caption: Lula at a campaign rally in Belem, Brazil. Photograph: Marx Vasconcelos/Reuters

blocks.text: “For Brazilian popular culture, Our Lady of Aparecida transcends altars … She is extremely powerful as a defining element of what we envision Brazilian popular culture to be,” Simas said, noting how Brazil’s “Black Madonna” was present in samba parades, football culture and Afro-Brazilian faiths.

While the debate flared up on the eve of the election, Simas said Our Lady of Aparecida was a long-running point of tension between Catholics and evangelicals, who oppose the Catholic veneration of saints and images. He recalled a major outcry in 1995 when a neo-Pentecostal pastor kicked a statue of Our Lady of Aparecida on TV.

Simas believed religious racism was at the heart of the outcry, given that Our Lady of Aparecida was a black representation of the Virgin Mary. “When all of this comes into contact with a turbulent political context, in a country experiencing the tensions of a highly contested pre-election scenario, all these controversies come to the surface,” Simas added.

articles.title: US pressures EU allies to release diesel stockpiles
articles.summary: The Trump administration has called on its European allies, particularly Germany and France, to release strategic diesel reserves in an effort to ease fuel prices. The EU will hold an emergency…

image.caption: The Trump administration wants Germany and France to release strategic diesel reserves to stem surging fuel pricesImage: Martin Meissner/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: The United States on Thursday told its European allies, particularly Germany and France, to "immediately" release their strategic reserves of diesel to help lower the soaring price of the refined fuel.
It comes after President Donald Trump on Wednesday floated the possibility of banning US diesel exports to stem the rise in prices.
Average US diesel prices have surged over 70% to $6.39 per US gallon (€1.50 per liter) since the start of the Iran war, according to AAA motor club data.
The surging cost of fuel has stoked public anger and intensified anxiety within Trump's Republican Party that it could lose control of Congress in November's midterm elections.
Germany's ADAC motoring club on Thursday reported an average diesel price of €2.409 per liter ($10.25 per US gallon).
Donald Trump blames Ukraine for record US diesel prices
What did US officials say?
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told Fox News on Thursday that he was "highly confident" Europe could ease fuel prices by drawing down emergency diesel inventories.

"This is a time for a coordinated release of diesel stores as we ⁠go into ​to harvest season and we go into winter heating oil season," Wright told the US broadcaster. "Now's the time to bring ​more diesel to the market, and that diesel is available. I think we have some positive news coming."

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington had done its share of an agreement struck in March among International Energy Agency ​members in releasing 172 million barrels of US diesel. "America is doing its part," Bessent said on X. "We look to our allies to match their commitments with action."
"Our European partners should accelerate delivery on their existing commitments and make additional supplies immediately available to address ongoing disruptions," he added.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, meanwhile, said there was an "eagerness on both sides to work together" on the diesel issue.

"We know that France, Germany, and Italy, ‌they're sitting on reserves ... ‌I won't ​put words in their mouth, of course, but ​I think they would love to have ⁠a ​cooperative path ​forward with the United ​States on how ‌we get more diesel ​to ⁠market," Greer told a news conference ⁠in ​Milwaukee.
How did the EU respond to the US demand?

European Union trade chief Maros Sefcovic, who was also attending a two-day G20 trade ministers' gathering in Milwaukee, met with Greer but told reporters that he did not go into details on energy exports.
The EU official said any move by the US to ban diesel exports would be "unexpected for Europeans."
He added that such a ban would have "very dramatic consequences for our economic performance."
Sefcovic said both sides "decided to stay in close touch to avoid any surprises here."

France's minister delegate for international trade, Nicolas Forissier, told the AFP news agency in Milwaukee: "I can't imagine that there will be a ban." He stressed that both sides will "try to find solutions."
Germany's Economy Ministry, meanwhile, said the International Energy Agency, the West's energy watchdog, has not yet asked Germany to release stocks.
On Friday morning, the EU's energy task force will hold an emergency meeting to discuss the situation, a Commission spokesperson said.
The task force is made up of the European Commission and the 27 EU member ​countries.

articles.title: Ex-Sara aide skips NBI appearance, denies Gracioso cash claims
articles.summary: Jefry Tupas says overseas trips contradict parts of Gracioso's sworn account.

blocks.text: October 2, 2026 | 11:47am

MANILA, Philippines — A former aide of Vice President Sara Duterte did not personally appear before the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) after being subpoenaed over allegations that he received cash on her behalf, but submitted a sworn statement denying the claims.

The NBI had ordered Jefry "Jepoy" Tupas, a former Davao City information officer who later worked at the Office of the Vice President, to appear at 10 a.m. on October 1 as part of its investigation into alleged plunder, graft and money laundering.
Tupas' lawyer Toby Diokno told Philstar.com that his client did not appear in person.
"I submitted his sinumpaang salaysay for him," Diokno said in a message.

Tupas' affidavit addresses allegations by dismissed police officer Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., who claimed that he delivered suitcases containing large amounts of cash to Duterte and other individuals on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
The Philippine National Police has confirmed that Gracioso had been detailed as a member of Velasco's security team, but his cash delivery allegations remain under investigation.
In his affidavit obtained by Philstar.com, Tupas denied Gracioso's allegations and said he wanted to be left out of what he described as politically motivated claims.

"Gaya ng sinabi ko na, isa na akong pribadong tao at wala na akong katungkulan na kahit ano sa gobyerno. Dahil dito, gusto ko na nang tahimik na buhay at sana naman ay hindi na ako idadawit muli sa mga gawa-gawang kwento lalo na sa mga kwento na ang lantarang pakay ay paninirang-puri lamang kalakip ng bangayan sa politika," Tupas said.

("As I have already said, I am now a private citizen and no longer hold any government position. Because of this, I just want a quiet life, and I hope I will no longer be dragged into fabricated stories, especially those whose clear purpose is character assassination tied to political infighting.")
What Gracioso alleged
Gracioso's sworn statement identified a "Jepoy" or "Jepoi," whom Tupas said he believed referred to him, as a trusted aide of Duterte when she was mayor of Davao City.

According to Gracioso, his first encounter with Tupas occurred around 2018, when he fetched Duterte from a private hangar in Pasay and drove her to the Diamond Hotel. Gracioso alleged that Duterte accepted a bag of chocolates but instructed him to hand a suitcase containing P20 million to Tupas.
Gracioso claimed that similar deliveries occurred between 2018 and 2020, with suitcases allegedly containing P10 million to P20 million handed either to Duterte or to Tupas when he accompanied her.

He also alleged that before the 2019 midterm elections, he delivered vehicles to Davao for Duterte, including vans he claimed contained cash and gifts, and was instructed to leave the vehicles with Tupas.

In another account, Gracioso alleged that during an April 2019 trip to Marinduque, Duterte directed him to turn over two large suitcases containing P50 million each, or P100 million in total, to Tupas.
Gracioso further claimed that on September 21, 2019, he delivered two more suitcases containing P50 million each to the Diamond Hotel and that Duterte instructed him to hand them to Tupas.
He also alleged making another cash delivery to Duterte and Tupas in Busay, Cebu, during the summer of 2020.

Gracioso's affidavit cited further alleged deliveries in 2021, including an incident in a house at Valle Verde 2 and another involving more than P200 million allegedly transported in two Toyota Grandia vans to the Diamond Hotel.
Tupas disputes timeline
These allegations were all denied by Tupas.
He said he did not receive money, gifts or vehicles for Duterte. He also sought to rebut several of Gracioso's claims by citing travel records and other documents.

On Gracioso's allegation involving two P50-million suitcases in Marinduque in April 2019, Tupas said he had never been to the province and submitted passport records, airline documents and social media posts that he said showed he was in South Korea at the time. Public reports on his affidavit say he left the Philippines on April 18 and returned on April 22.

Tupas also disputed the alleged September 21, 2019 delivery at the Diamond Hotel, saying he was in Japan during the period cited by Gracioso. He submitted travel records and social media posts in support of his account.

He also rejected Gracioso's account of a cash delivery in Busay, Cebu, during the summer of 2020, pointing to travel restrictions imposed during the COVID-19 lockdown. Tupas cited an executive order issued by then-Davao City Mayor Duterte suspending domestic air travel to and from Davao City beginning in March 2020.
Tupas also questioned the physical plausibility of Gracioso's account that he carried two suitcases allegedly containing P50 million each.

"Ako ay payat at maliit na tao at, dahil nga isa akong 'openly gay person' o halatang bakla, ang kadalasan kong suot na sapatos ay heels. Kaya, sa totoo lang, siguro ay makakadapa-dapa ako kung susubukan kong magbuhat ng dalawang maleta na puno, diumano, ng 50 Million Pesos bawat isa," Tupas said.
("I am thin and small, and as an openly gay person, I often wear heels. So, honestly, I would probably stumble if I tried to carry two suitcases allegedly containing P50 million each.")

Tupas further said he does not personally know Gracioso and denied ever visiting Velasco's residence in Valle Verde. Other accounts of his affidavit, however, differ on whether Tupas said he did not know Gracioso at all or merely did not recall him as part of Duterte's close-in security.
The NBI is continuing to verify Gracioso's allegations and has said it intends to seek the side of other individuals named in his affidavit.

articles.title: New crew makes the quickest US flight to ISS
articles.summary: The SpaceX spacecraft carrying the Crew-13 team docked with the International Space Station in 7 hours and 55 minutes, setting a new record.

image.caption: SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in the US state of FloridaImage: Philip Scott Andrews/REUTERS

blocks.text: Four astronauts docked at the International Space Station (ISS) port on Thursday after completing the fastest flight by a US spacecraft to the outpost, NASA officials said.

The SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket, with the Crew-13 aboard, lifted off at 11:10 a.m. local time (1510 GMT) from Cape Canaveral, Florida, and within 7 hours and 55 minutes, its capsule, SpaceX Dragon "Grace," docked at the ISS — setting a record for a US trip to the ISS.
The flight by the spacecraft was the quickest so far, not only for Elon Musk's company, but for any American entity, including NASA.
The time taken for a trip to the ISS mainly depends on the distance between the ISS and the spacecraft at the time of launch.
The space station's convenient location allowed the spacecraft to reach it faster.
The last crew, which took off from the United States, took more than 30 hours to reach the station.
A Russian Soyuz spacecraft set the overall record for a flight to the ISS in October 2020, reaching the station in just over three hours.
What do we know about the crew?
The new ISS crew was set to arrive in mid-September, however, its flight was delayed due to a leak aboard the Dragon.
It includes Americans Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian Joshua Kutryk, and Russian Sergey Teteryatnikov

Watkins, the Crew-13's commander, became the first Black woman to lead a crew to orbit. The crew is slated to stay at the ISS for six months and will be replacing Crew-12, which is set to return to Earth on Monday.

Despite many international cooperation agreements collapsing after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the United States and other ISS partners still work with Russia on the space station.
The ISS has been continuously in use for the last 25 years. NASA has committed to operating it through 2030.
